**Sūrat an-Najm (The Star)**
Sixty-two verses. Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By the star when it sets.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By the star when it sets.﴾ Before beginning the exegesis (tafsir, explanation of the Qur'an), we present some issues, and then we will devote ourselves to the tafsir, even though these issues are not part of it.

The first issue: The beginning of this sūrah is connected to the end of the preceding one, both verbally and in meaning. Verbally, the preceding sūrah (at-Ṭūr) ends with "the star," and this one begins with "the star" with the oath particle wāw. In meaning, Allah, may He be exalted, said to His Prophet ﷺ, ﴿And during the night glorify Him, and at the retreat of the stars﴾ [at-Ṭūr 52:49]. He then explained to him that He had made him (the Prophet ﷺ) a part of the plots against the Prophet ﷺ concerning the star and its setting, and He said: ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [an-Najm 53:2].

The second issue: The sūrahs that came before, which begin with an oath by nouns rather than by letters, are aṣ-Ṣāffāt, adh-Dhāriyāt, and aṭ-Ṭūr. This sūrah follows them, and it is most fitting. In the first (aṣ-Ṣāffāt), the oath is for establishing Divine Oneness, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, your God is One﴾ [aṣ-Ṣāffāt 37:4]. In the second (adh-Dhāriyāt), it is for the occurrence of the Gathering (ḥashr) and recompense, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true, and indeed, the Recompense is to occur﴾ [adh-Dhāriyāt 51:5–6]. In the third (aṭ-Ṭūr), it is for the continuance of the punishment after its occurrence, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur, there is none to repel it﴾ [aṭ-Ṭūr 52:7–8].

In this sūrah, it is for the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ, so that the three fundamentals are complete: Divine Oneness, the Gathering, and prophethood.

The third issue: Allah has not sworn oaths frequently for Divine Oneness or for prophethood. As for Divine Oneness, He swore by one thing in sūrat aṣ-Ṣāffāt. As for prophethood, He swore by one thing in this sūrah and by two things in sūrat aḍ-Ḍuḥā. He swore oaths much more often concerning the Gathering and what is related to it. For example, the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl 92:1]; His words: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [ash-Shams 91:1]; His words: ﴿By the sky containing the constellations﴾ [al-Burūj 85:1]; and so on. All of these contain the Gathering or what is related to it. The reason is that the proofs of Divine Oneness are many, and all of them are rational, as it has been said:

*"And in everything there is a sign indicating that He is One."*

The proofs of prophethood are also many; they are the famous and widely transmitted miracles. As for the Gathering, its possibility is established by reason, but its occurrence cannot be established except by revealed testimony (samʿ). Therefore, He swore many oaths so that the accountable person would be certain of it and believe in it with firm conviction.

As for the exegesis (tafsīr), it contains several issues.

The first issue: Is the wāw (in ﴿wa-n-najm﴾) an oath by the star, or by the Lord of the star? There is a difference of opinion on this, which we have already mentioned. The more apparent view is that it is an oath by the star. It is said: In origin, there is no particle that is specifically for oaths, but the bāʾ (ب) and the wāw (و) have been used for it due to an incidental meaning. This is because the bāʾ, in its original use in oaths, is the bāʾ of attachment and seeking help. Just as a speaker says: *"istaʿantu bi-llāh"* ("I sought help through Allah"), he says: *"uqsimu bi-llāh"* ("I swear by Allah"). And just as he says: *"aqūmu bi-ʿawni llāh ʿalā l-ʿadūww"* ("I stand up with the help of Allah against the enemy"), he says: *"uqsimu bi-ḥaqqi llāh"* ("I swear by the right of Allah"). The bāʾ in both is with the same meaning, as you say: *"kutiba bi-l-qalam"* ("it was written with the pen"). So the bāʾ in reality is not for oaths, except that the oath became so frequent in speech that it became unnecessary to mention it, whereas other uses were not frequent, so the verb could not be dispensed with. When a speaker says: *"bi-ḥaqqi Zayd"* ("by the right of Zayd"), the oath is understood from it, because if the intended meaning were like his saying: *"udkhul Zayd"* ("enter, Zayd") or *"idhhab bi-ḥaqqi Zayd"* ("go, by the right of Zayd"), or if he had not sworn by the right of Zayd, it would have been mentioned as it is mentioned with these other things, since the verb cannot be dispensed with in those cases. Since nothing was mentioned, it is known that the omission is due to its fame and its being understood without mention, and this does not occur in anything other than an oath. Thus it is known that the omitted element is the verb of swearing. It is as if he said: "I swear by the right of Zayd." So the bāʾ originally is not for oaths, but when the frequency and fame mentioned above occurred, it came to be said that the bāʾ is for oaths.

Then the speaker considered this and said: This is not free from ambiguity. For when I say *"billāh"* ("by Allah"), the listener pauses. If he hears after it a verb other than an oath, such as my saying: *"billāhi staʿantu"* ("by Allah I sought help"), *"billāhi qadirtu"* ("by Allah I was able"), *"billāhi mashaytu wa-akhadhtu"* ("by Allah I walked and took"), he does not interpret it as an oath. If he does not hear anything after it, he interprets it as an oath, provided he does not imagine the existence of a verb that I have mentioned but which he did not hear. But if he imagines that I mentioned something else along with my saying "billāh," and he did not hear it either, he hesitates, and there is hesitation in understanding. Therefore, when the wise speaker wants to remove this, while being concise and leaving out what is unnecessary, namely the verb of swearing, he replaces the bāʾ with the tāʾ (ت) and says: *"tallāh"* ("by Allah"). He speaks it with the word "Allah," because the word "Allah" is well known, and there is no fear of ambiguity. The tāʾ at the beginnings of words may be original, and it may be for address (second person) or for feminine gender. So if one swore with the letter tāʾ by someone whose name is *Dāʿī*, *Rāʿī*, *Hādī*, or *ʿĀdī*, one would say *tadāʿī*, *tarāʿī*, *tahādī*, or *taʿādī*, and this would be ambiguous. Likewise, for someone whose name is *Rūmān* or *Tūrān*: if you say *tarūmān* or *tatūrān*, intending to swear by the tāʾ, it becomes ambiguous with the tāʾ of address and feminine gender in the future tense. Therefore, they replaced it with wāw. It cannot be objected to in two ways:

The first objection: With the wāw, ambiguity is not avoided. We say *wallā*, so the original wāw becomes ambiguous with the wāw of oath. We answer: That does not apply to what we have proposed. The ambiguity would occur with the wāw only where it indicates and signifies coordination (ʿaṭf), even if the wāw is not used for oaths. How could it be otherwise, when this ambiguity exists with the bāʾ, which is like the original? You say *birām* as the plural of *burmah* (cooking pot), *bihām* as the plural of *bahmah* (lamb), and *bighāl* (mules). Due to the ambiguity of the original bāʾ in *bighāl* and *birām* with the bāʾ that you attach in phrases like *māla* and *raʾā*, you say *bimāl*. As for the tāʾ, when it was used for oaths, ambiguity resulted from that usage, since previously it was not one of the particles like the bāʾ and the wāw.

The second objection: Why is it not used in cases where there is no ambiguity, such as your saying *tārraḥīm* ("by the Merciful") and *tāl-ʿaẓīm* ("by the Mighty")? We say: Since the word of Allah, the Exalted, is at the utmost degree of fame and clarity, the tāʾ was used with it contrary to the original usage. This means that it is not permissible to analogize from it except to what is equally famous. As for other words, they may be obscure to some people. For whoever hears *ar-Raḥīm* and hears (the verb) *tarra* in the sense of "cut off" in rare usage, might say *tarahīm* as a verb and subject, or a verb and object, even though that is extremely remote. But equality in fame between the source and the derived form is necessary, and there is nothing as famous as the word of Allah. Moreover, we say: Why do you claim that when there is no ambiguity it is not used? Do you not see that it was transmitted from the Arabs: *birabbi l-Kaʿbah* ("by the Lord of the Kaʿbah")? What supports what we have said is that you say *uqsimu billāh* ("I swear by Allah") and you do not say *uqsimu tallāh* ("I swear by Allah," with tāʾ), because the tāʾ in it would cause fear of ambiguity when the verb of swearing is omitted. When the verb is present, the ambiguity is not feared, yet it was still not permitted.

The second issue: The lām in His words, ﴿wa-n-najm﴾ ("and the star"), is either the lām of definition by previous mention (ʿahd) according to one view, or the lām of definition by genus (jins) according to another. The first view is that of the one who said that ﴿an-najm﴾ refers to the Pleiades (ath-Thurayyā), and one of them said:

*"When the star appears in the evening, the shepherd seeks a blanket."*

The second view has several possibilities:

First: The star is a star of the sky, which is fixed in it for guidance. It was also said: No, rather the star is the shooting stars in it, which are missiles against the devils.

Second: The stars of the earth, which are plants without stalks.

Third: The stars of the Qur'an. Let us mention the appropriateness of each view and clarify which is preferred. As for our view that the intended meaning is the Pleiades, it is the most apparent of the stars to the observer, because it has a sign that is not confused with anything else in the sky, and it appears to everyone. The Prophet ﷺ was distinguished from everyone by clear signs, so Allah swore by him. Also, when the Pleiades rise from the east at dawn, the time for the fruits to ripen arrives, and when they appear at the beginning of the evening at the end of autumn, diseases decrease. When the Prophet ﷺ appeared, doubt and diseases of the heart decreased, and the fruits of wisdom and forbearance ripened.

As for our view that the intended meaning is the stars in the sky that are for guidance, we say: The stars are used for guidance in the wilderness. So Allah swore by them because of the resemblance and connection between them (the stars and the Prophet ﷺ).

As for our view that the intended meaning is the meteors among the stars, the stars keep the devils away from the inhabitants of heaven, and the prophets keep the devils away from the inhabitants of the earth.

As for our view that the intended meaning is the Qur'an, then He presented the miracle of the Prophet ﷺ as evidence of his truthfulness and innocence. This is like His words, the Exalted: ﴿Yā-Sīn. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers, upon a straight path﴾ [Yā-Sīn 36:1–4], meaning: you have not gone astray, nor have you erred.

As for our view that the star is the plant, we say: The plant is by it that the physical powers remain and are sound, while the intellectual power is more deserving of correction. This is through the messengers and the clarification of the paths. From this, it becomes apparent that the preferred view is that the stars which are in the sky are intended, because they are more apparent to the listener. His words ﴿when it sets﴾ point to this more clearly. After that, the Qur'an is also clearly apparent, and then the Pleiades.

The third issue: The discussion of ﴿wa-n-najm﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿wa-ṭ-ṭūr﴾ ("and the mount") [aṭ-Ṭūr 52:1], in that He did not say "wa-n-nujūm" (the stars) nor "al-aṭwār" (the mountains in their levels). He said ﴿wa-dh-dhāriyāt﴾ [adh-Dhāriyāt 51:1] and ﴿wa-l-mursalāt﴾ [al-Mursalāt 77:1], and this has already been mentioned.

The fourth issue: What is the benefit of restricting the oath to the star by a time in which it is (in that state)? We say: When the star is in the middle of the sky, it is far from the earth, and the traveler cannot be guided by it, because he does not know by it the east from the west, nor the south from the north. But when it sets, by its setting the side of the west is distinguished from the east, and the south from the north. Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ lowered his wing to the believers, and he was upon great character, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam 68:4]. And as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So by a mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them. And if you had been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:159].

If it is said: Being guided by the star when it is on the horizon of the east is like being guided by it when it is on the horizon of the west, so what you have mentioned is no answer to the objection, we say: Being guided by the star while it is inclining toward the west is more (effective), because it guides in both the worldly and the religious ways. As for the worldly, it is for the reason we have mentioned. As for the religious, it is as Khalīl (Abraham, peace be upon him) said: ﴿I do not love the setting ones﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:76].

There is a subtle point in this: When Allah swore by the star, He honored and exalted it. Some of the polytheists worshipped it. So along with its exaltation, He attached a description that shows it had not reached the rank of worship, for it is ephemeral and sets.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾. Most of the exegetes did not distinguish between ḍalāl (straying) and ghayy (error). What some of them said when attempting to distinguish them is: ḍalāl is the opposite of guidance (hudā), and ghayy is the opposite of rectitude (rushd). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they see the way of rectitude, they will not adopt it as a way; but if they see the way of error, they will adopt it as a way﴾ [al-A'rāf: 146], and He said: ﴿Rectitude has become clear from error﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256]. The fuller account of this is that ḍalāl is more general in usage in its basic sense: you say "my camel has strayed (ḍalla) and my saddle-bag," and you do not say "it has erred (ghawā)." So what is meant by ḍalāl is that the traveler cannot find any path at all to his destination, while ghayy is that there is no straight path for him to the destination. What proves this is that you say of a believer who is not on the course of uprightness that he is foolish (safīh) and not rightly guided (rashīd), and you do not say that he is astray (ḍāll), and the one who is astray is like the disbeliever, while the one who errs is like the transgressor. So it is as if He, the Exalted, said: ﴿has not strayed﴾, meaning he has not disbelieved, and not even less than that, so he has not transgressed. What supports what we have mentioned is His saying: ﴿But if you perceive in them rectitude, then hand over to them their property﴾ [al-Nisā': 6]. Or we may say: ḍalāl is like non-existence, and ghayy is like corrupt existence in rank and station.

As for His saying ﴿your companion (ṣāḥibukum)﴾, there are two interpretations: the first is "your master (sayyidukum)," and the other is "your companion who keeps company with you (muṣāḥibukum)"; one says ṣāḥib al-bayt and rabb al-bayt. It is also possible that what is meant by His saying ﴿has not strayed﴾ is "has not become mad (junn)," for the madman is astray. On this view it is like His saying: ﴿Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe. You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman. And indeed for you is a reward unending﴾ [al-Qalam: 1–3]. So it indicates that he has not erred; rather he is rightly guided and a guide, pointing to Allah through another guidance, as He said: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾ [Ṣād: 86], and He said: ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾ [Saba': 47]. And His saying: ﴿And indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4] is an allusion to His saying here: ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾, for this is a magnificent character.

To show the order, we say: He first said ﴿has not strayed﴾, meaning he is upon the road; ﴿nor has he erred﴾, meaning his road on which he is is straight; ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾, meaning he is riding its back and taking the direction of the destination. This is because whoever travels a road to reach his destination may remain without a road, or may find a road to it that is far, full of hardships and perils, or may find a wide and safe road but veer to the right and left, so the destination becomes distant from him and his arrival is delayed; but when he takes the main highway and rides its back, he arrives more quickly. It may also be said that ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ is a proof that he has neither strayed nor erred, its sense being: how could he stray or err when he does not speak from desire? Only one who follows desire strays, and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿Do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾ [Ṣād: 26].

If it is objected that what you mentioned of the first order, in the past tense in His saying ﴿has not strayed﴾, and the future form in His saying ﴿nor does he speak﴾, is most elegant, meaning: he did not stray when he withdrew from you and you worshipped what he worshipped in his youth; ﴿nor has he erred﴾ when he was alone by himself and saw his dream, "what he saw"; ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ now, since he has been sent to you and made a witness over you as a messenger, so he was not previously astray or erring, and now he has become a rescuer from misguidance and a guide and one who leads. And as for your claim that its sense is "how could he stray when he does not speak from desire," the form does not accord with this? We say: Yes, indeed. Its explanation is that Allah the Exalted protects whoever He intends to send in his youth from disbelief and shameful defects such as theft, fornication and habitual lying. So He said: ﴿has not strayed﴾ in his youth, because he does not speak from desire. The best thing said in explaining hawā (desire) is that it is love, but from the self; one says "hawiitu-hu" meaning "I loved him." However, the letters in the root h-w-y indicate descent, lowering and falling, and from it comes hāwiyah (the abyss). So when the self is base, and abandons lofty things and clings to trivialities, it has fallen; thus hawā becomes specific to the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sū'). Were you to say uhwī-hu bi-qalbī (I love him with my heart), its baseness would disappear; but the usage, after considering the Qur'anic usage, in which hawā is used only in contexts that oppose love, since love is used in a context of praise, shows this. What indicates what we have mentioned is His saying: ﴿As for he who transgressed, and preferred the life of this world, then indeed the Hellfire will be his refuge... and who forbade the self from desire﴾ [al-Nāzi'āt: 37–40], an allusion to the elevated rank of the self.

So He said: No. Rather, he speaks from Allah by revelation. There are several issues here.

**The first issue:** (in) is used in place of (mā) for negation, just as (mā) is used as a conditional in place of (in). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whatever We abrogate of a verse or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 106]. The resemblance between them is in form and in meaning. As for form: (in) consists of the hamza and the nūn, and (mā) consists of the mīm and the alif. The alif corresponds to the hamza, and the nūn corresponds to the mīm. The first (correspondence) is shown by the permissibility of metathesis (qalb), and the second by the permissibility and the obligation of assimilation (idghām). As for meaning: (in) indicates negation in one respect and affirmation in another, but its indication of negation is stronger and more emphatic. This is because, when the word (in) is used, the condition and the consequent must be non-existent when the aim is exhortation or prohibition. You say: "If you do good, you will have reward, and if you do evil, you will have punishment." But if the aim is to explain the state of two uncertain alternatives, as when you say: "If this gemstone is glass, its value is half, and if it is a jewel, its value is a thousand," then the existence of either of them is not known here, and the absence of knowledge is established. Here, the absence of knowledge is like the absence of occurrence in exhortation and prohibition. So in the uses of (in) there must be an absence, either in the matter, or in knowledge, or in existence. This is the case when the condition is present in explaining the state. For this reason the grammarians (nuḥāt) said: It is not good to say "If the unripe date turns red, I will come to you," because that is something that will certainly occur. But they permitted the use of (in) for what does not occur at all. It is said, in despairing of hope: "If the crow turns white, you will overcome me." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if it remains in its place, then you will see Me﴾ [Al-A'raf: 143], and neither the remaining nor the seeing has occurred. So it is known that its indication of negation is more complete, since its signified meaning is closer to a certain signified meaning, and so one of them is used in place of the other. This is the apparent view. As for what is said, that (in) and (mā) are both negating particles originally, there is no need for synonymy.

**The second issue:** Is (huwa) a known pronoun or a mentioned pronoun? We say there are two views, the more famous of which is that it is a known pronoun, referring to the Qur'an. It is as if He says: "The Qur'an is nothing but revelation." This is according to the view of those who say that (an-najm) does not refer to the Qur'an. As for the view of those who say it does refer to the Qur'an, then it refers to something mentioned. The second view is that it refers to something mentioned implicitly, which is the statement and speech of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is because His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ includes within it speaking (nuṭq), which is speech and utterance. So it is as if He, exalted is He, says: "His speech, which is his utterance, is nothing but revelation." There is another view, which is further and more subtle. It is that His saying: ﴿Your companion has not strayed﴾ [An-Najm: 2] has been explained, in one view, to mean that he is not possessed and the jinn have not touched him, so he is not a soothsayer. His saying: ﴿nor has he erred﴾ means there is no connection between him and error, so he is not a poet, for the poets are followed by the erring [Ash-Shu'ara: 42]. In that case, His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ is a refutation of them, since they said: "His speech is the speech of a soothsayer," and they said: "His speech is the speech of a poet." So He said: His speech is nothing but revelation, and it is not the speech of a soothsayer or a poet. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 41–42].

**The third issue:** Is (al-waḥy) a noun or a verbal noun (maṣdar)? We say it may be either. Al-waḥy is a noun whose meaning is "writing," and a verbal noun with several meanings, among them sending, inspiration, writing, speech and indication, and making understood. If we say that (huwa) refers to the Qur'an, then al-waḥy is a noun meaning "writing," as if He says: "The Qur'an is nothing but a writing," and (yūḥā) means "is sent." In this case it is also possible to say that it is a verbal noun, meaning: "The Qur'an is nothing but sending and inspiration," in the sense of the passive participle, that is, "sent." If we say that what is meant by His saying (innahu huwa) is His statement and His speech, then al-waḥy at that point is inspiration, inspired from Allah, or sent. There are issues concerning this.

*First issue:* The apparent meaning is contrary to what is famous among some exegetes, namely that the Prophet (ﷺ) never spoke except by revelation. There is no proof for those who imagine this from the verse. For His saying: ﴿It is not but a revelation that is revealed﴾, if (huwa) refers to the Qur'an, it is clear. If it refers to His statement, then what is meant by (huwa) is the speech about which they said that it is the speech of a poet, and Allah refuted them, saying: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 41], and that speech is the Qur'an. If we accept what they said, then (waḥy) should be explained as inspiration.

*Second issue:* This indicates that he (ﷺ) did not exercise ijtihad, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, for in wars he did exercise ijtihad, and he prohibited what Allah had not prohibited, and he gave permission to those about whom Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ [At-Tawbah: 43]. We say that, according to what is established, the verse does not indicate this.

*Third issue:* (yūḥā) may be from (waḥiya yaḥyā), and it may be from (awḥā yūḥī). You say ʿadima yaʿdamu and aʿdama yuʿdimu, and likewise ʿalima yaʿlamu and aʿlama yuʿlimu. So we say that (yūḥā) is from (awḥā), not from (waḥā). Although waḥiya and awḥā both came with the same meaning, Allah in the Qur'an, when mentioning the verbal noun, did not mention the īḥāʾ (the verbal noun of awḥā), and when mentioning the verb, did not mention waḥy, whose verbal noun is waḥy. Rather, when mentioning the verbal noun He said al-waḥy, and when mentioning the verb He said (awḥā) [Al-An'am: 19]. The same applies to aḥabba and ḥabba, for ḥabba and aḥabba have one meaning. When Allah, exalted is He, mentions the verbal noun, He does not mention al-ibāb in the Qur'an, and He mentions al-ḥubb, up to ﴿more intense in love﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 165]. When mentioning the verb, He does not say ḥabbahu Allāh, but He says: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 54], and He says: ﴿Would any of you like [to eat the flesh of his dead brother]?﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 12], and He says: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al-Imran: 92], and other examples. In this there is a secret of morphology (ʿilm al-ṣarf), namely that there is disagreement concerning the verbal noun and the triliteral past verb. Some morphologists said: the verbal noun is derived from the past verb, and the past verb is the original. The proof for this is of two kinds, verbal and conceptual.

As for the verbal proof: they say that the verbal noun of faʿala yafʿilu, when transitive, is faʿlun with a sukūn on the ʿayn, and when intransitive it is mostly fuʿūl. And they do not say that the past verb of fuʿūl is fuʿlā. This is the evidence for what we have mentioned.

As for the conceptual proof: things that exist exist only as particulars, and within them is the universal. An example is the human being, who exists and is realized as Zayd or ʿAmr or others, and within that he is Hindi or Turkish, and within that he is an animal and rational (nāṭiq). Human being does not first exist and then become Turkish, then become Zayd or ʿAmr.

Knowing this, the verb that is realized cannot be separated from being either past or future, and within it is that it is a verb regardless of its past or future. An example is striking (ḍarb), when it exists: it is either past or it has not yet passed. The first is past, the second is present or future. Striking does not exist as striking without past, present, or future. However, the intelligent person perceives from "he struck" (faʿala), and "he is striking now" (yafʿalu), and "he will strike tomorrow" (sayafʿalu), a common matter, and calls it an act (fiʿl). Likewise he perceives in "he struck" (ḍaraba), "he is striking now" (yaḍribu), and "he will strike tomorrow" (sayaḍribu), a common matter, and calls it striking (ḍarb). So ḍaraba exists first, and striking is extracted from it. The words were laid down for matters in which they are realized, and are thereby expressed. Common matters are realized only within other things. So the original positing is for what exists from it, and before striking the act is not perceived from it. This is what can be said to one who says that the past is the origin and the verbal noun is derived from it.

As for one who says that the verbal noun is the origin and the past is derived from it, he has evidences, among them: the noun is the origin, and the verb is a branch, and the verbal noun is a noun. Also, the verbal noun is inflected (muʿrab) and the past is indeclinable (mabnī), and inflection comes before indeclinability. Also, when we want to distinguish between qāla and qála, and rāʿa and rāʿa, we return their patterns to the verbal noun. We say: in qāla the alif is converted from a wāw, as in al-qawl; and in qála the alif is converted from a yāʾ, as in al-qīl. Likewise al-rawʿ and al-ray'.

As for the rational proof: words were laid down for things that are in minds, and the general comes before the particular in the mind. For when an existing thing is perceived, the perceiver says: "This existing thing is a substance (jawhar) or an accident (ʿaraḍ)." When he perceives that it is a substance, he says: "It is a body (jism) or not a body," according to one who makes the body a substance, which is the more correct and evident view. Then when he perceives that it is a body, he says: "It is complete." And so on until he reaches the most specific things, if reaching them is possible by division. So the first positing is the act, which is the verbal noun without addition. Then when time is joined to it, you say: "He struck," or "He will strike." So the verbal noun is before the past, and this is the more correct view.

Knowing this, we say: according to the view of those who say that in the triliteral the verbal noun is derived from the past, then ḥubb and aḥabba are both on one level, since both derive from ḥabba yuḥibbu, and the verbal noun of the triliteral comes before the verbal noun of the derived forms by one rank. But according to the view of those who say that in the triliteral the past is derived from the verbal noun, the triliteral verbal noun comes before the verbal noun of the derived forms by two ranks. So the verbal noun of the triliteral is used, because it comes before the verbal noun of the derived forms. As for the verb in aḥabba and awḥā, the alif in them gives a function that the bare triliteral does not give, because aḥabba is more effective in transitivity and further from the suspicion of intransitivity, so He used it.

**The fourth issue:** ﴿It is not but a revelation﴾ is more emphatic than the statement of a speaker who says: "He is a revelation." It has a benefit besides emphasis, namely that they used to say: "He speaks the word of a soothsayer," "He speaks the word of a poet." So He intended to negate their statement, and that is achieved by the form of negation. So He said: "It is not as they say." Then He added: "Rather, it is revelation." There is another benefit in His saying (yūḥā), which is like His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾ [Al-An'am: 38]. It establishes the reality. For a horse that runs very fast is sometimes called a bird. But when He says "flies with its wings," it removes the possibility of metaphor. Likewise, some who are not careful in speech and exaggerate in hyperbole say: "The speech of so-and-so is revelation," as they say "his poetry is magic," and "his statement is a miracle." But when He says (yūḥā), that metaphor disappears or becomes remote.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾. In this there are two possibilities, the most well-known among the exegetes being that the pronoun in ("عَلَّمَهُ", "he taught him") refers to the revelation, meaning: the revelation taught him, the one mighty in power. If the revelation is the Book, then this is clear; and if it is the inspiration (al-ilham), then it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193]. The better view is that the pronoun refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), its implied meaning being: Gabriel, the one mighty in power, taught Muhammad. In that case it refers to "your companion" (ṣāḥibukum), its implied meaning being: "taught your companion", and the one mighty in power is Gabriel, meaning that his powers, both cognitive and practical, are all strong, so he knows and he acts. His saying ﴿mighty in power﴾ contains several benefits. The first: praising the teacher is praising the student, for if He had said "Gabriel taught him" without describing him, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have gained any clear virtue. The second: in it is a refutation of them, since they said, "Tales of the ancients," (claiming) that he heard them at the time of his journey to Syria; so He said: no one among people taught him, rather his teacher is one mighty in power, and man was created weak, and he has been given only a little knowledge. The third: in it is a confirmation of the words of Gabriel, peace be upon him, for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾ combines what necessitates trust, because strength of perception is a condition for trusting the words of a speaker. For if we suspected a person of corrupted intellect, and then he transmitted to us from some of the great scholars a difficult issue, we would not trust his words and would say, "He did not understand what he said." Likewise, strength of memory, so that we do not say, "He grasped it but forgot it." Likewise, strength of trustworthiness, so that we do not say, "He distorted it and changed it." So He said: ﴿mighty in power﴾ to gather these conditions, so that it becomes like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Possessing power, with rank before the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 20], until He said: "trustworthy" (amin). The fourth: in consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is from the perspective that God, exalted is He, is not restricted to a place, so His relation to Gabriel is like His relation to Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore, if he were taught through an intermediary, that would be a decrease from his rank. So He said: "It is not so, for he is mighty in power, he is established for our conversing with you, and you, after you were leveled, will be like Moses when he fell down." It is as if God, exalted is He, taught him through an intermediary and then taught him without an intermediary, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa: 113]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My Lord disciplined me, and He made my discipline excellent."

Then God Most High said: ﴿Possessor of strength; so he stood firm﴾. Regarding His words ﴿Possessor of strength﴾ there are several interpretations:

The first: possessor of power.

The second: possessor of perfection in both intellect and religion together.

The third: possessor of a great appearance and awe-inspiring presence.

The fourth: possessor of good character. If it is said, according to our view that the meaning is possessor of power, the explanation of his having powers has already passed in His words ﴿Severe in power﴾, so how can we say his powers are severe and he has power? We say that this is not fitting if it comes as one description after another. As for if it comes as a substitute (badal), it is not permissible; it is as if He said: "He was taught by one possessing power," and omitted "severe in power," so it is not a description of him. Its estimate (taqdir) is: possessor of great or complete power. In that case it is like His words: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne secure﴾ [At-Takwir: 19–20], so it is as if He said: "He was taught by one possessing power, so he stood firm." The other answer is that singling out "power" by mention may be to show that his well-known powers are severe and that he has another power which God specially granted him, as one says: "So-and-so has much wealth," and he has a wealth that no one knows, meaning his apparent wealth is abundant and he has hidden wealth. Moreover, we say the intended meaning is possessor of intensity, and its estimate: he was taught by one whose powers are severe and who also has intensity in his essence, for a person may have severe powers while his body is small, weak and frail. There is also a subtle point here: God Most High intended by His words ﴿Severe in power﴾ his strength in knowledge.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿Possessor of strength﴾, that is, intensity in his body, so He put knowledge before physical strength, as God Most High said: ﴿And He increased him broadly in knowledge and physique﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 247]. Regarding His words ﴿so he stood firm﴾ there are two views. The well-known one is that the intended one is Jibril, that is, Jibril stood firm in his creation.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And he was at the highest horizon﴾. The well-known view is that "he" refers to Jibril, and its estimate: he stood firm as God Most High created him at the eastern horizon, and he blocked the east by his greatness. The apparent view is that the intended one is Muhammad (ﷺ); its meaning: he stood firm in a place, and he was in the lofty place of rank and station, in elevation of status, not literally in being located in a place. If it is said, how is this permissible when God Most High says: ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ [At-Takwir: 23], indicating that he saw Jibril at the clear horizon? We say: in that passage too we say, as we said here, that he (ﷺ) saw Jibril while he was at the clear horizon. One who says "I saw the crescent" is asked, "Where did you see it?" and he says, "Above the roof," meaning the seer was above the roof, not the seen. And "al-Mubin" (the clear) is the one that separates, from abana, meaning he separated, that is, he was at the horizon that separates between the rank of man and the station of the angel, for he (ﷺ) reached the end, attained the goal and became a prophet, just as some prophets became prophets, receiving revelation in their sleep and in his form, and he reached the highest horizon, and the horizon separates between the two stations. If it is said: what follows indicates something contrary to what you hold, for His words ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [An-Najm: 8] and other than that, and His words: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent, at the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ [An-Najm: 13–14], all of this indicates contrary to what you mentioned? We say: we will show its agreement with what we have mentioned, God willing, in its places when mentioning its interpretation. If it is said: the hadiths indicate something contrary to what you mentioned, since it is reported in the reports that Jibril (ﷺ) showed the Prophet (ﷺ) himself in his form, so he blocked the east; we say: we did not say that this did not happen, and the hadith does not say that God Most High intended this verse for that narration, so as to necessitate contradiction of the hadith. We only say that Jibril showed the Prophet (ﷺ) himself twice and spread his wings, and he covered and blocked the eastern side, but the verse was not revealed to explain that.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 53, verses 8–9:

Then God Most High said: ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾, and in this there are well-known interpretations.

The first: Gabriel drew near to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning, after he had extended his wing while on the horizon, he returned to the form in which he used to descend upon him, and he came close to the Prophet ﷺ. According to this, in (tadalla, "came down") there are three interpretations:

The first: there is inversion in the wording, its meaning being: then he descended from the highest horizon, so he drew near to the Prophet ﷺ.

The second: "drawing near" (dana) and "coming down" (tadalli) have one meaning, as if He said: he approached and so came near.

The third: "dana" means he intended nearness to Muhammad ﷺ and moved from the place where he was, so he "tadalla" (came down) and descended to the Prophet ﷺ.

The second interpretation: according to what we mentioned of the last view regarding His words ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾, that Muhammad ﷺ drew near to the creation and the community, was gentle toward them, and became like one of them. ﴿Then he came down﴾, meaning he came down to them with gentle speech and kind supplication, and so he said: ﴿I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me﴾ [Al-Kahf: 110]. According to this, the statement contains two perfections, as if He, exalted is He, said: except a revelation that is revealed, namely Gabriel, to Muhammad, so Muhammad became balanced and perfected; he drew near to the creation after his exaltation, came down to them, and conveyed the message.

The third: this is weak and foolish, namely that what is meant is His Lord, Exalted, and this is the view of those who affirm direction and place. Unless it is meant as nearness in rank, and in this case it would be like His words ﷺ, relating from his Lord, Exalted: "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running," which is an indication of the figurative meaning. Here, since He explained that the Prophet ﷺ rose and was exalted in intellectual rank, not in sensory place, He said: and God drew near to him, in confirmation of what is in His words, "Whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom."

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾, meaning: between Gabriel and Muhammad, upon both of them be peace, was the measure of two bows or less. This was rejected on the basis of the custom and practice of the Arabs: when two of their leaders or elders made a pact and covenant, they went out with their two bows, each of them stretched the end of his bow to the end of his companion's bow, and those below them among the common people placed their hand in the other's hand, and so they would finish with their two arms. For this reason it is called "musaya'a" (pledge of allegiance). According to this, there is a subtle point: His words ﴿two bow-lengths﴾ are on the supposition that they are both great, and His words ﴿or nearer﴾ are because of the superiority of one over the other. When the subjects pledge allegiance to a ruler, there is no bow between the one pledging and the ruler, so the ruler shakes his hand. So it is as if He, Exalted, informed that they were like two great leaders, so that between them was the measure of two bows; or Gabriel, upon him be peace, was an envoy between God Most High and Muhammad ﷺ, and so he was like a follower of Muhammad ﷺ, becoming like the one pledging who extends his arm, not the bow. This is according to the view of those who prefer the Prophet ﷺ over Gabriel, upon him be peace, which is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah except a few among them, since Gabriel is a messenger from God who must be honored and followed. Thus the Prophet ﷺ, according to the view of those who prefer Gabriel over the Prophet ﷺ, is like a follower of his.

There is another interpretation in this, according to what we mentioned: that the bow is an expression of a distance measured by a bow. According to this, we say: that distance is the specific distance that existed between the Prophet ﷺ and Gabriel, for he was in every state a human being, and Gabriel in every state was an angel. So the Prophet ﷺ, although he was free of the qualities that differ from those of angels, such as desire, anger, ignorance, and passion,
page 248
yet his humanity remained; and likewise Gabriel, although he abandoned the perfection and subtlety that prevent sight and veiling, yet he did not leave his being an angel. Therefore nothing remained between them except the difference of their realities. As for the other attributes that are possible to remove, they were removed from both of them. So the Prophet ﷺ rose until he reached the highest horizon of humanity, and Gabriel, upon him be peace, came down until he reached the lowest horizon of angelhood, and so they drew near, and nothing remained between them except their realities.

According to this, regarding the first agent of "awḥā" (revealed) there are two views:

One: that God Most High revealed. According to this, regarding "His servant" there are two views:

One: it is Gabriel, upon him be peace, and the meaning is: God revealed to Gabriel. According to this, regarding the last agent of "awḥā" there are two views:

One: God Most High also, and the meaning then is: God Most High revealed to Gabriel, upon him be peace, what He revealed to him, in magnification and honor of what was revealed.

Second: the agent of the second "awḥā" is Gabriel, and the meaning is: God revealed to Gabriel what Gabriel revealed to every messenger. In this is a statement that Gabriel is trustworthy and did not betray anything of what was revealed to him. This is like His words: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 193] and His words: ﴿Obeyed there, trustworthy﴾ [Al-Takwir: 21].

The second view regarding "His servant," on our saying that the one revealing is God, is that it is Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: God revealed to Muhammad what He revealed to him, for magnification and honor. This interpretation, as we mentioned, follows an order of utmost beauty. For Muhammad ﷺ, at first, attained in the highest horizon one of the stations of man, which is prophethood; then he drew near to Gabriel, who was in the station of prophethood, and so became a messenger; he became balanced and perfected; he drew near to the community with gentleness, came down to them with gentle speech, and kept going back and forth many times between his community and his Lord. Then God revealed to him, without the intermediary of Gabriel, what He revealed.

The second view regarding the agent of the first "awḥā" is that it is Gabriel: he revealed, meaning His servant to the servant of God, and God is known even though He is not mentioned. And in His words, Exalted: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them all, then says to the angels: "Did these used to worship you?" They will say: "Glory be to You; You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn"﴾ [Saba': 40–41], there is what necessitates certainty that this word may not be applied to the Prophet ﷺ. One: it is Gabriel, meaning Gabriel revealed to the servant of God what Gabriel had revealed, for magnification.

The first of them: "alladhi awḥā" is the prayer.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾, and in this there are well-known interpretations.

The first: Gabriel drew near to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning, after he had extended his wing while on the horizon, he returned to the form in which he used to descend upon him, and he came close to the Prophet ﷺ. According to this, in (tadalla, "came down") there are three interpretations:

The first: there is inversion in the wording, its meaning being: then he descended from the highest horizon, so he drew near to the Prophet ﷺ.

The second: "drawing near" (dana) and "coming down" (tadalli) have one meaning, as if He said: he approached and so came near.

The third: "dana" means he intended nearness to Muhammad ﷺ and moved from the place where he was, so he "tadalla" (came down) and descended to the Prophet ﷺ.

The second interpretation: according to what we mentioned of the last view regarding His words ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾, that Muhammad ﷺ drew near to the creation and the community, was gentle toward them, and became like one of them. ﴿Then he came down﴾, meaning he came down to them with gentle speech and kind supplication, and so he said: ﴿I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me﴾ [Al-Kahf: 110]. According to this, the statement contains two perfections, as if He, exalted is He, said: except a revelation that is revealed, namely Gabriel, to Muhammad, so Muhammad became balanced and perfected; he drew near to the creation after his exaltation, came down to them, and conveyed the message.

The third: this is weak and foolish, namely that what is meant is His Lord, Exalted, and this is the view of those who affirm direction and place. Unless it is meant as nearness in rank, and in this case it would be like His words ﷺ, relating from his Lord, Exalted: "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running," which is an indication of the figurative meaning. Here, since He explained that the Prophet ﷺ rose and was exalted in intellectual rank, not in sensory place, He said: and God drew near to him, in confirmation of what is in His words, "Whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom."

Then God Most High said: ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾, meaning: between Gabriel and Muhammad, upon both of them be peace, was the measure of two bows or less. This was rejected on the basis of the custom and practice of the Arabs: when two of their leaders or elders made a pact and covenant, they went out with their two bows, each of them stretched the end of his bow to the end of his companion's bow, and those below them among the common people placed their hand in the other's hand, and so they would finish with their two arms. For this reason it is called "musaya'a" (pledge of allegiance). According to this, there is a subtle point: His words ﴿two bow-lengths﴾ are on the supposition that they are both great, and His words ﴿or nearer﴾ are because of the superiority of one over the other. When the subjects pledge allegiance to a ruler, there is no bow between the one pledging and the ruler, so the ruler shakes his hand. So it is as if He, Exalted, informed that they were like two great leaders, so that between them was the measure of two bows; or Gabriel, upon him be peace, was an envoy between God Most High and Muhammad ﷺ, and so he was like a follower of Muhammad ﷺ, becoming like the one pledging who extends his arm, not the bow. This is according to the view of those who prefer the Prophet ﷺ over Gabriel, upon him be peace, which is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah except a few among them, since Gabriel is a messenger from God who must be honored and followed. Thus the Prophet ﷺ, according to the view of those who prefer Gabriel over the Prophet ﷺ, is like a follower of his.

There is another interpretation in this, according to what we mentioned: that the bow is an expression of a distance measured by a bow. According to this, we say: that distance is the specific distance that existed between the Prophet ﷺ and Gabriel, for he was in every state a human being, and Gabriel in every state was an angel. So the Prophet ﷺ, although he was free of the qualities that differ from those of angels, such as desire, anger, ignorance, and passion,

One: it is Gabriel, upon him be peace, and the meaning is: God revealed to Gabriel. According to this, regarding the last agent of "awḥā" there are two views:

One: God Most High also, and the meaning then is: God Most High revealed to Gabriel, upon him be peace, what He revealed to him, in magnification and honor of what was revealed.

Once both answers are known, we say:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 53, verses 10–11:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: He revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) what He had revealed to Jibril (Gabriel), meaning that Allah spoke to him that it was revelation, or He created in him necessary knowledge (*ʿilm ḍarūrī*, knowledge that arises in the mind without inference).

Second: He revealed to Jibril what He revealed to Muhammad, namely the sign by which it is known that it is revelation. On this view, *mā* may be understood as a verbal noun (*maṣdariyyah*), with the sense: He revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) the act of revelation (*al-īḥāʾ*), that is, the knowledge of revelation, so as to distinguish between the angel and the jinn.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Whose heart is it? The well-known view is that it is the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning that his heart did not lie. The definite article (*al-*) is used for a referent whose state is known, since Muhammad (peace be upon him) was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿His servant﴾, and in His saying ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ [53:7], and in the Exalted's saying ﴿Your companion has not gone astray﴾ [53:2]. It may also be said that ﴿the heart﴾ refers to the heart in general (*jins al-fuʾād*), because what is accused of lying is the imagination and fancy (*al-wahm wal-khayāl*). Fancy says: "How can he see Allah, or how can he see Jibril, since He is more subtle than the air, and air cannot be seen?" Likewise fancy says: "If he saw his Lord, he saw Him in a direction and a place and in a form, and all of this contradicts the object seen being God." If he saw Jibril, peace be upon him, even though he had taken the form of Dihya or someone else, then his reality would have been transformed, and if that were permissible, the trustworthiness of what is seen would be lifted. So we say: the seeing of Allah the Exalted and the seeing of Jibril, peace be upon him, as Muhammad (peace be upon him) saw them, is permissible according to whoever has a heart, and the heart does not deny this, although the imagining and fanciful soul denies it.

**The second issue:** What is the meaning of ﴿did not lie﴾? There are several views:

The first view is that of al-Zamakhshari, namely that his heart did not lie, and that it did not say that what his eye saw was untrue. Had the heart said that, it would have been lying in what it said. This is close to what al-Mubarrad said, where he stated: its meaning is that the heart spoke truthfully about what it saw; it saw something and was truthful about it.

Second: it was recited as *mā kaddhaba al-fuʾād* (with the doubled letter), and its meaning is that it did not claim that the object seen was an imagining with no reality.

Third: this confirms what we mentioned, that when Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Jibril, peace be upon him, Allah created in him necessary knowledge by which he knew that it was not imagination. His intention was not the truth in the way we described it. The meaning is: it did not allow that it could be false. The usage of negating possibility is common in both occurrences. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nothing among them is hidden from Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 16], and He said: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾ [al-Anʿam: 103], and He said: ﴿Your Lord is not heedless﴾ [al-Anʿam: 132]. All of these negate possibility. This is unlike His saying: ﴿We do not waste the reward of those who do good﴾ [Yusuf: 56], ﴿We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30], and ﴿Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 48], for these negate occurrence.

**The third issue:** In His saying ﴿what it saw﴾, who is the seer? Is it the heart, the eye, or something else? There are several views:

The first: the heart. It is as though He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The heart did not lie﴾ about what the heart saw, meaning it did not say that it was a jinn or a devil, but rather it was certain that what it saw with its heart was true and correct.

The second: the eye. That is, ﴿The heart did not lie﴾ about what the eye saw, and it did not say that what the eye saw was imagination.

The third: The heart did not lie about what Muhammad (peace be upon him) saw. This is clearly consistent with our view that *al-fuʾād* refers to the category, meaning the hearts bear witness to the truth of what Muhammad (ﷺ) saw [from the vision], even though the fancies do not acknowledge it.

**The fourth issue:** What is the object seen in His saying ﴿what it saw﴾? According to the earlier disagreement, and what the expression allows, there are three possibilities:

First: the Lord, the Exalted.

Second: Jibril, peace be upon him.

Third: the wondrous divine signs.

If it is asked: how can the seeing of Allah the Exalted be possible without this being a flaw, and without its implying that He is a body in a direction? We say: know that when a rational person reflects on a man who exists in a place and says, "This is the object seen by Allah the Exalted, and Allah sees him," and when he reflects on a matter that does not exist at all and says, "This is the object seen by Allah the Exalted, and Allah sees it," he finds a difference between the two. His intellect affirms the first statement and rejects the second. This does not mean that He is aware of it, because if one said, "The existent is known to Allah, and the non-existent is known to Allah," he would find no flaw in his words nor any strangeness. Thus Allah is a seer in the sense that He is knowing. Then Allah is a seer without becoming opposite the object seen, and without being located in a direction, nor being opposite to it. What makes this difficult for the imagination is only that it has never seen anything except in a direction, so it says that this is necessary. Something that confirms this is that you see the moon in water, while in reality you do not see the moon, when looking at the water, except in its place above the sky. You see the moon in the water because the ray emitted from the eye reaches it, and the water reflects that ray back to the sky. But your fancy, when it saw most of what it sees in front of it, did not become accustomed to seeing something located behind it except by facing toward it. It says, "I see the moon," and there is no seeing except when the object seen is opposite the pupil, and nothing is opposite the pupil except the water. So on this basis it judges that he sees the moon in the water. Thus, in this world, fancy overcomes the intellect, because most of the immediate matters are imaginary and sensory, while in the Hereafter the imaginings disappear and the understandings are made clear, so one sees things by their existence and not by their being contained in space.

Know that whoever denies the permissibility of seeing Allah the Exalted must also deny the permissibility of seeing Jibril, peace be upon him. This entails the denial of prophethood, which is disbelief, and it contains what almost amounts to disbelief. That is because whoever doubts the seeing of Allah the Exalted says: "If Allah the Exalted were permissible to be seen, He would necessarily be seen, because our senses are sound, and Allah the Exalted is not behind a veil, nor is He at an extreme distance from us, since He is not in a direction or place. So if it were permissible for Him to be seen and we do not see Him, it would entail a flaw in what is perceived and observed, since it would then be possible for there to be a mountain near us that we do not see." To that speaker it is said: it is established that Jibril, peace be upon him, used to descend upon Muhammad (ﷺ) while others were present with him, and he saw him, and if what is permissible were necessary, everyone would have seen him. If it is argued that there is a veil there, we say: it would then be necessary for a veil to be seen there, since a veil is not veiled when it is visible, according to their doctrine. Moreover, the texts have stated that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord with his heart, so his sight was placed in his heart, or he saw Him with his eye, so his heart was placed in his eye. And why not? According to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*), seeing is by the will of Allah, not by the power of the servant. So when Allah the Exalted produces knowledge of a thing through the eye, it is seeing, and if He produces it through the heart, it is knowing. Allah is able to produce knowledge through a created perceiver in the eye of the known object, just as He is able to produce it through a created perceiver in the heart. This matter is mentioned in the foundational sciences (*al-uṣūl*), so we will not lengthen it.

It may also be said that this verse emphasizes the meaning that preceded it, because one who is certain of something may be such that doubt does not depart from his soul.

He reinforced this with the words of the Exalted: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ ﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾. This is because when the Prophet ﷺ saw him while he was on the expanse of the earth, it was possible to say that he was a jinn, which is an extremely remote possibility, since we have explained that the Prophet ﷺ obtained the necessary knowledge that he was a sent angel. The remote possibility does not undermine resolute certainty. Do you not see that when we sleep at night and wake up by day, we are certain

that the seas did not dry up or sink during our sleep, nor did the mountains vanish or move away, even though it is possible that this happened, for Allah is able to do that during our sleep and return them to what they were on our day. So when he saw him at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, above the seventh heaven, it was not possible that there was a jinn or a human there, so this possibility was also negated. Thus the Exalted said: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ — the seeing of the eye. And how, when he saw him in the heaven? So what do you conjecture about it? There are several issues here:

We say there are several views on this, and they are arranged according to the question: to whom does the pronoun in "he saw" refer? And there are two opinions on this. The first: it refers to Allah the Exalted, meaning he saw Allah in another descent. This is according to the view of one who said that "what he saw" in His saying ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ is Allah the Exalted. The first: the view of those who permit motion and displacement upon Allah the Exalted, and this is false.

One of them: that the Prophet ﷺ descended upon the back of desire and the vehicle of the self; for this reason it is said of one who rides the back of his desire that he "exalted himself in the earth and was arrogant," as the Exalted said: ﴿exalted himself in the earth﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 4].

He chose the word "descent" because the ascent in the Hereafter has no descent, so He said "descent" so that it might be known that it is of the kind that was in this world. The second opinion: that the pronoun refers to Gabriel, peace be upon him, meaning he saw Gabriel in another descent. If it is asked, "Why did He say 'another (ukhrā)'?" We say: because the Prophet ﷺ, regarding the matter of prayer, went back and forth many times, so perhaps he would pass beyond him each time and descend to Gabriel. It is possible that the descent was for Gabriel, peace be upon him, and both are transmitted. On this view, "another descent" is clear, because Gabriel had descents, and he had two descents upon him while he was in his own form. As for His saying ﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾: the well-known view is that the lote-tree is a tree in the seventh heaven, and upon it are things like the nabq fruit. It has been said it is in the sixth heaven. A report has come that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants."

We say: the well-known view is that it is an adverb of place, its implied sense being: he saw Gabriel or another near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. The remote possibility does not undermine resolute certainty. Do you not see that when we sleep at night and wake up by day, we are certain

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 53, verse 16:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When there covered the lote tree that which covered it﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** What governs (al-'amil fi) *idh* (إذ, "when")? Is it what precedes it or what follows it? On this there are two views. If we say it is what precedes it, then there are two possibilities:

[Page 253]

The more apparent of them is *ra'ah* (he saw), meaning: he saw him at the time when that which covers the lote tree covered it. The other possibility is that what governs it is the verb that is in the *nazlah* (descent), its estimated sense being: he saw him in another descent, that descent being at the time when that which covers the lote tree covered it. That is, his descent did not occur except after the wonders had appeared at the lote tree, ﴿then there covered it that which covered it﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. Then Muhammad descended a (second) descent, indicating that he did not return without benefit.

If we say it is what follows it, then what governs it is ﴿His sight did not swerve﴾ [al-Najm: 17], meaning: his sight did not swerve at the time the lote tree was covered by what covered it. We will mention this when we explain the verse.

**The second issue:** I have mentioned that according to some interpretations, ﴿the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾ is the furthest limit of bewilderment. Saying ﴿which covers the lote tree﴾ according to that interpretation seems to contradict it. Can it be corrected? We say: it is possible to say that what is meant by covering is the covering of one state over another state, i.e., the state of sight and certainty came upon the state of bewilderment. Muhammad ﷺ saw, when the intellect was bewildered, what he saw at the time there came upon that state what came of the grace of God, the Exalted, and His mercy. The first view is the correct one, for the transmitted report we mentioned, that its lote fruit is like the jars of Hajar (Hajar: a region known for its pottery), indicates that it is a tree.

**The third issue:** What covered the lote tree? We say there are several views:

The first: butterflies or locusts of gold. This view is weak, because such a thing is not established except by a textual (sam'i) proof. If a report about it is authentic, then it is not far-fetched to interpret it; and if it is not authentic, then there is no basis for it.

The second: those who cover the lote tree are angels who surround it as if they were birds. This is close to the truth, because the place is one that no angel may transgress. They ascend to it honouring it, seeking blessing, visiting, just as people visit the Ka'bah and gather around it.

The third: the lights of God, the Exalted. This is evident, because when the Prophet ﷺ reached it, his Lord manifested Himself to it, just as He manifested Himself to the mountain, and the lights appeared. But the lote tree was stronger and firmer than the mountain, so the mountain was made level dust, and the tree did not move, and Moses fell down unconscious, while Muhammad did not tremble.

The fourth: it is something left indefinite out of glorification. One says: "I saw what I saw at the king's (court)," pointing to disclosure in one respect and concealment in another respect.

**The fourth issue:** ﴿yaghsha﴾ (يغشى) means "covers, veils," from which come *al-ghawashi* (coverings), or it is derived from the sense of "coming." It is said: "He does not come to me (la yaghshani) every time," meaning, he does not come to me. Both meanings are possible. According to the view of those who say that God comes and goes, then "coming" is closer.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

First issue: The lam in (al-basar, "the sight") may carry two meanings:

The first: It refers to what is well known, namely the sight of Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning that the sight of Muhammad did not swerve. On this reading, the non-swerving has several aspects. If we say that what covered the Lote-tree (sidrah) was locusts and moths, then the meaning is that he did not turn towards them, did not occupy himself with them, and did not cut off his gaze from the intended object. On this reading, the covering by the locusts and moths is a trial and a test for Muhammad (ﷺ). If we say that it was the lights of Allah, then there are two aspects:

The first: he did not turn right or left, but occupied himself with contemplating them.

The second: his sight did not swerve from the awe-struck shock (ṣa'qah), unlike Moses (peace be upon him), who cut off his gaze and fainted. In the first, there is a demonstration of the courtesy (adab) of Muhammad (ﷺ), and in the second, a demonstration of his strength.

The second aspect: The lam is for defining the genus (lam al-jins), meaning that no sight at all swerved in that place because of the greatness of the awe. If it is objected that were this the case he would have said "ma zaagha basar" (no sight swerved), since it is more indicative of generality, because an indefinite noun in the context of negation is general, we answer: it is like His saying ﴿Eyes do not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103], and He did not say "no sight perceives Him."

Second issue: If the intended one is Muhammad, then if He had said "his heart did not swerve," would the benefit of His saying "the sight did not swerve" have been obtained? We say no. This is because one who attends before a great king feels within himself that he is in awe of him and trembles, displaying his greatness, while his heart is strong. So when He says "the sight did not swerve," the benefit is obtained that the matter was great, and his sight did not swerve without the choice of the one who possesses the sight.

Third issue: "Wa ma taghaa" (nor did it transgress) is a conjunction of an independent sentence to another sentence, or a conjunction of an implied sentence to a sentence. An example of the independent: "Zayd went out and 'Amr entered." An example of the implied: "Zayd went out and entered." We say: both aspects are permissible. As for the first: it is as if He, exalted, said when the light appeared: "The sight of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not swerve, and Muhammad did not transgress by means of turning," and had he turned he would have been a transgressor. As for the second: it is clear on all the aspects. As for our saying that a locust covered the Lote-tree and he did not turn towards it, "nor did it transgress" means he did not turn towards other than Allah, so he did not turn to the locust, nor to anything other than the locust except Allah. As for our saying that a light covered it, then His saying "did not swerve" means he did not incline away from the lights, and "nor did it transgress" means he did not seek anything beyond them. There is a subtle point here: Allah, exalted, said "did not swerve and did not transgress" and did not say "did not incline and did not exceed," because inclining and exceeding at that place are both blameworthy, so He used zaygh and tughyan for them. There is another aspect: that this is an explanation of Muhammad's (ﷺ) arrival at the Lote-tree of certainty (sidrat al-yaqin), beyond which there is no certainty. The reasoning is that the sight of Muhammad (ﷺ) "did not swerve," meaning it did not deviate from the path, so he did not see things contrary to what they are, unlike one who looks at the disc of the sun for example and then looks at something white, and sees it yellow or green, his sight swerving from the course of sights. "Nor did it transgress" means he did not imagine the non-existent as existent, so he did not see the non-existent exceeding its limit.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: In it there is evidence that the Prophet ﷺ saw the signs of Allah on the night of the Mi'raj, and did not see Allah. There is disagreement on this. The reasoning is that Allah, exalted is He, concluded the account of the Mi'raj here with the seeing of the signs, and said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra' 17:1] up to His saying: ﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾ [al-Isra' 17:1]. Had he seen his Lord, that would have been the greatest possible, and the sign would have been the seeing, and the greatest thing would have been the seeing. Do you not see that when someone has wealth it is said to him: "Travel so that you may profit," and it is not said: "Travel so that you may enjoy the sights," because profit is greater than enjoyment.

The second issue: Some of the exegetes said: ﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ refers to his seeing Jibril, peace be upon him, in his (true) form. Is it as they say? We say: the apparent meaning is that these signs are other than that, because although Jibril, peace be upon him, is great, it has been reported in the traditions that Allah has angels greater than him. The word al-Kubra is the feminine of al-Akbar, so it is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: he saw of the signs of his Lord signs which are the greatest of signs. If it is said that Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed it is one of the greatest (calamities)﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:35], although the greatest of the wonders of Allah is Saqar, so likewise the greatest signs are Jibril and what is in him, even if Allah has signs greater than him. We say: Saqar is "one of the greatest," i.e., one of the great calamities, and there is no doubt that among calamities Saqar is great and immense; but as for the signs of Allah, Jibril is not the greatest of them. Moreover, Saqar in itself is greater and more wondrous than Jibril, peace be upon him, so describing it as great does not necessitate describing it as "the greatest."

The third issue: To what is al-Kubra an attribute? We say there are two views on this:
One of them: it is an attribute of a omitted noun, its estimate being: he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest sign.

The second: it is an attribute of "signs of his Lord," and in this case the object of ra'a is omitted, its estimate being: he saw of the greatest signs a sign or a thing.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾, ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾. When He had established the prophethood, He mentioned what the Messenger should begin with, which is tawhid and preventing the creation from associating partners with Allah. So the saying of Him, exalted is He, "Have you considered" is an indication of nullifying their statement by the very statement itself, just as when a weak person claims kingship and sensible people see him to be very far from what he claims, they say: "Look at this one who claims kingship," denouncing him without offering any proof, because his matter is evident. Therefore He said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾, meaning: as they are, so how do you associate them with Allah? The "ta'" in al-Lat is a feminine ta' as in al-Manat, but it is written elongated so that one does not stop on it and it becomes a ha', thereby resembling the name of Allah, exalted is He, for the ha' in Allah is original and is not a feminine ta' that changed into a ha' when pausing. It is an idol that belonged to Thaqif in al-Ta'if. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is fa'lah from lawa yalwi, because they used to circle around it (lawa 'alayha). According to what he said, its original form is lawyah; the ya' was made sukun and dropped due to the meeting of two sukuns, leaving lawah; the waw was changed to alif because of the fatha before it, becoming Lat. It was also read al-Latt with shaddah, from latta. It is said that it is derived from a man who used to knead food with ghee and feed people, so after his death an idol was made in his form and worshipped, and they named it al-Lat. According to this, al-Lat is masculine. As for al-'Uzza, it is the feminine of al-A'azz, and it was a tree that was worshipped. The Prophet ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, who cut it down, and from it came out a female devil with uncovered head and loose hair, striking her head and calling for woe and destruction. Khalid killed her while saying:

O 'Uzz, disbelief in you, no glorification of you! Indeed I have seen that Allah has humiliated you.

He returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of what he had seen and done, and he said: "That was al-'Uzza, and she will never be worshipped again." As for Manat, it is fa'alah, the idol of al-Safa, a rock that belonged to Hudhayl and Khuza'ah. On it there are issues:

The first issue: "al-akhar" (the other) cannot properly be used unless the first shares with the second, so one does not say "I saw a woman and another man," but one says "I saw a man and another man," because the first and second share in being men. Here His saying ﴿the third, the other﴾ according to what we mentioned requires that al-'Uzza be "third, first" and Manat "third, other," and that is not so. The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: "al-ukhra" is also used for dispraise. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Its first said to its last﴾ [al-A'raf 7:39], meaning to its later ones, who are the followers, and they are called the "tails" because of their lateness in rank, so it is an attribute of dispraise. It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: and Manat, the third, the latecomer, the humiliated. We say on this basis: there is an order among the three idols, because the first was an idol in the form of a human, al-'Uzza's form is that of a plant, and Manat's form is that of a rock, which is inanimate. The human is nobler than the plant, and the plant is nobler than the inanimate, so the inanimate is later, and Manat is inanimate, so it is among the "last" in rank.

The second answer: there is an omission in it, its estimate being: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾, the two worshipped falsely, ﴿and Manat, the third﴾, the worshipped other.

The third answer: the idols were many, and if al-Lat and al-'Uzza are taken as the first two, then every idol that is found is a third, so there are many thirds. It is as if He says to them: there are many thirds, and this is the third, the other. This is like the saying of a speaker: "day after day."

The fourth answer: there is inversion in it, its estimate being: and Manat, the other, the third. It may be said that "the other" is used for something imagined or understood even if it is neither well-known nor mentioned. Someone who is greatly troubled by people, when a person harms him, says: "The other one came to harm us," and he may remain silent at the saying "you are the other," and his purpose is understood; so likewise here.

The second issue, which is more appropriate in order: what is the purpose of the fa' in His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾, since it is used in other places without fa'? We say: since He had mentioned the greatness of the signs of Allah in His dominion, that the Messenger of Allah to the Messengers, who fills the horizons with some of his wings and destroys cities with his might and power, cannot exceed the Lote-tree of the Boundary in the station of the majesty and might of Allah, He said: have you considered these idols, with their insignificance and worthlessness, as partners of Allah, along with what has preceded? So He said it with fa', meaning: immediately after what you have heard of the greatness of the great signs of Allah, exalted is He, and the execution of His command in the highest assembly and what is beneath the soil.
