The second issue, which is more appropriate in order: what is the purpose of the fa' in His saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾, since it is used in other places without fa'? Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah?﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:4], ﴿Have you considered your partners?﴾ [Fatir 35:40]. We say: since He had mentioned the greatness of the signs of Allah in His dominion, that the Messenger of Allah to the Messengers, who fills the horizons with some of his wings and destroys cities with his might and power, cannot exceed the Lote-tree of the Boundary in the station of the majesty and might of Allah, He said: have you considered these idols, with their insignificance and worthlessness, as partners of Allah, along with what has preceded? So He said it with fa', meaning: immediately after what you have heard of the greatness of the great signs of Allah, exalted is He, and the execution of His command in the highest assembly and what is beneath the soil. So look at al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and you will know the corruption of what you have gone to and relied upon.

The third issue: where is the completion of the speech which conveys a meaning? We say it has already been explained: it says, "Have you seen these truly, the seeing?" If you had seen them, you would know that they are not fit to be partners. Its parallel is what we mentioned about one who denies that a weak person claims kingship: he says to his companion, "Do you not know so-and-so, limited to him," pointing to the falsity of what he goes to.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 53, verses 21–22:

﴿Is it for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ ﴿That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is it for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ We have already mentioned what must be mentioned about this in Surat al-Tur, in His words ﴿Or has He daughters while you have sons?﴾ [al-Tur: 39]. Here we repeat some of that, or something close to it. We say: When He mentioned al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat and did not mention anything else, He said: These things which you have seen and recognised, and which you take as partners to Allah, you have heard of the majesty and greatness of Allah. The angels, despite their elevated rank and loftiness, reach the Lote Tree (al-Sidrah) and stop there. There remains no doubt that they are further from the way of reason (al-ma'qul) than they are from the way of transmission (al-manqul). It is as if they said: We do not doubt that none of these is a likeness of Allah, the Exalted, nor close to resembling Him. We only fashioned these things in the forms of the honoured angels whom the prophets have acknowledged. They said that the angels ascend and stop at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), that commands and prohibitions descend upon them, and that they convey to Allah what proceeds from His servants on His earth, and that they are the daughters of Allah. So we took images in the forms of females and named them with female names. Al-Lat is the feminine of al-Lawah, and its original form should have been al-Lahah. But in the feminine it is pausal, so it becomes al-Lahah, and one of the two hes is dropped, leaving the word on two original letters plus the feminine ta'. We treated it as if it were original, just as we did with dhat mal and dha mal. Al-'Uzza is the feminine of al-A'azz. Then He said to them: How do you attribute daughters to Allah when you yourselves acknowledge that daughters are deficient and sons are complete, while Allah is complete in majesty? How can you attribute to Him what you have made deficient, when you are in the utmost lowliness and humiliation, in that you have made yourselves more abject than a donkey, a slave, then a rock and a tree, and then you attribute to yourselves the complete? So this division is also unjust by your own standard, in that you have abased yourselves and attributed to them the greatest of the two weights (the jinn and humankind), and you have hated daughters and attributed them to the greatest, who is Allah, the Exalted. By your custom, you were to make the greatest for the great and the least for the lowly. Thus you have contradicted reason, intellect and the custom that you hold.

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ There are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: To what does "that" (tilka) refer? We say it refers to something omitted, whose estimate is: That division is an unjust division, meaning not equitable. It may also be said that its meaning is: That attribution is a division. This is because they did not divide, nor did they say: For us the sons, and for Him the daughters. Rather, they attributed daughters to Allah, while they disliked them, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike﴾ [al-Nahl: 62]. So when they attributed daughters to Allah, an unjust division arose from that attribution. This difference does not burden the matter.

The second issue: What is the answer ("jawab") of "idhan" (then)? We say it may have several possibilities:

The first: Your attributing daughters to Allah, when you have sons, is an unjust division.

The second: Your attributing daughters to Allah while believing that they are deficient, and your choosing sons while believing that they are complete, when you are in the utmost lowliness and Allah, the Exalted, is in the utmost greatness, is an unjust division.

If it is asked: What is the origin of "idhan"? We say: It is "idha" (when), which is used for time, from which the annexation (idafah) has been cut off, so it takes nunation (tanwin). Its explanation is that you say: "I will come to you when the sun rises," as if you had annexed "idha" to the rising of the sun and said: "I will come to you at the time of the sunrise." If someone then says: "I will come to you," you say to him: "Idhan, I will honour you," meaning: "If you come to me, I will honour you." Because you omitted the coming, since it had been mentioned in the speaker's words, you substituted nunation for it and said "idhan," as you say: ﴿And to each We gave﴾ [al-Anbiya': 74].

The third issue: "Dhiza" has been read with a hamzah and without a hamzah. According to the first reading, it is "fi'la" with a kasrah on the fa', like "dhikra," being a verbal noun described by the adjective, like "rajul 'adl" (a just man), meaning an unjust division. According to the second reading, it is "fu'la," and its original form was "dhuza," but the 'ayn of the word was a ya'-type letter, so the fa' was given a kasrah in order that the 'ayn be saved from conversion (qalb). The same was done with "bid" (white ones). The plural of "af'al" is "fu'l": one says "aswad" and "sud," and "ahmar" and "humr." One also says "abyad" and "bid," and the pattern would have been "bu'd," which would necessarily have entailed converting the 'ayn, so the ba' was given a kasrah and the ya' was left in its place. On this basis, "dhiza" is an intensive form from "da'iza" (unjust). One says: "fadil," "afdal," "fadila," and "fudla," and "kabir," "akbar," "kabira," and "kubra." Likewise "da'iz," "duwaz," "da'iza," and "duwza." On this basis we say: "adwaz" (more unjust) than "da'iz," and "dhiza" (more unjust) than "da'iza."

If it is objected: You said earlier that His words ﴿Or has He daughters while you have sons?﴾ [al-Tur: 39] do not mean the denial of both matters, but rather the denial of the first and the showing of reproof by means of the second, as you say: "Do you make rivals for Allah while you know that He created everything other than Himself?", where the second is not denied. Here, His words ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ indicate that He denied both matters together. We say: We have already mentioned there that both matters are possible. As for denying both, it is apparent according to the well-known view. As for denying the first, it is established by several considerations. As for the second, what we mentioned is that He, the Exalted, said: How do you attribute daughters to Allah when sons have come to you by His power? As He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He bestows females upon whom He wills and bestows males upon whom He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 49]. The Creator of sons for you does not have daughters. As for His words ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾, we say: We have made clear that "that" refers to the attribution, meaning your attribution of daughters to Allah, the Exalted, while you have sons, is an unjust division. So what is denied is that attribution. If what is denied is the division itself, we say it is possible that its estimate is: Is it permissible to assign daughters to Allah, the Exalted, just as, when one has a shared thing between himself and his partner in equal measure, he takes half for himself, and gives from the remaining half a half to his oppressor and a half to his companion? So he said: This is an unjust division, not because he took the half, for that is his right, but because he did not deliver to him the remaining half.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They are nothing but names you and your fathers have named; God has sent down no authority for them﴾. In this verse there are subtle points which, if one has a great share of the linguistic sciences, one can grasp. Let us first mention what has been said about it, so we say: it has been said that its meaning is: ﴿They are nothing but names﴾, that is, their being females and their being worshipped are names without anything named by them, for they are not really females, nor are they gods. It has also been said: "names" means you called some of them "al-'Uzza" and there is no might (*'izza*) for them. And it has been said: you claimed that they are gods, and they are not gods. What we say is that this is a response to their statement, and that is in accordance with what we have explained, that they said: "We do not doubt that God has not begotten as women beget, nor been begotten as men are begotten through intercourse and impregnation." However, we have seen the word *walad* (child) used among the Arabs for that which is caused: they say *bint al-jabal* (daughter of the mountain) and *bint al-shafa* (daughter of the lip), because of what appears and comes into being from them. So the angels are "children of God" in the sense that they came into being through Him without an intermediary, and so we say they are His children. Then, since the angels carry the feminine *ta' marbuta*, we say they are feminine children, and a feminine child is a *bint* (daughter), so we say to them: "daughters of God," meaning there is no intermediary between them and God, exalted is He, in bringing into existence, as the philosophers say. Then God said: these names you have devised by your own whims and you have applied to God what gives the impression of deficiency, and that is impermissible. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Alas, my regret over what I neglected concerning God﴾ [az-Zumar: 56], and the saying "In Your hand is the good," are names that give an impression (of deficiency), except that He, exalted is He, sent them down, and He may name Himself by what He chooses. But no one may name [God] by what gives the impression of deficiency without the revelation of the Law concerning it. Now let us explain the exegesis (*tafsir*, explanation of the Qur'an) in several issues:

The first issue: To what does the pronoun in *hiya* (they) refer? We say: the apparent reference is to a known matter, namely the names, as if He said: "What are these names that you have set down?" This is the well-known view. It is also possible to say that *hiya* refers to the idols themselves, meaning: "These idols are nothing but names." In that case it is by way of exaggeration and figurative speech, as one says to belittle a person: "Zayd is nothing but a name," and "The king is nothing but a name" when he does not possess a quality that is regarded as significant in speech among people. This view is supported by His saying: ﴿You worship besides Him nothing but names﴾ [Yusuf: 40], meaning: "These idols are nothing but names."

The second issue: What is the benefit in His saying ﴿you named them﴾, given that all the names were set down by them, or some of them were set down by them and He did not reject that from them? We say: the matter is disputed, and the blame is not complete except by His saying ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾. Its explanation is that if God sent down the names, there is no discussion of them; but if they set them down for mutual understanding, then there should not be within that benefit a corruption greater than it. Yet the giving the impression of deficiency in the attributes of God is greater than that. So God did not permit assigning names to realities except where it is safe from what is forbidden. Thus there is found in these names neither a transmitted proof nor a rational reason, because committing a great corruption for the sake of a small benefit is not permitted by a sensible person. So when ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾, and the name is assigned, this can only be by a transmitted or rational proof, namely that it occurs free from the prevailing harms.

The third issue: How did He say ﴿you named them﴾ when these designations for their idols existed before them? We say there is a subtle point in this, namely that if they had said, "We did not name them; they were set down before us," it would be said to them: everyone who uses these terms is like the first one who set them down. For the first setter of these names, since he set them down without a rational proof, it is not obligatory to follow him. So whoever uses a term because so-and-so used it, that is not valid for him, just as it is not valid for him to say: "The blind man misled me." And if he said it, it would be said to him: "Rather, you misled yourself when you followed one whom you knew was not fit to be followed."

The fourth issue: Names are not named; rather, one is named by them. How then did He say ﴿you named them﴾? We say there are two answers concerning this. One is linguistic: naming (*tasmiya*) is the setting of a name, so it is as if He said: "names you set down," and He used *sammaytumuhā* in the sense of *waḍa'tumuhā* (you set them down). One says *sammaytuhu Zaydan* and *sammaytuhu bi-Zayd*, so *sammaytumuhā* means *sammaytum bihā* (you named with them).

The second is semantic: if He had said "names you named with them," there would be something other than the name to which the *bāʾ* in His saying *bihā* (with them) attaches, because the speaker's saying "I named him with it" requires a second object. One says: "I named him with Zayd, my son, or my slave, or other than that," so that he has given the idols a consideration beyond their names. But when He said ﴿They are nothing but names you named﴾, meaning: "You set them down in themselves, not as having referents," this would not be the case. If it is objected that this is invalid in view of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I named her Maryam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 36], where He did not say "I named her with Maryam," and what you mention was not intended, otherwise Maryam would not be regarded as the object of attention, as you said about the idols: We say there is a great difference between them. For there He said ﴿I named her Maryam﴾, mentioning both objects. So He considered the reality of Maryam by His saying ﴿I named her﴾, and her name by His saying "Maryam." But here He said ﴿They are nothing but names you named﴾, meaning: there is nothing here but names that have been set down. So the reality was not considered here, whereas it was considered in the case of Maryam.

The fifth issue: ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾. In what manner is the *bāʾ* used in His saying ﴿for them no authority﴾? We say it is used as when a speaker says "So-and-so departed with his family and his goods," meaning he departed and with him were the family and the goods. So it is here as well.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture and what the souls desire, and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾. In this verse there are issues:

The first issue: It was recited *in tattabi'ūna* with the *tā'* (second person), which is apparent and suitable to His saying ﴿you and your fathers﴾, and [the usual reading] is in the third person. In it there are two views:

One: the address is with them, but it is an *iltifāt* (shift of person), as if He broke off speech with them and said to His Prophet: "They do not follow anything but conjecture, so do not turn to their statement."

The second: the intended people are others, and in this there are two possibilities:

One: the intended are their fathers, and the meaning is that when He said ﴿you named them﴾, it was as if they said: "These are not names we set down; rather they are like other names that we received from those before us, from our fathers." So He said: "And their fathers named them, and they follow nothing but conjecture." If it is objected: it should have been in the past tense, we say: it may also be in the future tense, as if He envisages a time after the time of speech, as in His saying: ﴿and their dog stretches out its forelegs﴾ [al-Kahf: 18].

The second: the intended are the unbelievers in general, as if He said: "The unbelievers follow nothing but conjecture."

The second issue: What is the meaning of "conjecture" (*zann*), and how does He blame them for it, when it has been made obligatory for us to follow it in jurisprudence (*fiqh*), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, on the authority of God, exalted is He: "I am according to My servant's expectation of Me"? We say: as for *zann*, it is the opposite of knowledge (*'ilm*). It has been used figuratively in place of knowledge and knowledge in its place. The root of knowledge is manifestation, and from it come *'ilm* and *'alam* (sign). We have explained in the tafsir of ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾ that the letters *ʿ-l-m* in their permutations carry the meaning of manifestation. From them: *lamaʿa al-ālu* (the mirage shone) when it appeared; *miyḍ al-sarāb* (the shimmering of the mirage); *lamaʿa al-ghazāl* (the gazelle shone) when it ran; likewise the ostrich, where there is manifestation; and likewise *ʿalimtu* (I knew). But *zann*, when it stands in opposition to knowledge, carries obscurity, and from it comes *bi'r ẓanūn* (a well whose water is unknown, one does not know whether there is water in it or not), and from it *al-ẓanīn* (the suspected one), who is accused and one does not know what he suspects. We say: it is permissible to base a matter on the prevailing conjecture when one is unable to reach certainty. Belief is not like that, because certainty has not been made impossible for us. To this is the allusion in His saying ﴿and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾, meaning: they followed conjecture, although it was possible for them to take hold of certainty. And in action too that is also impossible.

The third issue: Is *mā* in His saying ﴿and what the souls desire﴾ a relative (*khabariyya*) or a verbal (*maṣdariyya*) one? We say there are two views:

One: it is verbal, as if He said: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture﴾ and the desire of the souls. If it is asked: what is the benefit in turning away from the explicit verbal noun to the verb with the addition of *mā*, which entails lengthening? We say there is a benefit in it, and it is in the original form; then we mention it here: when a speaker says "Your handiwork pleased me," it is known from the form that the pleasure derives from a completed action; likewise if he says "What you do pleased me," it is known that the pleasure derives from an action in which it is. But if he said "Your handiwork pleased me," and he has a handiwork of yesterday and a handiwork of today, it is not known which handiwork pleased him. If you understand this, we say: here His saying ﴿and what the souls desire﴾ indicates that they follow what their souls desire in the present and the future, an indication that they are not steadfast on a single error. Nor did their souls desire, in the past, any kind of worship which they committed to and persisted in; rather every day they devise a worship, and when their idols are broken today they bring another tomorrow, changing the form of their worship according to the demand of their desire today.

The second: it is relative (*khabariyya*), its implied sense being: "and what their souls desire." The difference between the verbal and the relative is that what is followed in the first is the desire itself, and in the second is what the desire requires, as when I say "Your made thing pleased me."

The fourth issue: Why did He say ﴿and what the souls desire﴾ in the plural, when they do not follow what every soul desires, for some souls do not desire what others desire? We say it is from the type of matching plural with plural, meaning each one of them followed what his own soul desires, just as one says "The people went out with their families," meaning each one with his family, not each one with the family of the whole group.

The fifth issue: Explain the meaning of the speech as a whole. We say: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture and what the souls desire﴾ mentions two matters, and it may be that their mention is for two matters: a distinction between *yattabi'ūna al-ẓann* (they follow conjecture) in belief, and *yattabi'ūna mā tahwā al-anfus* (they follow what the souls desire) in action and worship. Both are corrupt, because belief should be founded on certainty, and how is it permissible to follow conjecture in a grave matter? The greater and more dangerous the matter, the more obligatory and cautious the precaution in it. As for action, worship opposes desire, so how could it be based on following it? It may also be that in a single matter, by way of descending by degrees, He said: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture and what the souls desire﴾, meaning: and what falls below conjecture, because the vulgar desire what is not even thought to be good. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾ is an indication that they are in a state not to be regarded, because certainty is within their power, and it was realized by the coming of the messengers. ﴿The guidance﴾ here has three meanings:

The first: the Qur'an.

The second: the messengers.

The third: the miracles.

[Page 261 (in the source)]

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ It is well known that "am" here is disjunctive (munqati'a), and its meaning is: "Does man have what he chose and desired?" Regarding ﴿whatever he wishes﴾ there are several interpretations:

The first: They wished for intercession, though they had no intercession.

The second: Their saying, ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50].

The third: The saying of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ [Maryam: 77].

The fourth: A group wished to be prophets, but that lofty rank was not attained by them. If you ask, "Can 'am' here be connected (muttasila)?" We say: Yes. In that case, the first sentence may have two interpretations:

One of them: It is mentioned in His saying, ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ as if He had said: "Is the male for you and the female for Him in reality, or do you attribute to yourselves what you desire and wish for?" On this view, His saying ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾ and others are sentences inserted between two connected statements.

The second: It is omitted. The explanation of this is that we have shown that His saying, ﴿Have you considered?﴾ serves to show the corruption of their statement and to point to its being evident without evidence, like when one says, "So-and-so is fit for kingship," and another says to a third, "Did you not see what so-and-so says, and not mention that he is unfit for kingship?" and his intent is that, so he mentions it alone as evidence of its unfitness. Here, the Exalted said, ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ That is: Do they deserve worship, or does man have the right to worship what his nature desires even if it does not deserve worship? On this view, His saying "am li-l-insan" means: Does he have the right to worship through wishing and desiring? This is supported by His saying, ﴿And what the souls desire﴾, that is: You worshipped, by the desire of your souls, what does not deserve worship. So do you have that?

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first [life]﴾, and concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Concerning the connection of the fa' (fa') to the discourse, and there are several interpretations:

The first: Its implied sense is: If man chooses a deity in his worldly life according to what he wished and desired, then to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first [life]. He will punish him for his act in this world, and if He does not punish him in this world, He will punish him in the Hereafter. His saying, ﴿And how many an angel [there is] in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing﴾ [An-Najm: 26], up to His saying ﴿Their intercession will not avail﴾ [An-Najm: 26], serves as an emphasis for this meaning, that is: Their punishment will occur and no one will intercede for them, and the intercession of an intercessor will not benefit them.

The second: When He, exalted, made clear that taking al-Lat and al-'Uzza was by following conjecture and the desires of souls, it was as if He affirmed it and said: If you do not know this, then to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first [life]. These idols have no share of the affair, so how is associating partners permissible? His saying, ﴿And how many an angel﴾, on this view, is an answer to a statement, as if they had said: "We do not associate anything with Allah; these idols are only our intercessors, for they are the form of angels brought near," so He said: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession avails them nothing﴾ [An-Najm: 26].

The third: This is consolation, as if the Exalted had said that to His Prophet, when he had made clear his message and the oneness of Allah, and they did not believe. So He said: Do not grieve. ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first [life]﴾, that is: They cannot overpower Allah.

The fourth: It is the arrangement of a truth upon its proof. Its explanation is that when He, exalted, made clear the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ by His saying, ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾, up to its end, and made clear some of what Muhammad ﷺ brought, which is monotheism, He said: When you know the truthfulness of Muhammad through the clarification of the message of Allah, the Exalted, then ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first [life]﴾, because he ﷺ informed you about the Gathering, so he is truthful.

The fifth: It is that the disbelievers used to say to the believers, "Are these better guided than us?" and they said, ﴿If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 11]. So the Exalted said: Allah chose for you the worldly life and gave you wealth, and He did not give the believers part of that matter. Rather, you said: "If Allah had willed, He would have made them rich," and you were certain of this matter. ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first [life]﴾. Say in the Hereafter what you said in this world, ﴿Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [Al-Qasas: 56], just as He enriches whom He wills.

The second issue: "al-Akhirah" (the Hereafter) is an adjective of what? We say: It is an adjective of "al-hayah" (life) or of "al-dar" (the abode). It is an active participle (ism al-fa'il) of a verb that is not used. You say "akhkhartuhu, fa-ta'akhkhara" (I delayed it, so it was delayed), and by analogy it should be "fa-ukhkhira" just as you say "ghabbartuhu, fa-ghubbira." So you are prevented from it by hearing. There is a benefit to this inquiry that will come, God willing.

The third issue: "al-Ula" (the first) is of the form fu'la for the feminine, so "al-awwal" is then af'al as an adjective. Concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: There must be a root from which af'al and fu'la are derived, for every fu'la and af'al for the feminine and masculine has a root, so it must be derived from it, like "al-fudla" and "al-afdal" from "al-fadila" and "al-fadil." So what is that? We say: Here it is derived from a root that is not used, just as we said that "al-akhir" is an active participle of a verb that is not used. The reason for this is that every used verb has an "akhir" (end), because it has a past tense, and when you use its past tense it implies the completion of the act; otherwise the doer would still be within the act, and so it would not be past. For you do not say of one who is after eating "akala" (he ate), except figuratively when a little remains for him, so he says "akala," indicating that what remains is not significant. And you say to one who is near completion, "faraghta" (you have finished), and he says "faraghtu" (I have finished), meaning that what remains is a little and not significant, so it is as if I have finished. As for the past in its reality, it is valid only when a thing is complete and finished. Thus, for a used verb there is an "akhir." If our saying "akhir" were on the pattern fa'il from a verb "akhara, ya'khuru" like "amara, ya'muru," its meaning would be "its source has occurred," like "jalasa" (he sat) means the sitting occurred from him completely and perfectly. So it would follow that when one says "fulan akhar" (so-and-so is last), its meaning is that the completion of being last has occurred from him and he is finished with it, so after he is last there is no further last. But it has been established that every verb has an "akhir" after it. It is not objected that this is contradicted by our saying "ta'akhkhara" (it was delayed), for its meaning is "it became last," because we say that the pattern of the verb speaks for the validity of what we mentioned, for it is of the category of affectation and arrogance when used of something other than the arrogant one, that is, it is considered last while in reality it is not so. Having known this, we say: "al-akhir" is an active participle with no verb. Its intensive form is with af'al, and it is like our saying "a'akhar," so the hamza was moved to the place of the alif and the alif to the place of the hamza, so the alif became a hamza and the hamza an alif. This is shown by the interpretation of the meaning, for the end of a thing is a part of it connected to it, while the "akhir" is separate from it and detached, and the detached is after the connected. The "akhir" is more delayed from the thing than its end. The "awwal" is af'al with no doer and no verb. The "awwal" is further from the verb than the "akhir," because the past verb is known to have an end from its being described as past; without that description, its end would not be known. As for the verb, to explain its being a verb, its beginning is known, because the verb must have a doer who performs it or from whom it proceeds. So the doer is first, then the verb. When the doer is the first of the verb, how can the "awwal" have a verb proceeding from it, while it has neither verb nor doer? So one does not say "al" (ala) of a thing meaning "preceded," as one says "qala" from speech or "nala" from attainment. It is not said that our saying "sabaqa" (he preceded) is derived from it "al-sabiq" and from "al-sabiq" "al-asbaq," even though the doer precedes the verb. Likewise it is said "taqaddama al-shay'" (the thing advanced), though the doer is prior to the verb, and so on. We say: As for "taqaddama," the answer about it has already passed in "ta'akhkhara." As for "sabaqa," the speaker says "sabaqtuhu, fa-sabaqtuhu" (I raced him, so I outran him). We answer that this requires a matter proceeding from a doer. So "al-sabiq," if used of the first, is by way of resemblance, not in reality. The doer is the first of the verb in the sense of "before the verb," not the "preceding" of the verb, because the doer and the verb do not race each other, so the doer does not outrun it. What clarifies what we have mentioned is that the "akhir" is further from the first with respect to the verb, unlike the "akhir." As for what is said, that "awwal" means "making the last first" in order to extract a meaning from the speech, it is far-fetched; otherwise "akhir" would not be inferior to it in conveying that. Rather, the interpretation (ta'wil) is from "ala al-shay'," when a thing returns, that is, returns it to the intended meaning. And further from the two words "qabl" and "ba'd": the "akhir" is a doer without a verb, and the "awwal" is af'al without a doer and without a verb, while "qabl" and "ba'd" have neither doer nor af'al, so nothing is understood from a verb at all. For the "awwal" is "awwal" because of what is in it of the meaning of "qabl," and "qabl" is not "qabl" because of what is in it of the meaning of "awwal." And the "akhir" is "akhir" because of what is in it of the meaning of "ba'd," and "ba'd" is not "ba'd" because of what is in it of the meaning of "akhir." What shows you this is that you explain one of them by the other and do not reverse it. You say, "This is the last of those who came, because he came after all," and you do not say, "He came after all, because he is the last of those who came." What supports this is that the "akhir" is not realized except with a specific "after-ness," which is the one that has no after-ness after it, while "ba'd" is not realized except with the "akhir," for the one in the middle after the first is not the last. This discussion is one of the discussions on time, and from it is known the meaning of his saying ﷺ: "Do not revile time, for time is Allah." That is, time is that from which the notion of "before" and "after" is understood, and Allah, the Exalted, is the one from whom that is understood. "Before" and "after" are real in affirming Allah, and time has no meaning except what gives it "before" and "after." So do not revile time, for what you understand from it is realized only in Allah and through Allah, and were it not for Him, there would be no "before" and no "after."

The second discussion: The Arabic usage "al-uwla" (feminine of "al-awwal") occurs, and this contradicts the validity of using "al-ula" as the feminine, because "al-ula" indicates that "al-awwal" is an af'al of comparison (tafdil), and an af'al of comparison does not take the feminine ta' ending. Thus one does not say "Zayd a'lam" and "Zaynab a'lamah," for a reason whose mention is long, and we will mention it in another place, God willing, the Exalted. We say in answer: "Awwal," since it is an af'al and has no doer, resembled "al-arba'" and "al-arnab," so it is permissible to attach the ta' to it. And since it is an adjective, it resembled "al-akbar" and "al-asghar," so it was said "uwla."

The fourth issue: "Ula" indicates that "awwal" is not declinable (la yanṣarif). How then can one say "af'aluhu awwalan" (I do it first) and say "jā'a Zayd awwalan wa-'Amr thāniyan" (Zayd came first and 'Amr second)? If it is said that both are permissible based on "uwlah" and "ula," then whoever holds that the feminine of "awwal" is "uwlah" is like "al-arba'" and "al-arba'ah," so tanwin is permissible; and whoever says "ula" is not permissible. We say: If that is so, then the more common usage is to omit the tanwin, because the more common view is that its feminine is "ula," and the Qur'an's usage is according to it. So the answer is: In the feminine, "ula" should be said, looking at the meaning, while for the Arabs "uwlah" is the root, and it is indicated by evidence, even if it is weaker than the other. It may be said that the prohibition of declension of af'al occurs only when its feminine is only fu'la. As for when its feminine is with the ta' or it is permissible for it, it is not undeclinable.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing, except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and is pleased with.﴾

The connection of this verse with what precedes it has already been explained in the earlier aspects concerning His words ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾, if we say that its meaning is that al-Lat, al-'Uzza and others have no share of the affair at all. ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ It is therefore not permissible to associate partners with Him, for they would say, "We do not associate anything with Allah; we only say these are our intercessors." So He said, "How can these intercede when whoever is in the heavens does not possess intercession?" And there are issues in this:

**The first issue:** *kam* (كَمْ) is a word used for quantities. It is either interrogative, when one seeks to know the quantity, as in your saying *kam dhiraan tooluhu* (كَمْ ذِراعًا طُولُهُ, "how many cubits is its length?") and *kam rajulan jaa'aka* (كَمْ رَجُلًا جاءَكَ, "how many men came to you?"), meaning "what is the number of those who came?", seeking to know the amount; it is like *kayfa* (كَيْفَ) for seeking to know states, *ayy* (أيُّ) for seeking to know individuals, and *ma* (ما) for seeking to know realities. Or it is used to state the quantity in general, in which case it is declarative (khabariyya), as in your saying *kam rajulin akramani* (كَمْ رَجُلٍ أكْرَمَنِي, "many a man honoured me"), meaning "many of them honoured me." However, there are questions on this:

The first: why was *min* (مِن) not permitted to be inserted after the interrogative *kam*, while it was permitted after the declarative? The second: why was the specification (*tamyiz*, the noun that clarifies a number, the accusative of specification) of the interrogative put in the accusative, while that of the declarative is put in the genitive? The third: the declarative *kam* is used in contrast to *rubba* (رُبَّ, "many a"/"a few"), so why was it made a noun when *rubba* is a particle?

As for the answer to the first, *min* is used in a position that is specified by an annexation (*idafa*). You say *khatamun min fiddatin* (خاتَمٌ مِن فِضَّةٍ, "a ring of silver") just as you say *khatamu fiddatin* (خاتَمُ فِضَّةٍ). Since the interrogative is not annexed, it was not permissible to use what resembles it. We shall clarify this answer. As for the answer to the second question, we say that the original state of the *tamyiz* is the annexation. As for the third, *kam* can be preceded by a preposition, so you say *ila kam tasbiru* (إلى كَمْ تَصْبِرُ, "until when will you endure?"), *fi kam yawmin ji'ta* (فِي كَمْ يَوْمٍ جِئْتَ, "on how many days did you come?"), and *bi kam rajulin marrarta* (بِكَمْ رَجُلٍ مَرَرْتَ, "with how many men did you pass?"). In terms of meaning, when *kam* is joined with *min* and its specification is made plural, as in the saying of the speaker *kam min rijalin khadamtuhum* (كَمْ مِن رِجالٍ خَدَمْتُهم, "how many men have I served?"), its meaning is "many of the men I served." *Rubba*, although it denotes paucity, does not stand in the place of a small number. Therefore one cannot say of *rubba* that it expresses a few, as we said of *kam* that it expresses many.

**The second issue:** He said *shafa'atuhum* (شَفاعَتُهم, "their intercession") with the pronoun referring to the meaning (of the plural noun), whereas had He said *shafa'atuhu* (شَفاعَتُهُ, "his intercession") the pronoun would have referred to the wording (of the singular). It would then be permissible to say *kam min rajulin ra'aytuhu* (كَمْ مِن رَجُلٍ رَأيْتُهُ, "how many a man have I seen him") and *kam min rajulin ra'aytuhum* (كَمْ مِن رَجُلٍ رَأيْتُهم, "how many a man have I seen them"). If you ask, "Is there a semantic difference between the two?" I say: yes. When He, exalted is He, said *la tughni shafa'atuhum* (لا تُغْنِي شَفاعَتُهُمْ, "their intercession avails nothing"), it means the intercession of all of them together. Had He said *shafa'atuhu*, its meaning would have been "many angels, each of whose intercession avails nothing," and so it might occur to someone that their intercession would avail if it were gathered together. On this basis, the statement contains matters all of which point to the greatness of the affair:

First: *kam*, for it denotes multiplicity.
Second: the word *malak* (مَلَك, "angel"), for it is the noblest of the kinds of created beings.
Third: *fi as-samawat* (فِي السَّماواتِ, "in the heavens"), for it is an indication of the loftiness of their rank and the nearness of their station to the abode of felicity.
Fourth: the plural pronoun in His words *shafa'atuhum* (شَفاعَتُهُمْ), indicating that they are gathered in the matter.

All of this serves to demonstrate the corruption of their claim that the idols intercede. That is, how can they intercede, given their lowliness, weakness and the baseness of their rank? Inanimate matter is the basest of kinds, while the angels are the noblest of them, and they are in the highest heavens, yet the intercession of the angels is not accepted. So how could the intercession of inanimate things be accepted?

[Page 264]

**The third issue:** What is the benefit of His words *wa kam min malak* (وكَمْ مِن مَلَكٍ, "and how many an angel"), in the sense of "many of the angels," although each one of those in the heavens does not possess intercession? We say: the purpose is to refute them in their claim that these idols intercede, and this is not achieved by showing that a single angel's intercession is not accepted. So He contented Himself with mentioning the many, and did not say "none of them possesses intercession," because the latter is closer to dispute about it than the statement "many," although the intended purpose is achieved by it.

Then there is a point here: in some contexts the form of generality is used while the meaning is the many, and in others the many is used while the meaning is all, and both follow one method, namely the disregarding of the remainder and not giving it consideration. In His words *tudammiru kulla shay'* (تُدَمِّرُ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ, "it destroys everything") [al-Ahqaf 46:25], it is as if He makes what lies outside the ruling not worthy of attention. In His words *wa kam min malak* and His words *bal aktaruhum la ya'lamun* (بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ, "but most of them do not know") [an-Nahl 16:75], and His words *aktaruhum bihi mu'minun* (أكْثَرُهم بِهِمْ مُؤْمِنُونَ, "most of them are believers in Him") [Saba 34:41], the exception is made not worthy of attention, so it is treated as if it were not excluded, like a matter that lies outside the ruling, as if it had not gone out. This varies according to the intended purpose of the speech. If the speech is mentioned for a matter in which exaggeration is made, the word "all" is used. An example: one says to a king, "All the people pray for you," when the aim is only to show the abundance of prayer for him and nothing else. If the speech is mentioned for a matter outside of it, exaggeration is not made in it, because the purpose is something other than it, so "all" is not used. An example: when a king says to someone who has said to him, "Seize the opportunity of my prayer," "Many of the people pray for me," it indicates that he has no need of his prayer, not to show the abundance of prayer for him. So it is likewise here.

**The fourth issue:** He said *la tughni shafa'atuhum* (لا تُغْنِي شَفاعَتُهُمْ, "their intercession avails nothing") and did not say *la yashfa'una* (لا يَشْفَعُونَ, "they do not intercede"), although their claim was that these are their intercessors, not that their intercession benefits or avails. And He said in other places: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255], thus negating intercession without permission. And He said: ﴿You have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾ [al-An'am 6:51], negating the intercessor. Here He negated the availing. We say: they used to say "these are our intercessors," and they believed in the benefit of their intercession, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that they may bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [az-Zumar 39:3]. Then we say that negating their claim contains a great benefit. As for negating their claim, it is because they said: "The idols intercede for us with an intercession that brings near and avails," so He said: ﴿their intercession avails nothing﴾, as proven by the fact that the intercession of the angels does not avail. As for the benefit, it is that when He made an exception by His words ﴿except after Allah gives permission﴾, meaning that then they would intercede, this did not show whether it is accepted and avails or is not accepted. But when He said: ﴿their intercession avails nothing﴾ and then said: ﴿except after Allah gives permission﴾, its meaning becomes that it does avail, and so good tidings are achieved. For He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir 40:7], and He said: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for whoever is on the earth﴾ [ash-Shura 42:5]. And seeking forgiveness is a form of intercession.

As for His words ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255], the intended meaning is not the negation of intercession and its acceptance, as in this verse, where He refuted their statement. Rather the intended meaning is the greatness of Allah, exalted is He, and that no one speaks in His presence or utters a word, as in His words: ﴿They will not speak except those whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ [an-Naba 78:38].

**The fifth issue:** The *lam* (لام, "for") in His words ﴿for whom He wills and is pleased with﴾ (لِمَن يَشاءُ ويَرْضى) may bear two interpretations:

One: it is connected to the permission (*idhn*). This has two ways. The first: it is said, "except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills among the angels to intercede for whom He wills, and is pleased with." The second: the permission is regarding the one for whom intercession is made, because permission has been granted to all to intercede for the believers, since they all ask forgiveness for them, so there is no sense in specification. But this may be disputed.

The second: it is connected to the availing, meaning: "except after Allah gives them permission to intercede, and their intercession avails for whom He wills." It may be said that this is far-fetched, because that requires the angels to intercede, and the availing occurs only for whom He wills. It is answered that the point is to draw attention to the meaning of the greatness of Allah, exalted is He, for when an angel intercedes, Allah, exalted is He, according to His will after their intercession, forgives whom He wills.

**The sixth issue:** What is the benefit of His words ﴿and is pleased with﴾ (ويَرْضى)? We say that in it there is the benefit of guidance. For when He said ﴿for whom He wills﴾, the one under obligation was uncertain, not knowing His will, so He said ﴿and is pleased with﴾, so that he might know that it is the one who worships and is grateful, not the stubborn disbeliever. For He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need from you, and He does not approve disbelief for His servants; but if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾ [az-Zumar 39:7]. So it is as if He said: "for whom He wills," then said: "and is pleased with," as an explanation of whom He wills.

Another answer, according to our statement "their intercession avails nothing of whom He wills," is that the subject of "is pleased with," understood from "for whom He wills," is as if He said: "and he is pleased," meaning the intercession benefits him with something good, so that his pleasure is achieved by it. Likewise He said: "and he is pleased," meaning the intercession benefits him. In that case "is pleased with" serves as an explanation, for when He said ﴿their intercession avails nothing﴾, indicating the negation of every little and much, it followed by way of the exception that their intercession avails something, even if little. And the one for whom intercession is made is pleased, so that it is known that it avails more than what is implied by the exception.

It may also be said that ﴿and is pleased with﴾ is to clarify that His word "wills" (يَشاءُ) does not mean the will which is approval. For when Allah, exalted is He, wills misguidance for a servant, He is not pleased with it, and when He wills guidance, He is pleased. So He said: ﴿for whom He wills and is pleased with﴾, so that it may be known that the will is not the general will, but the specific one.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females.﴾ We have already explained this in Surah al-Tur and used this verse as evidence, and we will mention here what is close to it, so we say: ﴿Those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ are those who do not believe in the messengers and do not follow the Sharia, but only follow what they claim is reason. They say that the names of God Most High are not tawqifiyya (fixed by revelation), and they say that the child is what is produced from another, and they cite the saying of the lexicographers: "So-and-so is produced from such-and-such," as in "glass is produced (yatawallad) from brick," meaning it is found from it. The same is said of "daughter of the vine" and "daughter of the mountain." Then they said: the angels were brought into existence by God Most High, so they are His offspring in the sense of bringing into existence. Then they saw that the angels have the feminine ta' (tā' al-ta'nīth), and it was valid in their view to say "the angels prostrated" (sajadat), so they said: "daughters of God." So He said: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females﴾, i.e., just as females are named "daughters" (banāt). And in this there are issues:

The first issue: How can it be said that they do not believe in the Hereafter when they used to say, "These are our intercessors with God," and it was their custom to tie a riding animal at the grave of one who died, believing that he would be resurrected upon it? We say the answer to this is in two respects:

One: Since they were not certain of it, they would say there is no resurrection, but if there is, then we have intercessors; this is indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will come; and if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50].

Two: They did not acknowledge the Hereafter in the [true] manner that the messengers brought.

The second issue: Some people said that "unthā" is "fu'lā" from "af'ala," and it is said of its verb "anatha" and of its agent "anīth," as in "a hadid dhakar" and "hadid anīth." The truth is that "unthā" is used in most cases otherwise, as evidenced by its plural "inath."

The third issue: Why did He say "tasmiyat al-unthā" and not "tasmiyat al-inath"? We say there are two answers to this. One is apparent and the other subtle. As for the apparent: the purpose is to specify the genus, and this word is more fitting for this context, since the end of the verses conforms to it. The subtle: if He had said "yusammūnahum tasmiyat al-inath," it could have two meanings:

One: daughters.

Two: the customary proper names for females, such as ʿĀʾisha and Ḥafṣa, for the naming of females is of that kind. So when He said "tasmiyat al-unthā," it was determined to be for the genus, which is daughter and daughters. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when they were told that the idol is inanimate and cannot intercede, and it was explained to them that the greatest kinds of creation have no intercession except by permission, they said: "We do not worship idols because they are inanimate; rather we worship the angels by worshiping them, for they are in their images, and we set them before us so that the witnessed reminds us of the unseen, and we honor the angel whom it is established is near, of great rank and high station." So God Most High replied to them: "How do you honor them when you name them with the naming of females?" Then He mentioned their basis for this, which is the word "angels," and He did not say "those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the naming of females," but He said: ﴿name the angels﴾. They were deceived by the ta' (tā'), and their deception is false, because the ta' comes for meanings other than true feminine gender, and "bint" is not applied except to the truly feminine by absolute usage, and the ta' in it is to emphasize the meaning of plurality, as in ṣayāqila, and it resembles that ta'. This is because "malā'ika" is, in the commonly held view, the plural of "malak," and "malak" is a contraction of "malāk" with the hamza removed, and "al-mal'ak" is a transposition of "al-ma'lak" from "al-ulūka," which is the message. So "malā'ika" on this view is "mafā'ila," the original being "mafāʿil," and it was returned to "malā'ika" in the plural, so it resembles "fa'ā'il" and "fa'ā'ila." The apparent view is that "malā'ika" is "fa'ā'il," the plural of "malīkī," a nisba to "al-Malīk," as evidenced by God's words: ﴿in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Qamar: 55] in the promise to the believers, and He said in describing the angels: ﴿But those who are with your Lord﴾ [Fussilat: 38], and He also said in the promise: ﴿And indeed for him with Us is a near station﴾ [Sad: 40], and He said in describing the angels: ﴿nor the near angels﴾ [al-Nisa': 172]. So they are then honored servants whom God has singled out with greater nearness, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6], like the command of kings and attendants at the courts of sultans who stand at their doors waiting for an order to come to them. So they are attributed to the Sovereign, the All-Powerful, in the present state, so they are "malīkiyyūn" and "malā'ika." The ta' is then for the nisba in the plural, as in "al-sayārifa" and "al-bayāṭira."

If it is said that this is false in several respects:

The first: no one was used with "malīkī" for one of them as "ṣayrafī" is used.

The second: a human, when he comes to be near God Most High, must be of the angels, and this is not so, because what is understood by "malā'ika" is a genus other than the human.

The third: "fa'ā'ila" in the plural of "fa'īlī" has not been heard; rather it is said "fa'īla," as one says "jā'a bil-namīma" and "al-ḥaqība."

The fourth: if this were so, "malak" would not have been pluralized.

We say:

The answer to the first: As for the non-use of its singular, this is conceded, and it is for a reason: the more exalted a king is, the more his rule, servants and retinue are numerous; when he is described with greatness he is described with plurality, so it is said "the owner of a large army," and he is not described with a singular as a description of honor. As for that singular, if it is attributed to the Sovereign, it is specified for the predicate, by saying "this is malīkī," and that is when its identity is known, so you make it the subject and inform about it with "malīkī." The angels were not known by their individual identities except a few of them, such as Jibrīl and Mīkā'īl, and then there is no benefit in our saying "Jibrīl is malīkī," because the predicate defines... and the copula is not formed except to show the predicate's establishment for the subject, so one does not say of a human "animal" or "body," because that is an obvious clarification, except that it is used for giving an example or in a rare form for a purpose. As for being attributed to the Sovereign while being the subject, this is not so, because the greatness lies in one saying "one of the angels," thereby indicating the multitude of those near to Him, just as you say "one of the companions of the king," and you do not say "the companion of the king." So when you want the utmost honor, for the singular it uses the name "malak" unattributed, rather it is placed for its intensity and strength, as God Most High said: ﴿possessor of strength﴾ and ﴿possessor of power﴾, so He said: ﴿Mighty in strength﴾, and "m-l-k" indicates intensity in its permutations, as is known. And for the plural it uses "malā'ika" for honor, as He said: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

The answer to the second: We say the name may at first be for an attribute specific to some of those who have it, and another who comes to have that attribute is not named with that name, like "dābba," which is "fā'ila" from "dabba." One does not call a woman who has a "dabb" (a kind of walk) a "dābba" as a name, though she may be called so as a description at the time she walks with a particular walk other than the general walking common to all, as if she walked at night to take something or for other purpose. Or it is said: the angels were called angels because of their long attachment and standing before the creation of Adam by years whose number none knows but God. Whoever has not reached God and stands at His door does not attain the covenant and attachment, so he is not named with that name.

The answer to the third: We say: regular plurals have no impediment, like "fi'āl" as the plural of "fa'al," such as "jibāl" and "thimār," and "af'āl" such as "athqāl" and "ashjār," and "fa'lān" and others. As for what is heard, even if it came only rarely, it suffices with what it contains of exaltation through attributing plurality to any but God's door, and it is of the type of "al-mar'a" and "al-nisā'."

The answer to the fourth: The denial, and perhaps this is from it; or we say "fa'īlī" was treated as "fa'īl" in the plural, just as "fay'il" was treated as "fa'īl" in the plural, so it is said in the plural of "jayyid" "jiyād," and one does not say "afā'il" of "fa'īl." What supports what we have mentioned is that Iblis, while he was standing at the door, was within the group of angels. So we say God's words: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis﴾ [al-Baqara: 34] — when he was turned away and expelled, he went out from them and became one of the jinn.

As for what some lexicographers said, that "malā'ika" is the plural of "mal'ak," and the original of "mal'ak" is "ma'lak" from "al-ulūka," which is the message, there are contrivances in it much more than what we have mentioned. Among them: "malak" is not "fa'al" but "maf'al," and this is contrary to the apparent. And why was "ma'ālik" not used in its original form, like "ma'ārib," "ma'āthim," "ma'ākil," and others, which are only counted with contrivance? Among them: why was "malak" made "mal'ak," and this was not done with its siblings we have mentioned? Among them: why was the ta' attached to its plural, and why was it not said "malā'ik" as in the plural of every "maf'al"? And what refutes their view is His words: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1]: they are other than the messengers, so it is not valid to say "the angels were made messengers," just as it is not valid to say "the messengers were made sent ones," or "the near one was made near," because making (ja'l) necessarily involves change. And among what indicates the opposite of what they said is that all of them are attributed to Him, standing before Him, awaiting His command, for orders come upon them.

[Page 268]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they have no knowledge of it. They follow only conjecture﴾. There are several views on what the pronoun in (bihi, "of it") refers back to:

First: what al-Zamakhshari reported, namely that it refers to what they used to say without knowledge.

Second: that it refers to what preceded in the previous verse, "knowledge" (ʿilm), meaning: they have no knowledge of God, so that they associate partners with Him. It was also read as "ma lahum bihā" ("they have no knowledge of it"). This reading also has several views:

First: they have no knowledge of the Hereafter.

Second: they have no knowledge of the naming (al-tasmiyah).

Third: they have no knowledge of the angels. If we say ﴿He has nothing in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20], then it is an answer to what we mentioned, that although they used to say the idols are their intercessors with God, and used to tie camels at the graves of the dead so that they could ride them, yet what they said was not based on knowledge. If we say it refers to the naming, then it may be as follows: knowledge of the naming is available to them, for they know that they are not in doubt, since the naming may be a primary imposition (waḍʿ awwalī), and that is not by conjecture but by knowledge that it is an imposition. It may also be a figurative usage (istiʿmāl maʿnawī), which admits of truth, falsehood and knowledge. An example of the first: whoever first assigned the name "sky" to its referent and said, "this is a sky." An example of the second: if after that we say to water and stone, "this is a sky," then it is false, and whoever believes it is ignorant. Likewise their saying about the angels that they are "daughters of God" was not a naming by imposition; they only meant that they are described by a quality that makes it necessary to use the word "daughters" for them. That is false, and whoever believes it is ignorant. This is what is meant by our statement that conjecture is followed in matters of benefit (maṣlaḥah), in customary or legal actions, when certainty cannot be reached. As for beliefs (iʿtiqādāt), conjecture gives nothing of the truth at all.

If it is said: does conjecture not sometimes hit the mark? How then can it be judged that it gives nothing at all? We say: the responsible person (al-mukallaf) needs a certainty that distinguishes truth from falsehood, so that he believes the truth, and distinguishes good from evil, so that he does good. However, regarding truth, one must be decisive in believing what corresponds to it, and the one who conjectures is not decisive. Regarding good, conjecture is sometimes taken into account in certain cases. It is also possible to say that the intended meaning of "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) is God, the Exalted, and the meaning is that conjecture gives nothing of God, the Exalted; that is, the divine attributes are not derived by conjectures. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿That is because God is the Truth﴾ [al-Hajj: 6].

There is a subtle point here: God, the Exalted, prohibited conjecture in three places, and in all those places the prohibition came directly after naming and calling upon something by a name. Two of them are in this surah. The first is His saying: ﴿They are only names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority. They follow only conjecture﴾. The second is His saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture, and conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾. The third is in al-Hujurat, where God said: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames. Wretched is the name of defiance after belief. And whoever does not repent, it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and then: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of conjecture﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12], following the calling by the heart. All of this is evidence that guarding the tongue is more important than guarding the other members, and that lying is more ugly than the visible evil deeds of the hands and feet.

These three places involve: first, praising one who does not deserve praise, such as al-Lat and al-Uzza, derived from "al-ʿizz" (might). Second, blaming one who does not deserve blame, namely the angels, who are the servants of the Merciful, whom they name with the designation of females. Third, blaming one whose condition is not known. As for praising one whose condition is not known, He did not say concerning him "they follow only conjecture"; rather, conjecture is taken into account in that case, and acting upon the outward condition of a sane person is obligatory.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So turn away from him who turns away from Our remembrance and desires none but the worldly life﴾. That is, leave off arguing with them, for you have conveyed and done what was incumbent upon you. Most of the exegetes say that every instance of His saying "fa-aʿriḍ" (so turn away) in the Qur'an is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of killing. This is false, for the command to turn away agrees with the verse of fighting, so how could it be abrogated by it? This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to call with wisdom and good admonition. When they opposed him with their falsehoods, it was said to him: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. Then, when that did not benefit, his Lord said to him: "Turn away from them and do not confront them with proof and evidence, for they follow only conjecture and do not follow the truth. Confront them with turning away from debate, on the condition that confronting is permissible." So how could it be abrogated? The turning away (iʿrāḍ) is of the pattern of "ashkāhu" (he made him complain), and the hamzah in it is for negation (li-l-salb), as if He said: "remove the presentation (ʿarḍ)," and do not present any matter to them after this.

His saying ﴿from him who turns away from Our remembrance﴾ explains the priority of the benefit of presentation and debate, for how can one who does not listen to speech understand its meaning?

Concerning "dhikrinā" (Our remembrance) there are several views:

First: the Qur'an.

Second: the proof and evidence.

Third: the remembrance of God, the Exalted, for one who does not reflect on a thing cannot know its attributes. They used to say: "We do not reflect upon the bounties of God, because we have no connection to God; our affair is only with the one who created us," meaning the angels, or time (al-dahr), according to the differences in their sayings and the diversity of their falsehoods.

His saying ﴿and desires none but the worldly life﴾ is an allusion to their denial of the Gathering (al-ḥashr), as they said: ﴿There is only our worldly life﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Are you pleased with the worldly life?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], meaning they did not affirm anything beyond it for which they would work. So His saying ﴿from him who turns away from Our remembrance﴾ is an allusion to their denial of the Gathering, for when one abandons reflection upon the bounties of God, the Exalted, he does not know Him, so he does not follow His Messenger, and so his speech does not benefit him. And when one does not affirm the Gathering and the Reckoning, he does not fear, so he does not turn back from what he is upon. Then there remains no benefit in calling.

Know that the Prophet (ﷺ) was a physician of hearts, and he proceeded according to the order of physicians. Their order is that when a condition can be remedied by nourishment, they do not use medicine; and when it can be remedied by a weak medicine, they do not use a strong one. Then, when they are unable to treat by drinks and other things, they turn to the knife and cautery, and it is said: the last of the remedies is cautery. The Prophet (ﷺ) first commanded the hearts to remember God only, for "by the remembrance of God hearts are at rest" [al-Ra'd: 28], just as by nourishment souls are at rest. So remembrance is the nourishment of the heart. For this reason he first said: "Say: there is no god but God." He commanded remembrance for those who benefited, such as Abu Bakr and others who benefited. For those who did not benefit, he mentioned the proof to them and said: ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾ [al-A'raf: 184], ﴿Say: look﴾ [Yunus: 101], ﴿Will they not look?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17], and other such things. Then he brought the threat and the warning. When these did not benefit them, He said: turn away from the treatment, and cut off the corrupt so that it does not corrupt the good.

The twenty-eighth part is complete, and after it comes the twenty-ninth part, whose beginning is the interpretation of His saying (That is the extent of their knowledge).
