Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge﴾. There are several views concerning "dhālika" (that):

First: the most apparent is that it refers to conjecture, meaning: the furthest that they reach with it is that they act upon conjecture.

Second: the preference of the worldly life is the extent of their knowledge, meaning that preference is the furthest they have attained of knowledge.

Third: ﴿So turn away from him who turns away﴾ [al-Najm: 29]. That turning away is the furthest that they have attained of knowledge. Knowledge here would mean knowledge of the known (al-ʿilm bi-l-maʿlūm), and the alif and lam would be for definition, and the knowledge of the known is what is in the Qur'an. The explanation of this is that when the Qur'an came, some of them received it with acceptance and their chests were expanded, so they reached the utmost goal. Some of them accepted it because it is a miracle and followed the Messenger, so they reached the middle rank. Some of them hesitated about it, like Abu Talib, and that is the lowest of the ranks. Some of them rejected it and found fault with it. The first group could not be turned away from, while the others had to be turned away from. The place of its reaching knowledge is that it cut off speech with him; turning away from him is the placement of the knowledge. There is an objection to this, namely: God has explained that their furthest extent is that: ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. The insane person who has no knowledge and the child are not commanded beyond their capacity, so how does God punish them?

We say: it was mentioned before that they turned away from the remembrance of God. So their lack of knowledge is due to their not accepting knowledge. God decreed their turning away so that ignorance would be attributed to that, thereby confirming the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is the extent of their knowledge" is a parenthetical statement between two statements, and the connected one is His saying: ﴿So turn away from him who turns away from Our remembrance and desires none but the worldly life﴾ ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge. Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾ [al-Najm: 29–30]. According to what we have mentioned, the intended meaning is not complete except with it. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Turn away from them, for that is their furthest extent, and there is nothing beyond what has appeared from them." And His saying ﴿from him who turns away﴾ is an allusion to cutting off their excuse through ignorance, for the ignorance was by their turning away and their preference of the immediate.

Then He began and said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾. Concerning the connection (al-munāsabah) there are several views:

First: when He said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Turn away," and the Prophet (ﷺ) was very eager for the faith of his people, and it sometimes occurred to his mind that there might still be benefit in the reminder, and that perhaps other people among the disbelievers might believe without fighting, He said to him: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾. He knows that no one among the responsible persons will believe merely by calling, and that what benefits them is that the sword and fighting should strike. So turn away from debate and turn to fighting. On this view, His saying ﴿and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ means: He knew in eternity who would go astray in His decree and who would be guided, so the two matters are not confused for Him, and there is no harm in turning away, and it is considered in custom to be a benefit.

Second: it is in the sense of His saying: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord will judge between us﴾ [al-A'raf: 87]. Its meaning is that they used to say: "We are upon guidance and you are the falsifiers." The Prophet (ﷺ) established the proof against them, but it did not benefit them. So He, exalted is He, said: "Turn away from them, and your reward has fallen upon God, for He knows that you are guided and He knows that they are astray." When two disputants argue before a powerful king, their aim is that the matter become manifest before the king. If the opponent acknowledges the truth, that is well; otherwise the purpose of the one who is right becomes manifest before the king. So He, exalted is He, said: "You have argued and done well, and God is most knowing of the one who is right from the one who is false."

Third: when He, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to turn away, and great harm had come from them, and the Prophet (ﷺ) bore it in hope that they would believe, all of that was abrogated. When they did not believe, it was as if He said: "My striving and my bearing of their harm has fallen as dust." So God, exalted is He, said: Indeed God knows the condition of those who misguide and those who are guided: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did, and recompense those who did good﴾ [al-Najm: 31], from among the guided. In this there are several issues.

First issue: ﴿huwa﴾ (He) is called ʿimād (a support pronoun) and faṣl (a separator). If he had said "inna rabbaka aʿlam" (indeed your Lord is more knowing), the sentence would have been complete. However, when the sentence is free of this ʿimād, the hearer may sometimes pause to hear what follows, to know whether "aʿlam" is the predicate of "rabbaka" or whether it is with something else as the predicate. For example, if one said: "inna Zaydan aʿlamu minhu ʿAmrun" (indeed Zayd, ʿAmr is more knowing than him), then the predicate of Zayd would be the sentence that follows. But if he says ﴿huwa aʿlam﴾ (He is most knowing), that suspicion is removed.

**The second issue: "a'lam" requires a comparative object.** It is said: Zayd is a'lam (more knowing) than 'Amr; God is a'lam than whom? We say: af'al often comes in the sense of 'alim (knowing), not that there is any other knower like Him. In that case, if there is a knower, then that is the one compared against; and if there is not, then in reality He is the only knower. In many places, af'al in the attributes of God has this meaning. It is said: Allah is Akbar (the Greatest), and in reality there is nothing greater like Him, nor anything greater than Him except Him. What fits this is that it occurs in supplications: "O Most Generous of the generous" (ya akram al-akramin), as if he said: there is no one more generous than You; in reality there is no one more generous than Him. This is the meaning of the statement of those who say that a'lam means 'alim (knowing) with regard to the guided and the astray. It may also be said: He is more knowing than every knower, on the assumption of another knower.

**The third issue: "'alimtuhu" and "'alimtu bihi" are both used.** God, Exalted, said in al-An'am: ﴿He knows best who strays from His way﴾. Then the knowing that is meant by the object should be the knowing whose connection to the object is stronger, either because the knowing is stronger, or because the object is manifest, or to emphasize the obligation of knowing it, or because the action itself has strength. As for the strength of knowing, it is as in His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and He said: ﴿Does he not know that God sees?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14]. Since God's knowledge is complete and all-encompassing, He connected it directly to the object, which is a state of His servant, who is before Him, without a preposition. Since the servant's knowledge is weak and temporal, he connected it to the object, which is an attribute of God Exalted, which human knowledge does not encompass, by means of a preposition. Or, since God's seeing is not something perceived or witnessed by the senses, the verb was connected to the object directly, and to the other by means of a preposition. As for the manifestness of the object, it is as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not know that God extends provision to whom He wills?﴾ [al-Zumar: 52], and it is an evident, manifest matter. As for emphasizing the obligation of knowing it, as in His saying: ﴿So know that there is no god but God﴾ [Muhammad: 19]. It may be said that this belongs to the category of the manifest. Likewise His saying: ﴿And know that you cannot escape God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2]. As for the strength of the action, God Exalted said: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and He said: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) nearly...﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Since the word used is an attribute of the action, He connected it to the object without a preposition. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who...﴾, just as the word used is a noun denoting an action, whose governing power is weakened by its connection to the object.

**The fourth issue: the knowledge of "who has gone astray" is placed before the knowledge of "the guided" in many places,** among them in Surat al-An'am, and among them in Surat (Nun) [al-Qalam], and among them in this surah (al-Najm), because in all these places the one mentioned is His Prophet ﷺ and the obstinate opponents. So He mentioned them first, as a threat to them and as consolation to the heart of His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

**The fifth issue: in one place He said: ﴿He knows best who strays from His way﴾, and in another He said: ﴿who has gone astray﴾.** Do you have anything on this? I say: Yes. We clarify this with a rational argument and another transmitted one. As for the rational: the eternal knowledge relates to the known as it is. If something existed yesterday, it is known that it existed yesterday during yesterday. This is unlike our knowledge, where a thing may have occurred yesterday and we do not know it except today. Rather: ﴿Nothing escapes Him, the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Saba': 3], and what occurs is not delayed from His knowledge even for the blink of an eye. As for the transmitted argument: the active participle (ism al-fa'il) works as the verb does when it has the sense of the future, and does not work as the verb does when it is in the past. So you do not say: "I am striking Zayd yesterday." What is required, if you want it to govern an object, is to say: "I struck Zayd." And if you use the active participle, then the required form is the genitive construction (idafah). You say: "Striker of Zayd yesterday, I am," and it is permissible to say: "I am striking Zayd tomorrow." The reason for this is that when an action has occurred, it has no renewal outside the future, and no realization in the present, so it is nonexistent and too weak to govern. As for the present and what is anticipated, it has existence, so it is possible for it to govern. Since this is established, we say: When he said "dalla" (he went astray), the matter was in the past, and His knowledge was connected to it at the time of its existence, so it was known. His saying "a'lam" means 'alim (knowing), so it becomes as if he said: knowing of who has gone astray. So if he dropped the preposition, it would be governing the active participle in the sense of the past. When He said "yadilla" (goes astray), He knows the straying at the moment it occurs, even though He knew in eternity that he would stray. However, after that, knowledge has another connection which will come into existence, namely its connection to the straying having occurred and taken place, which was not in eternity. For it is not said: God knew in eternity that so-and-so had gone astray. Rather the correct statement is: it was known in eternity that he would stray, so that it is as if He knows that he goes astray, and the active participle is then in the sense of the future and works as the verb does. Thus it is not said: "Zayd is more knowing our question than 'Amr." Rather the required form is: "Zayd is more knowing of our question than 'Amr." For this reason the grammarians said regarding Surat al-An'am: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who goes astray﴾ means: He knows who goes astray. They also said: "a'lam" for the elative (tafdil, comparative) is formed only from an intransitive verb; if it is transitive, it is reduced to an intransitive one. Our saying "'alima" is as if it were from the pattern "'ulima" with a damma, and likewise in the exclamative when we say: "ma a'lamahu bi-kadha" (how knowing he is of such-and-such), as if it were from an intransitive verb.

As for me, I have answered this by saying that His saying ﴿most knowing of who goes astray﴾ means: knowing (alim). We have already presented what must be believed about the attributes of God, that for the most part it means that He is knowing, and there is no one knowing like Him, so a'lam is in its real sense. This is better than saying: it means simply knowing and nothing more. If it is asked: Why did He say here "bi-man dalla" (of who has gone astray) and there "yadilla" (goes astray)? We say: Because here the straying happened in the past, and it was confirmed when the Messenger's despair occurred and he was commanded to turn away. As for there, God Exalted had said previously: ﴿If you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God﴾ [al-An'am: 116].

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who goes astray﴾, meaning: if you go astray, God knows you, so the straying was not occurring in Him, and therefore He did not use the past form.

**The sixth issue: He said "from His way" with regard to straying, and did not say "to His way" with regard to guidance.** This is because straying from the way is straying itself, and it is sufficient for straying, since straying occurs only on the way; but after arrival there is no straying. Or because whoever strays from His way does not reach the intended goal, whether he has traveled a road or not. As for whoever is guided to a road, there is no arrival unless he travels it. This is supported by the fact that whoever strays in other than His way is astray, and whoever is guided to it is not guided unless he is guided to every matter whose ignorance harms faith. So certain guidance is absolute guidance, and therefore He said: ﴿of those who are guided﴾ and said: ﴿the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 117].

[Page 268]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they have no knowledge of it. They follow only conjecture﴾. There are several views on what the pronoun in (bihi, "of it") refers back to:

First: what al-Zamakhshari reported, namely that it refers to what they used to say without knowledge.

Second: that it refers to what preceded in the previous verse, "knowledge" (ʿilm), meaning: they have no knowledge of God, so that they associate partners with Him. It was also read as "ma lahum bihā" ("they have no knowledge of it"). This reading also has several views:

First: they have no knowledge of the Hereafter.

Second: they have no knowledge of the naming (al-tasmiyah).

Third: they have no knowledge of the angels. If we say ﴿He has nothing in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20], then it is an answer to what we mentioned, that although they used to say the idols are their intercessors with God, and used to tie camels at the graves of the dead so that they could ride them, yet what they said was not based on knowledge. If we say it refers to the naming, then it may be as follows: knowledge of the naming is available to them, for they know that they are not in doubt, since the naming may be a primary imposition (waḍʿ awwalī), and that is not by conjecture but by knowledge that it is an imposition. It may also be a figurative usage (istiʿmāl maʿnawī), which admits of truth, falsehood and knowledge. An example of the first: whoever first assigned the name "sky" to its referent and said, "this is a sky." An example of the second: if after that we say to water and stone, "this is a sky," then it is false, and whoever believes it is ignorant. Likewise their saying about the angels that they are "daughters of God" was not a naming by imposition; they only meant that they are described by a quality that makes it necessary to use the word "daughters" for them. That is false, and whoever believes it is ignorant. This is what is meant by our statement that conjecture is followed in matters of benefit (maṣlaḥah), in customary or legal actions, when certainty cannot be reached. As for beliefs (iʿtiqādāt), conjecture gives nothing of the truth at all.

If it is said: does conjecture not sometimes hit the mark? How then can it be judged that it gives nothing at all? We say: the responsible person (al-mukallaf) needs a certainty that distinguishes truth from falsehood, so that he believes the truth, and distinguishes good from evil, so that he does good. However, regarding truth, one must be decisive in believing what corresponds to it, and the one who conjectures is not decisive. Regarding good, conjecture is sometimes taken into account in certain cases. It is also possible to say that the intended meaning of "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) is God, the Exalted, and the meaning is that conjecture gives nothing of God, the Exalted; that is, the divine attributes are not derived by conjectures. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿That is because God is the Truth﴾ [al-Hajj: 6].

There is a subtle point here: God, the Exalted, prohibited conjecture in three places, and in all those places the prohibition came directly after naming and calling upon something by a name. Two of them are in this surah. The first is His saying: ﴿They are only names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority. They follow only conjecture﴾. The second is His saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture, and conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾. The third is in al-Hujurat, where God said: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames. Wretched is the name of defiance after belief. And whoever does not repent, it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and then: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of conjecture﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12], following the calling by the heart. All of this is evidence that guarding the tongue is more important than guarding the other members, and that lying is more ugly than the visible evil deeds of the hands and feet.

These three places involve: first, praising one who does not deserve praise, such as al-Lat and al-Uzza, derived from "al-ʿizz" (might). Second, blaming one who does not deserve blame, namely the angels, who are the servants of the Merciful, whom they name with the designation of females. Third, blaming one whose condition is not known. As for praising one whose condition is not known, He did not say concerning him "they follow only conjecture"; rather, conjecture is taken into account in that case, and acting upon the outward condition of a sane person is obligatory.

He knows that no one among the responsible persons will believe merely by calling, and that what benefits them is that the sword and fighting should strike. So turn away from debate and turn to fighting. On this view, His saying ﴿and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ means: He knew in eternity who would go astray in His decree and who would be guided, so the two matters are not confused for Him, and there is no harm in turning away, and it is considered in custom to be a benefit.

Second: it is in the sense of His saying: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord will judge between us﴾ [al-A'raf: 87]. Its meaning is that they used to say: "We are upon guidance and you are the falsifiers." The Prophet (ﷺ) established the proof against them, but it did not benefit them. So He, exalted is He, said: "Turn away from them, and your reward has fallen upon God, for He knows that you are guided and He knows that they are astray." When two disputants argue before a powerful king, their aim is that the matter become manifest before the king. If the opponent acknowledges the truth, that is well; otherwise the purpose of the one who is right becomes manifest before the king. So He, exalted is He, said: "You have argued and done well, and God is most knowing of the one who is right from the one who is false."

Third: when He, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to turn away, and great harm had come from them, and the Prophet (ﷺ) bore it in hope that they would believe, all of that was abrogated. When they did not believe, it was as if He said: "My striving and my bearing of their harm has fallen as dust." So God, exalted is He, said: Indeed God knows the condition of those who misguide and those who are guided: ﴿And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did, and recompense those who did good﴾ [al-Najm: 31], from among the guided. In this there are several issues.

First issue: ﴿huwa﴾ (He) is called ʿimād (a support pronoun) and faṣl (a separator). If he had said "inna rabbaka aʿlam" (indeed your Lord is more knowing), the sentence would have been complete. However, when the sentence is free of this ʿimād, the hearer may sometimes pause to hear what follows, to know whether "aʿlam" is the predicate of "rabbaka" or whether it is with something else as the predicate. For example, if one said: "inna Zaydan aʿlamu minhu ʿAmrun" (indeed Zayd, ʿAmr is more knowing than him), then the predicate of Zayd would be the sentence that follows. But if he says ﴿huwa aʿlam﴾ (He is most knowing), that suspicion is removed.

**The second issue: "a'lam" requires a comparative object.** It is said: Zayd is a'lam (more knowing) than 'Amr; God is a'lam than whom? We say: af'al often comes in the sense of 'alim (knowing), not that there is any other knower like Him. In that case, if there is a knower, then that is the one compared against; and if there is not, then in reality He is the only knower. In many places, af'al in the attributes of God has this meaning. It is said: Allah is Akbar (the Greatest), and in reality there is nothing greater like Him, nor anything greater than Him except Him. What fits this is that it occurs in supplications: "O Most Generous of the generous" (ya akram al-akramin), as if he said: there is no one more generous than You; in reality there is no one more generous than Him. This is the meaning of the statement of those who say that a'lam means 'alim (knowing) with regard to the guided and the astray. It may also be said: He is more knowing than every knower, on the assumption of another knower.

**The third issue: "'alimtuhu" and "'alimtu bihi" are both used.** God, Exalted, said in al-An'am: ﴿He knows best who strays from His way﴾. Then the knowing that is meant by the object should be the knowing whose connection to the object is stronger, either because the knowing is stronger, or because the object is manifest, or to emphasize the obligation of knowing it, or because the action itself has strength. As for the strength of knowing, it is as in His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and He said: ﴿Does he not know that God sees?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14]. Since God's knowledge is complete and all-encompassing, He connected it directly to the object, which is a state of His servant, who is before Him, without a preposition. Since the servant's knowledge is weak and temporal, he connected it to the object, which is an attribute of God Exalted, which human knowledge does not encompass, by means of a preposition. Or, since God's seeing is not something perceived or witnessed by the senses, the verb was connected to the object directly, and to the other by means of a preposition. As for the manifestness of the object, it is as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not know that God extends provision to whom He wills?﴾ [al-Zumar: 52], and it is an evident, manifest matter. As for emphasizing the obligation of knowing it, as in His saying: ﴿So know that there is no god but God﴾ [Muhammad: 19]. It may be said that this belongs to the category of the manifest. Likewise His saying: ﴿And know that you cannot escape God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2]. As for the strength of the action, God Exalted said: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and He said: ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) nearly...﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Since the word used is an attribute of the action, He connected it to the object without a preposition. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who...﴾, just as the word used is a noun denoting an action, whose governing power is weakened by its connection to the object.

**The fourth issue: the knowledge of "who has gone astray" is placed before the knowledge of "the guided" in many places,** among them in Surat al-An'am, and among them in Surat (Nun) [al-Qalam], and among them in this surah (al-Najm), because in all these places the one mentioned is His Prophet ﷺ and the obstinate opponents. So He mentioned them first, as a threat to them and as consolation to the heart of His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

**The fifth issue: in one place He said: ﴿He knows best who strays from His way﴾, and in another He said: ﴿who has gone astray﴾.** Do you have anything on this? I say: Yes. We clarify this with a rational argument and another transmitted one. As for the rational: the eternal knowledge relates to the known as it is. If something existed yesterday, it is known that it existed yesterday during yesterday. This is unlike our knowledge, where a thing may have occurred yesterday and we do not know it except today. Rather: ﴿Nothing escapes Him, the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Saba': 3], and what occurs is not delayed from His knowledge even for the blink of an eye. As for the transmitted argument: the active participle (ism al-fa'il) works as the verb does when it has the sense of the future, and does not work as the verb does when it is in the past. So you do not say: "I am striking Zayd yesterday." What is required, if you want it to govern an object, is to say: "I struck Zayd." And if you use the active participle, then the required form is the genitive construction (idafah). You say: "Striker of Zayd yesterday, I am," and it is permissible to say: "I am striking Zayd tomorrow." The reason for this is that when an action has occurred, it has no renewal outside the future, and no realization in the present, so it is nonexistent and too weak to govern. As for the present and what is anticipated, it has existence, so it is possible for it to govern. Since this is established, we say: When he said "dalla" (he went astray), the matter was in the past, and His knowledge was connected to it at the time of its existence, so it was known. His saying "a'lam" means 'alim (knowing), so it becomes as if he said: knowing of who has gone astray. So if he dropped the preposition, it would be governing the active participle in the sense of the past. When He said "yadilla" (goes astray), He knows the straying at the moment it occurs, even though He knew in eternity that he would stray. However, after that, knowledge has another connection which will come into existence, namely its connection to the straying having occurred and taken place, which was not in eternity. For it is not said: God knew in eternity that so-and-so had gone astray. Rather the correct statement is: it was known in eternity that he would stray, so that it is as if He knows that he goes astray, and the active participle is then in the sense of the future and works as the verb does. Thus it is not said: "Zayd is more knowing our question than 'Amr." Rather the required form is: "Zayd is more knowing of our question than 'Amr." For this reason the grammarians said regarding Surat al-An'am: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who goes astray﴾ means: He knows who goes astray. They also said: "a'lam" for the elative (tafdil, comparative) is formed only from an intransitive verb; if it is transitive, it is reduced to an intransitive one. Our saying "'alima" is as if it were from the pattern "'ulima" with a damma, and likewise in the exclamative when we say: "ma a'lamahu bi-kadha" (how knowing he is of such-and-such), as if it were from an intransitive verb.

As for me, I have answered this by saying that His saying ﴿most knowing of who goes astray﴾ means: knowing (alim). We have already presented what must be believed about the attributes of God, that for the most part it means that He is knowing, and there is no one knowing like Him, so a'lam is in its real sense. This is better than saying: it means simply knowing and nothing more. If it is asked: Why did He say here "bi-man dalla" (of who has gone astray) and there "yadilla" (goes astray)? We say: Because here the straying happened in the past, and it was confirmed when the Messenger's despair occurred and he was commanded to turn away. As for there, God Exalted had said previously: ﴿If you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God﴾ [al-An'am: 116].

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who goes astray﴾, meaning: if you go astray, God knows you, so the straying was not occurring in Him, and therefore He did not use the past form.

**The sixth issue: He said "from His way" with regard to straying, and did not say "to His way" with regard to guidance.** This is because straying from the way is straying itself, and it is sufficient for straying, since straying occurs only on the way; but after arrival there is no straying. Or because whoever strays from His way does not reach the intended goal, whether he has traveled a road or not. As for whoever is guided to a road, there is no arrival unless he travels it. This is supported by the fact that whoever strays in other than His way is astray, and whoever is guided to it is not guided unless he is guided to every matter whose ignorance harms faith. So certain guidance is absolute guidance, and therefore He said: ﴿of those who are guided﴾ and said: ﴿the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 117].

[Page 268]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they have no knowledge of it. They follow only conjecture﴾. There are several views on what the pronoun in (bihi, "of it") refers back to:

First: what al-Zamakhshari reported, namely that it refers to what they used to say without knowledge.

Second: that it refers to what preceded in the previous verse, "knowledge" (ʿilm), meaning: they have no knowledge of God, so that they associate partners with Him. It was also read as "ma lahum bihā" ("they have no knowledge of it"). This reading also has several views:

First: they have no knowledge of the Hereafter.

Second: they have no knowledge of the naming (al-tasmiyah).

Third: they have no knowledge of the angels. If we say ﴿He has nothing in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20], then it is an answer to what we mentioned, that although they used to say the idols are their intercessors with God, and used to tie camels at the graves of the dead so that they could ride them, yet what they said was not based on knowledge. If we say it refers to the naming, then it may be as follows: knowledge of the naming is available to them, for they know that they are not in doubt, since the naming may be a primary imposition (waḍʿ awwalī), and that is not by conjecture but by knowledge that it is an imposition. It may also be a figurative usage (istiʿmāl maʿnawī), which admits of truth, falsehood and knowledge. An example of the first: whoever first assigned the name "sky" to its referent and said, "this is a sky." An example of the second: if after that we say to water and stone, "this is a sky," then it is false, and whoever believes it is ignorant. Likewise their saying about the angels that they are "daughters of God" was not a naming by imposition; they only meant that they are described by a quality that makes it necessary to use the word "daughters" for them. That is false, and whoever believes it is ignorant. This is what is meant by our statement that conjecture is followed in matters of benefit (maṣlaḥah), in customary or legal actions, when certainty cannot be reached. As for beliefs (iʿtiqādāt), conjecture gives nothing of the truth at all.

If it is said: does conjecture not sometimes hit the mark? How then can it be judged that it gives nothing at all? We say: the responsible person (al-mukallaf) needs a certainty that distinguishes truth from falsehood, so that he believes the truth, and distinguishes good from evil, so that he does good. However, regarding truth, one must be decisive in believing what corresponds to it, and the one who conjectures is not decisive. Regarding good, conjecture is sometimes taken into account in certain cases. It is also possible to say that the intended meaning of "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) is God, the Exalted, and the meaning is that conjecture gives nothing of God, the Exalted; that is, the divine attributes are not derived by conjectures. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿That is because God is the Truth﴾ [al-Hajj: 6].

There is a subtle point here: God, the Exalted, prohibited conjecture in three places, and in all those places the prohibition came directly after naming and calling upon something by a name. Two of them are in this surah. The first is His saying: ﴿They are only names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority. They follow only conjecture﴾. The second is His saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture, and conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾. The third is in al-Hujurat, where God said: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames. Wretched is the name of defiance after belief. And whoever does not repent, it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and then: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of conjecture﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12], following the calling by the heart. All of this is evidence that guarding the tongue is more important than guarding the other members, and that lying is more ugly than the visible evil deeds of the hands and feet.

These three places involve: first, praising one who does not deserve praise, such as al-Lat and al-Uzza, derived from "al-ʿizz" (might). Second, blaming one who does not deserve blame, namely the angels, who are the servants of the Merciful, whom they name with the designation of females. Third, blaming one whose condition is not known. As for praising one whose condition is not known, He did not say concerning him "they follow only conjecture"; rather, conjecture is taken into account in that case, and acting upon the outward condition of a sane person is obligatory.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So turn away from him who turns away from Our remembrance and desires none but the worldly life﴾. That is, leave off arguing with them, for you have conveyed and done what was incumbent upon you. Most of the exegetes say that every instance of His saying "fa-aʿriḍ" (so turn away) in the Qur'an is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of killing. This is false, for the command to turn away agrees with the verse of fighting, so how could it be abrogated by it? This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to call with wisdom and good admonition. When they opposed him with their falsehoods, it was said to him: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. Then, when that did not benefit, his Lord said to him: "Turn away from them and do not confront them with proof and evidence, for they follow only conjecture and do not follow the truth. Confront them with turning away from debate, on the condition that confronting is permissible." So how could it be abrogated? The turning away (iʿrāḍ) is of the pattern of "ashkāhu" (he made him complain), and the hamzah in it is for negation (li-l-salb), as if He said: "remove the presentation (ʿarḍ)," and do not present any matter to them after this.

His saying ﴿from him who turns away from Our remembrance﴾ explains the priority of the benefit of presentation and debate, for how can one who does not listen to speech understand its meaning?

Concerning "dhikrinā" (Our remembrance) there are several views:

First: the Qur'an.

Second: the proof and evidence.

Third: the remembrance of God, the Exalted, for one who does not reflect on a thing cannot know its attributes. They used to say: "We do not reflect upon the bounties of God, because we have no connection to God; our affair is only with the one who created us," meaning the angels, or time (al-dahr), according to the differences in their sayings and the diversity of their falsehoods.

His saying ﴿and desires none but the worldly life﴾ is an allusion to their denial of the Gathering (al-ḥashr), as they said: ﴿There is only our worldly life﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Are you pleased with the worldly life?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], meaning they did not affirm anything beyond it for which they would work. So His saying ﴿from him who turns away from Our remembrance﴾ is an allusion to their denial of the Gathering, for when one abandons reflection upon the bounties of God, the Exalted, he does not know Him, so he does not follow His Messenger, and so his speech does not benefit him. And when one does not affirm the Gathering and the Reckoning, he does not fear, so he does not turn back from what he is upon. Then there remains no benefit in calling.

Know that the Prophet (ﷺ) was a physician of hearts, and he proceeded according to the order of physicians. Their order is that when a condition can be remedied by nourishment, they do not use medicine; and when it can be remedied by a weak medicine, they do not use a strong one. Then, when they are unable to treat by drinks and other things, they turn to the knife and cautery, and it is said: the last of the remedies is cautery. The Prophet (ﷺ) first commanded the hearts to remember God only, for "by the remembrance of God hearts are at rest" [al-Ra'd: 28], just as by nourishment souls are at rest. So remembrance is the nourishment of the heart. For this reason he first said: "Say: there is no god but God." He commanded remembrance for those who benefited, such as Abu Bakr and others who benefited. For those who did not benefit, he mentioned the proof to them and said: ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾ [al-A'raf: 184], ﴿Say: look﴾ [Yunus: 101], ﴿Will they not look?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17], and other such things. Then he brought the threat and the warning. When these did not benefit them, He said: turn away from the treatment, and cut off the corrupt so that it does not corrupt the good.

The twenty-eighth part is complete, and after it comes the twenty-ninth part, whose beginning is the interpretation of His saying (That is the extent of their knowledge).

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge﴾. There are several views concerning "dhālika" (that):

First: the most apparent is that it refers to conjecture, meaning: the furthest that they reach with it is that they act upon conjecture.

Second: the preference of the worldly life is the extent of their knowledge, meaning that preference is the furthest they have attained of knowledge.

Third: ﴿So turn away from him who turns away﴾ [al-Najm: 29]. That turning away is the furthest that they have attained of knowledge. Knowledge here would mean knowledge of the known (al-ʿilm bi-l-maʿlūm), and the alif and lam would be for definition, and the knowledge of the known is what is in the Qur'an. The explanation of this is that when the Qur'an came, some of them received it with acceptance and their chests were expanded, so they reached the utmost goal. Some of them accepted it because it is a miracle and followed the Messenger, so they reached the middle rank. Some of them hesitated about it, like Abu Talib, and that is the lowest of the ranks. Some of them rejected it and found fault with it. The first group could not be turned away from, while the others had to be turned away from. The place of its reaching knowledge is that it cut off speech with him; turning away from him is the placement of the knowledge. There is an objection to this, namely: God has explained that their furthest extent is that: ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. The insane person who has no knowledge and the child are not commanded beyond their capacity, so how does God punish them?

We say: it was mentioned before that they turned away from the remembrance of God. So their lack of knowledge is due to their not accepting knowledge. God decreed their turning away so that ignorance would be attributed to that, thereby confirming the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is the extent of their knowledge" is a parenthetical statement between two statements, and the connected one is His saying: ﴿So turn away from him who turns away from Our remembrance and desires none but the worldly life﴾ ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge. Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾ [al-Najm: 29–30]. According to what we have mentioned, the intended meaning is not complete except with it. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Turn away from them, for that is their furthest extent, and there is nothing beyond what has appeared from them." And His saying ﴿from him who turns away﴾ is an allusion to cutting off their excuse through ignorance, for the ignorance was by their turning away and their preference of the immediate.

Then He began and said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾. Concerning the connection (al-munāsabah) there are several views:

First: when He said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Turn away," and the Prophet (ﷺ) was very eager for the faith of his people, and it sometimes occurred to his mind that there might still be benefit in the reminder, and that perhaps other people among the disbelievers might believe without fighting, He said to him: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way﴾. He knows that no one among the responsible persons will believe merely by calling, and that what benefits them is that the sword and fighting should strike. So turn away from debate and turn to fighting. On this view, His saying ﴿and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ means: He knew in eternity who would go astray in His decree and who would be guided, so the two matters are not confused for Him, and there is no harm in turning away, and it is considered in custom to be a benefit.

Second: it is in the sense of His saying: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24], and His saying: ﴿Our Lord will judge between us﴾ [al-A'raf: 87]. Its meaning is that they used to say: "We are upon guidance and you are the falsifiers." The Prophet (ﷺ) established the proof against them, but it did not benefit them. So He, exalted is He, said: "Turn away from them, and your reward has fallen upon God, for He knows that you are guided and He knows that they are astray." When two disputants argue before a powerful king, their aim is that the matter become manifest before the king. If the opponent acknowledges the truth, that is well; otherwise the purpose of the one who is right becomes manifest before the king. So He, exalted is He, said: "You have argued and done well, and God is most knowing of the one who is right from the one who is false."

Third: when He, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to turn away, and great harm had come from them, and the Prophet (ﷺ) bore it in hope that they would believe, all of that was abrogated. When they did not believe, it was as if He said: "My striving and my bearing of their harm has fallen as dust." **The fifth issue: in one place He said: ﴿He knows best who strays from His way﴾, and in another He said: ﴿who has gone astray﴾.** Do you have anything on this? I say: Yes. We clarify this with a rational argument and another transmitted one. As for the rational: the eternal knowledge relates to the known as it is. If something existed yesterday, it is known that it existed yesterday during yesterday. This is unlike our knowledge, where a thing may have occurred yesterday and we do not know it except today. Rather: ﴿Nothing escapes Him, the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Saba': 3], and what occurs is not delayed from His knowledge even for the blink of an eye. As for the transmitted argument: the active participle (ism al-fa'il) works as the verb does when it has the sense of the future, and does not work as the verb does when it is in the past. So you do not say: "I am striking Zayd yesterday." What is required, if you want it to govern an object, is to say: "I struck Zayd." And if you use the active participle, then the required form is the genitive construction (idafah). You say: "Striker of Zayd yesterday, I am," and it is permissible to say: "I am striking Zayd tomorrow." The reason for this is that when an action has occurred, it has no renewal outside the future, and no realization in the present, so it is nonexistent and too weak to govern. As for the present and what is anticipated, it has existence, so it is possible for it to govern. Since this is established, we say: When he said "dalla" (he went astray), the matter was in the past, and His knowledge was connected to it at the time of its existence, so it was known. His saying "a'lam" means 'alim (knowing), so it becomes as if he said: knowing of who has gone astray. So if he dropped the preposition, it would be governing the active participle in the sense of the past. When He said "yadilla" (goes astray), He knows the straying at the moment it occurs, even though He knew in eternity that he would stray. However, after that, knowledge has another connection which will come into existence, namely its connection to the straying having occurred and taken place, which was not in eternity. For it is not said: God knew in eternity that so-and-so had gone astray. Rather the correct statement is: it was known in eternity that he would stray, so that it is as if He knows that he goes astray, and the active participle is then in the sense of the future and works as the verb does. Thus it is not said: "Zayd is more knowing our question than 'Amr." Rather the required form is: "Zayd is more knowing of our question than 'Amr." For this reason the grammarians said regarding Surat al-An'am: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who goes astray﴾ means: He knows who goes astray. They also said: "a'lam" for the elative (tafdil, comparative) is formed only from an intransitive verb; if it is transitive, it is reduced to an intransitive one. Our saying "'alima" is as if it were from the pattern "'ulima" with a damma, and likewise in the exclamative when we say: "ma a'lamahu bi-kadha" (how knowing he is of such-and-such), as if it were from an intransitive verb.

As for me, I have answered this by saying that His saying ﴿most knowing of who goes astray﴾ means: knowing (alim). We have already presented what must be believed about the attributes of God, that for the most part it means that He is knowing, and there is no one knowing like Him, so a'lam is in its real sense. This is better than saying: it means simply knowing and nothing more. If it is asked: Why did He say here "bi-man dalla" (of who has gone astray) and there "yadilla" (goes astray)? We say: Because here the straying happened in the past, and it was confirmed when the Messenger's despair occurred and he was commanded to turn away. As for there, God Exalted had said previously: ﴿If you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of God﴾ [al-An'am: 116].

* * *

Then God Exalted said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who goes astray﴾, meaning: if you go astray, God knows you, so the straying was not occurring in Him, and therefore He did not use the past form.

**The sixth issue: He said "from His way" with regard to straying, and did not say "to His way" with regard to guidance.** This is because straying from the way is straying itself, and it is sufficient for straying, since straying occurs only on the way; but after arrival there is no straying. Or because whoever strays from His way does not reach the intended goal, whether he has traveled a road or not. As for whoever is guided to a road, there is no arrival unless he travels it. This is supported by the fact that whoever strays in other than His way is astray, and whoever is guided to it is not guided unless he is guided to every matter whose ignorance harms faith. So certain guidance is absolute guidance, and therefore He said: ﴿of those who are guided﴾ and said: ﴿the guided﴾ [al-An'am: 117].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 53, verse 31:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did and recompense those who did good with the best (reward)﴾. This indicates the perfection of His self-sufficiency (ghina) and power, so that after this He says: "Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided" (cf. 53:30). The one who knows but has no power cannot bring about the recompense, so He said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Zamakhshari said: "What indicates that he holds the view that the lam in His saying ﴿liyajziya (that He may recompense)﴾ is like the lam in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride them﴾ (An-Nahl: 8)." He proceeded on this according to his school, and said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ means: He created what is in them for the purpose of recompense. He does not shy away from what he mentioned, because of the known doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds human beings have free will and God is bound by justice and wisdom). Al-Wahidi said: the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah, the lam indicating the outcome of an action rather than its intended purpose), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that it may become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (Al-Qasas: 8), meaning they took him, and the consequence was that he became an enemy to them. The verification of this matter is that "hatta" (until) and the lam of purpose (lam al-gharad) are close in meaning, because the purpose is the end of the act, and "hatta" indicates absolute termination (al-ghaya al-mutlaqah), so there is a closeness between them, and one of them is used in place of the other. It is said: "I walked until I enter it" and "in order that I enter it." So the lam of consequence is the one used in the place of "hatta" for termination. It may be said that here there is a more likely view, though it is more hidden than the two views: that His saying ﴿liyajziya﴾ is connected to His saying "went astray and was guided" (dalla wa-htada), not to the knowledge nor to the creation of what is in the heavens. Its estimated meaning is as if He said: "He is most knowing of the one who has gone astray and the one who is guided, so that the one who went astray and the one who was guided may be recompensed with recompense, and Allah knows it." Thus His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ becomes a parenthetical statement. It may also be said that it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so turn away﴾ (53:29), meaning: turn away from them so that the recompense may occur, as the one who wants to do something says to someone who prevents him from it: "Leave me so that I may do it." That is because as long as the Prophet ﷺ had not despaired, the punishment would not descend, and turning away is at the time of despair. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ is then mentioned so that it is known that the punishment which occurs at his turning away is not like the one about which He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾ (Al-Anfal: 25). Rather, it is specific to those who did wrong, while for others there is the best (reward).

As for His saying, exalted is He, concerning the wrongdoer: ﴿according to what they did﴾, and concerning the doer of good: ﴿with the best﴾, there is a subtle point in it. The recompense of the wrongdoer is punishment, so He drew attention to what removes injustice and said: He does not punish except for a sin. As for the best (reward), He did not say "according to what they did," because if the reward is not in return for a good deed, it is in the utmost bounty, and this does not spoil the meaning. This applies if we say that "al-husna" (the best) is the reward with the best. But if we say: "the good deeds" (al-a'mal al-husna), then there is a different subtle point in it, which is that their deeds were not described as equal. He said about the deeds of the good-doers: "al-husna" (the best), indicating generosity and forgiveness, since He mentioned the better of the two names. "Al-husna" is an adjective placed in the position of the noun it modifies, as if He, exalted is He, said: "with the good deeds," like His saying: ﴿the most beautiful names﴾ (Al-A'raf: 180). In that case it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will surely remove from them their evil deeds and We will surely recompense them with the best of what they used to do﴾ (Al-'Ankabut: 7), meaning He takes the best of their deeds and makes the reward of everything that came from them in return for that best. Or it is an adjective of the reward, as if He said: "and recompense those who did good with the best reward, or with the best outcome," meaning their recompense is a good outcome. This is a recompense only; as for the increase which is grace upon grace, it is not included in it.

[Page 7]

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Those who avoid the grave sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾. "Those who" (alladhina) may be a substitute (badal) for "those who did good" (alladhina ahsanu), and this is the apparent reading. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: "that He may recompense those who did evil and recompense those who did good." This shows that the doer of good does not benefit God in any way by his good deeds, and that He is the one who does not do evil or commit the ugly act which is an evil in itself in the sight of his Lord. So "those who did good" are those who avoided [sins], and for them is the finest reward. By this, the evildoer and the doer of good are distinguished, because whoever does not avoid the grave sins is an evildoer, and whoever avoids them is a doer of good. On this basis there is a subtle point: since the doer of good is the one who avoids sins, the one who performs supererogatory acts is above the doer of good. But God the Exalted promised the doer of good an increase, so the one above him has increases beyond them, and these are the ones for whom is the reward of double. It is also possible that this is the beginning of a new statement, its implied meaning being: "those who avoid the grave sins, God will forgive them." What indicates this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. On this basis, this verse together with what precedes it clarifies the state of the evildoer and the doer of good, and the state of one who neither did good nor did evil, and these are the ones who committed no evil deed, even if no good deeds came from them. They are like children in whom the conditions of legal accountability have not been found, and for them is forgiveness, which is below the finest reward. This is made clear by His saying after it: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth and when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers﴾ [al-Najm: 32], i.e., He knows the condition in which there is neither good nor evil, just as He knows the one who did evil and went astray and the one who did good and was guided. Concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: If it is a substitute for "those who did good," why does it differ from what follows it in tense, past and present, where He said: ﴿those who did good﴾ and said: ﴿those who avoid﴾, and did not say "avoided"? We say: it is like the speaker saying, "Those who asked me, I gave them; those who keep coming to me asking" — i.e., those whose habit is coming back and asking, who asked me, and I gave them. Likewise here He said: ﴿those who avoid﴾, i.e., those whose habit and constant practice is avoidance, not those who avoided once and then returned to it another time. If it is said: in many places He said regarding the grave sins: ﴿And those who avoid the grave sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive﴾ [al-Shura: 37], and He said regarding worshippers of idols: ﴿And those who avoided the idols, not worshipping them, and turned back to God﴾ [al-Zumar: 17]. What is the difference? We say: worship of idols relates to belief, and belief, once it exists, persists as an outward state; whoever avoids it believes in its falsehood, and so it continues. As for drinking and fornication, these are matters in which people's conditions differ: one leaves it for a time and returns to it. For this reason the sinful person is tested when he repents, but the unbeliever is not tested when he embraces Islam. So He said regarding sins: ﴿those who avoid﴾ (present), constantly, and they persevere in abstention forever. Regarding the worship of idols: ﴿avoided﴾ in the past tense, so that it indicates more clearly that the avoidance has been achieved. Also, the grave sins are of many kinds, so one should avoid one kind, avoid another, and avoid a third; there is repetition and renewal in it, so the present tense is used for it. The worship of an idol is one single, unified matter, so this usage is dropped and the past tense is used, indicating that avoidance of it occurs all at once.

The second issue: "grave" (kabā'ir) is the plural of kabīrah, which is an adjective, so what is the noun it modifies? We say: it is an adjective of the act, as if He were saying: "the grave acts of sin." If it is said: why is "kabīrah" used specifically for sins in usage, and if someone said, "the grave good deed," nothing would prevent it? We say: a good deed is not grave, because when it is compared with what a servant ought to render in return for God's blessings, it is at the utmost smallness; were it not that God accepts it, it would be dust scattered. But the evil deed of a servant upon whom God has bestowed kinds of blessings is grave. Were it not for God's grace, occupation with eating and drinking and turning away from His worship would be an evil deed; but God forgave some evil deeds and lightened others.

The third issue: when "grave" is mentioned, what are the "immoralities" after it? We say: "grave" points to the magnitude of evil in them, and "immoralities" point to the ugliness in them, as if He said: "great in magnitude, ugly in form." In the language, "fāḥish" is specific to what is ugly, whose ugliness exceeds the limit of concealment, and the arrangement of the letters in their permutations indicates this: when you reverse them and say ḥashafa, it carries the meaning of extreme vileness beyond limit. It is said faḥashat al-nāqah when the she-camel stands in a specific posture for urinating. So fuḥsh is accompanied by ugliness. For this reason He did not say "the immoralities of sin," but said regarding the grave sins: "kabā'ir al-ithm," because if the grave sins are not distinguished by their relation to sin, the purpose would not be achieved, unlike the immoralities.

The fourth issue: many opinions have been given regarding the grave sins and immoralities. It was said: the grave sins are those for which God threatened the Fire explicitly and plainly, and the immoralities are those for which He prescribed a legal punishment in this world. It was said: the grave sins are those whose permissibility-denier becomes a disbeliever. It was said: the grave sins are those which God does not forgive their doer except after repentance, and this is according to the Mu'tazilah. All these definitions define a thing by something equal to it in obscurity or above it. We have mentioned that the grave sins are those whose magnitude is great, and the immoralities are those whose ugliness is evident. So "grave" is an attribute referring to magnitude, and "fāḥishah" is an attribute referring to quality, just as one says, for example, of the leper: a large patch of white has covered him, clearly visible in color. So "grave" expresses quantity, and "evident" expresses quality.

On this basis, we say, according to what we have said: the default for every act of disobedience is that it is grave, because God's blessings are abundant, and opposing the Benefactor is a great evil. However, God, exalted is He, has removed from His servants error and forgetfulness, because these do not indicate abandonment of reverence, either because of their generality among servants or because of their frequent occurrence among them, like a lie or backbiting once or twice, and a glance, and ugly acts which carry an element of doubt, for those who abstain from them are few in every age. For this reason our companions said: listening to singing accompanied by stringed instruments makes one a sinner, but if one listens to it in a town whose people do not believe in its prohibition, one is not made a sinner. Thus the minor sin returns to what we have mentioned: if rational people do not regard it as a sign of abandoning reverence, it is not a commission of a grave sin. On this basis, matters vary according to times and persons. A scholar who is pious, if he pursues women or indulges much in play, commits a grave sin; the broker, the merchants, and the one free of occupation who has nothing to do are not in that case. Likewise, play at the time of prayer, and play at other times. On this basis, every sin is a grave sin, except what the accountable person knows or presumes God will remove by His grace and pardon from the grave sins.

The fifth issue: concerning "lamam" (minor lapses), there are several opinions. The first: what the believer intends but does not carry out; on this view it comes from lamma yalummu, when one gathers, as if he gathered his resolve and resolved upon it. The second: what the believer commits and regrets at once; it is from the lamam which is a touch of madness, as if it touched him and departed. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember God and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾. The third: the minor sin, from alamma, meaning to descend without a long stay; and it is said alamma bi-l-ṭaʿām when he consumed a little of food. On this basis, His saying: ﴿except for minor lapses﴾ admits several interpretations:

The first: that it is an exception from the immoralities, and in that case there are two views:
One: it is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), because minor lapses are not among the immoralities.
The second: it is not disjunctive, because, as we have shown, every act of disobedience, when considered in relation to the side of God and what He is due, is both grave and an immorality. For this reason God said: ﴿and when they commit an immorality﴾ [al-A'raf: 28]. However, God excepted from them certain matters; it is said: the immoralities are every act of disobedience
[page 9]
except those God has excepted from them and promised pardon for.

The second: "illā" is in the sense of "ghayr" (other than), and the sense is "and the immoralities other than minor lapses." If this is for description, as one says, "the men other than those with desire," then minor lapses are the very immorality; and if it is for something else, as one says, "the men other than the women came to me," it is for emphasis and clarification, so "fa-lā" (then no).

The third: it is an exception from the verb indicated by His saying: ﴿those who avoid﴾, because that indicates that they do not approach it, so it is as if He said: they do not approach it except approaching without intercourse, and that is the minor lapse.

* *
* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾. According to our reading ﴿those who avoid﴾ as the beginning of a statement, this is very clear: the doer of good is rewarded and his sin is forgiven; and one who avoids the grave sins, likewise his minor sin is forgiven; and one who commits grave sins but repents is forgiven. So there remains none to whom forgiveness does not reach except those who did evil and persisted in it. Forgiveness is vast. There is also another subtle meaning: when He excluded the evildoer from forgiveness, He clarified that this is not due to any narrowness in forgiveness; rather it is by the will of God, exalted is He. Had God willed the forgiveness of everyone, both those who did good and those who did evil, He would have done so, and His forgiveness would never have been too narrow for them. Forgiveness derives from covering, and it occurs only over something ugly. Every creature God created, when you look at his action and relate it to God's blessings, you will find him deficient and remiss, for whoever repays the Benefactor with blessings beyond counting, despite the Benefactor's evident self-sufficiency and manifest greatness, with a dirham or less than that, needs to cover up what he has done.

* * *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth, and when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers. So do not claim your own purity; He knows best who has piety﴾. Regarding the connection there are several aspects:

The first: it is a confirmation of what passed, His saying: ﴿He knows best who has gone astray﴾. It is as if a disbeliever who acts says: "We do things in the dark of night and in closed houses; how would God know them?" So He said: "Your deeds are not more hidden than your states when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers, and God knows those states."

The second: it is an indication of the one who strayed and the one who was guided, each reaching what he is in by God's decree, for the Truth knew their states while they were in their mothers' wombs, so He wrote for one that he is astray and for the other that he is guided.

The third: it is a confirmation and clarification of the recompense. For when He said: ﴿that He may recompense those who did evil for what they did﴾, the disbelievers said: "This recompense cannot be realized except by resurrection, and gathering the parts after they have been scattered, and restoring to Zayd the parts that belonged to his body without mixing, is impossible." So He said: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you﴾, and He will gather them by His power in accordance with His knowledge, as He produced you. Concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: the operator of "idh" (when) may be what is indicated by "best knows" — i.e., He knew you at the time of your production. It may also be "remember," making it an affirmation of His being knowing; its sense would be: "He knows you best," and the speech is complete; then he says: if you are in doubt about His knowledge of you, then remember the state of your production from dust.

The second issue: we have mentioned repeatedly that His saying "from the earth" — some people said it refers to Adam, since he was from dust; and we have established that every person's origin is from dust, for it becomes nourishment, then becomes a drop of sperm.

The third issue: if someone says that "when He produced you from the earth" must be referred to Adam, because "and when you were embryos in the wombs of your mothers"

[page 10]

The first part refers to something else, since it was not an embryo. If you say that His saying, ﴿when He produced you﴾, refers to all people, then all people should have been embryos in their mothers' wombs, which is the view of the philosophers (al-falasifa). We say that this is not so, because we say: the address is to those who exist at the time of the address. His saying, ﴿He is most knowing of you﴾, is an address to everyone after the revelation according to one view, and to those present at the time of the revelation according to another view. There is no doubt that all of these were from the earth, and they had been embryos.

The Fourth Issue: The embryos are those in the wombs of their mothers. After birth, one is called only a child or a miscarriage. So what is the benefit of His saying, ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾? We say: it is to draw attention to the perfection of knowledge and power, for the inside of the mother's womb is in the utmost darkness, and whoever knows the condition of the embryo within it, nothing about the condition of the servants that becomes apparent is hidden from him.

The Fifth Issue: Someone may say: if we say that His saying, ﴿He is most knowing of you﴾, is a confirmation that He knows who has gone astray, then His saying, ﴿so do not justify yourselves﴾, has a clear connection to it. But if we say that it is an emphasis and an explanation of the recompense, then He knows the parts and returns them to the bodies of their owners; so how can ﴿so do not justify yourselves﴾ be connected to it? We say: its meaning then is: do not absolve yourselves from the punishment, and do not say that the parts have scattered so the punishment will not occur. For the one who knows you at the time of creation knows you at the time of resurrection. Accordingly, His saying, ﴿He knows best who is mindful of Him﴾ means: He knows its parts and returns them to Him, and rewards him for what he has done.

The Sixth Issue: To whom is the address? There are three possibilities. The first: it is to the disbelievers. This is according to our view that they said, "How could God know it?" So His words were a rebuttal of their statement. The second: it is to everyone who existed at the time of the address and after it, among the believers and the disbelievers. The third: it is to the believers. Its explanation is that when God Most High said, ﴿So turn away from whoever turns away from Our remembrance﴾ [al-Najm: 29], He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): It is known that you and those with you are upon the truth, and that the polytheists are upon falsehood; so turn away from them. And do not say, "We are upon the truth and you are upon error," for they would respond to you with the same. Entrust the matter to God Most High, for He knows best who is mindful and who transgresses. Accordingly, the view of the one who said that ﴿turn away﴾ is abrogated (mansukh) is more apparent. This is like His saying, Most High: ﴿Indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in manifest error﴾ [Saba: 24]. And God knows best the totality of matters.

It is possible to say: on this third aspect, it is guidance for the believers, so God addressed them and said: He knows you best, O believers. He knows what has been due to you from the beginning of your creation to the end of your day. So do not justify yourselves out of showing off and self-admiration, and do not say to another, "I am better than you, I am purer than you and more God-fearing," for the matter is with God. There is another aspect, which indicates the obligation of fear regarding the outcome, meaning: do not be certain of your salvation, O believers, for God knows the outcome of the one who is upon piety. This supports the view of the one who says, "I am a believer, if God wills," for the referral to the outcome.

[Page 11]

Then Allah, exalted is He, said:

﴿Have you seen the one who turned away,﴾ ﴿and gave a little and then held back?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Some of the commentators (mufassirun) said: The verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. He sat with the Prophet ﷺ and heard his admonition, and the wisdom had a strong effect on him. A man said to him: "Why are you abandoning the religion of your fathers?" Then he said to him: "Do not fear, and give me such-and-such, and I will bear your burdens (of sin) for you." So he gave him part of what he had committed to, and he turned away from the admonition and from listening to the words of the Prophet ﷺ. And some others said:

[Page 12]

It was revealed concerning Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. He used to give away a great deal of his wealth, and his half-brother from his mother, Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, said to him: "Your wealth will soon run out, so hold back." Uthman said to him: "Indeed I have sins, and I hope that Allah will forgive me because of the giving." His brother said to him: "I will bear your sins for you if you give me your she-camel along with such-and-such." So he gave him what he asked for and withheld his hand from giving, and the verse was revealed. But this statement is false and must not be mentioned, because it was not transmitted by mass narration (tawatur) and was not well known, and the apparent condition of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, rejects it. Rather, the truth is to say: When Allah, exalted is He, had said to His Prophet ﷺ earlier: ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance and desires nothing but the life of this world﴾ [An-Najm: 29], and turning away was among its kinds the turning away of one who considers himself self-sufficient, since one who knows a thing does not attend gatherings that mention that thing and does not strive to obtain something else. So He said: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away﴾ out of self-sufficiency: does he have knowledge of the unseen?

**The second issue:** The particle *al-fa'* (فاء, "so/then") requires a statement that this follows from. What is it? We say: it is what preceded regarding the demonstration of Allah's knowledge and power, and His promise of recompense to the evildoer and the doer of good. Its meaning is this: when Allah, exalted is He, made clear that recompense must certainly occur for both evil and good, and that the doer of good is the one who avoids the major sins, a person is not free of need to hear the words of the Prophet ﷺ and his followers. After this, one who turns away does so only after reaching the utmost need and the extreme of poverty (before the truth).

**The third issue:** The relative pronoun *alladhi* (الَّذِي, "the one who") according to what some of the commentators said refers to something known, namely that man, who is al-Walid. The apparent view, however, is that it refers to something already mentioned, for Allah, exalted is He, said earlier: ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance﴾, and this is what is known, because the command to turn away is not specific to one of the opponents. So He said: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away﴾, meaning the one whose mention has preceded.
