**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 53, verses 36–37:**

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾ ﴿and Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]?﴾ This is another state, opposed to the first, in which the one who turns away is excused, and that is absolute ignorance. For whoever knows a thing with complete knowledge is not commanded to learn it, and whoever is absolutely ignorant of it, being utterly heedless like a sleeper, is likewise not commanded. So this one who turns away is asked: Did he know everything, so that turning away is permitted for him? Or did he not hear anything, and no call ever reached him at all, so that he would be excused? Neither of the two is the case, so he is not excused in turning away. And in this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿of what is in﴾, may carry two meanings.

The first: the intended meaning is "what is in them" without regard to the attribute of being in them. It is as if He, Exalted, says: "Has he not been informed of the Tawhid (Oneness of God), the Resurrection, and other things that are mentioned in the scriptures of Moses?" An example: a person says to one who performed ablution with something other than water, "Perform ablution with what the Prophet ﷺ performed it with." According to this, the address is to everyone, because the polytheist and the People of the Book were informed by the Prophet ﷺ of what is in the scriptures of Moses.

The second: the intended meaning is what is in the scrolls together with its being in them, just as one who says in the example we mentioned, "Perform ablution with what is in the waterskin, not with what is in the jar," means that very thing and not its kind. According to this, the address is to the People of the Book, because they are the ones who were informed of it.

**The second issue:** Are the scriptures of Moses and Abraham collectively so called because they are many scrolls, or because they are attributed to two, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Your hearts have inclined﴾ (al-Tahrim 66:4)? The apparent meaning is that they are many, for God, Exalted is He, said, ﴿He took the tablets﴾ (al-A'raf 7:154), and He said, Exalted is He, ﴿and he threw down the tablets﴾ (al-A'raf 7:150), and every tablet is a scroll (sahifah).

**The third issue:** What is meant by "that which" (alladhi) in them? We say: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ and ﴿that man will have nothing but what he strives for﴾ (al-Najm 53:38–39), and what follows it of the matters mentioned, according to the reading of the one who reads anna (that) with a fatha, and according to the reading of the one who reads it with a kasra and says, ﴿and that to your Lord is the finality﴾ (al-Najm 53:42). In this there are several possibilities:

First: it is what is mentioned by His saying, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ (al-Najm 53:38), and this is the apparent meaning. Other things were only considered possible because the scriptures of Moses and Abraham do not contain this alone, and this is not the main purpose, unlike the reading with a fatha, for in it all the fundamentals are included, as has been explained.

Second: it is that the Hereafter is better than the first life, which is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ (al-A'la 87:18–19).

Third: all the fundamentals of the religion (usul al-din) are mentioned in all the books, and God did not leave any book devoid of them. For this reason He said to His Prophet ﷺ, ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ (al-An'am 6:90). The intended meaning is not the subsidiary rulings (furu'), because the subsidiary rulings of his religion differ from the subsidiary rulings of theirs, without doubt.

**The fourth issue:** Moses is mentioned first here, and He did not say it as He said in ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ (al-A'la 87:1). Is there a benefit in this? We say: Such a thing in the speech of the eloquent does not require a benefit to be sought for it. Rather, anteriority and posteriority are equal in their speech, so it is valid to limit oneself to this answer. It may also be said: the mention there was merely for the purpose of informing and warning, whereas here the purpose is to show the absence of excuses. Therefore, there He mentioned in the order of existence the scrolls of Abraham before the scrolls of Moses in the sending down. As for here, we have said that the address is to the People of the Book, who are the Jews, so He mentioned their scripture first. And if we say the address is general, the scrolls of Moses, peace be upon him, were abundant in existence. It is as if it was said to them: Look into them and you will know that the message is true, that messengers were sent before Moses, that monotheism is true, and that the Resurrection is certain. Since the scrolls of Moses were abundant among the Jews, He mentioned them first. As for the scrolls of Abraham, they were remote, and the admonitions in them were not well known among them, as were the scrolls of Moses, so He postponed their mention.

**The fifth issue:** God often mentioned Moses and postponed his mention, peace be upon him, because he was for the most part tested by those around him, and they were polytheists and Judaizers. The polytheists used to revere Abraham, peace be upon him, because he was their father. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿who fulfilled﴾, there are two interpretations.

The first: it is the fulfilling of the kind found in covenants. According to this, the doubling of the letter is for emphasis. It is said: waffa and waffa, like qata'a and qatta'a and qatala and qattala. This is clear, because he fulfilled the vow and laid his son down for slaughter. And it came concerning him: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ (al-Saffat 37:105), and God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, this is the manifest trial﴾ (al-Saffat 37:106).

The second: it is from tawfiyah, which is from wafa', meaning completeness, fulfilment, and completion. It is said: waffahu, that is, he gave it to him complete. According to this, it is from His saying, ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:124). It was also said: "waffa" means he gave the rights of God in his body. According to this, it is the opposite of the one about whom God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and gave a little and then ceased﴾ (al-Najm 53:34). He praised Abraham and did not describe Moses, peace be upon him.

We say: As for explaining his fulfilment, there is a subtle point in it: he never entered into a covenant without fulfilling it. He said to his father, ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ (Maryam 19:47), so he asked forgiveness and fulfilled the covenant, yet God did not forgive him. Thus he knew ﴿that man will have nothing but what he strives for﴾, and that his burden would not be borne by another soul. As for the praise of Abraham, peace be upon him, it is because it was agreed upon among the Jews, the polytheists, and the Muslims, and no one denied that he was faithful and one who fulfilled. Perhaps the polytheists hesitated in describing Moses, peace be upon him. Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and its interpretation has already been mentioned in Surah al-Mala'ikah (Fatir). What is appropriate to this place are the following issues:

The first: We have explained that the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿of what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾, is what He clarified by His saying, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear﴾. The first: the intended meaning is that the Hereafter is better and more enduring.

The second: the fundamentals.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 53, verses 36–37:**

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾ ﴿and Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]?﴾ This is another state, opposed to the first, in which the one who turns away is excused, and that is absolute ignorance. For whoever knows a thing with complete knowledge is not commanded to learn it, and whoever is absolutely ignorant of it, being utterly heedless like a sleeper, is likewise not commanded. So this one who turns away is asked: Did he know everything, so that turning away is permitted for him? Or did he not hear anything, and no call ever reached him at all, so that he would be excused? Neither of the two is the case, so he is not excused in turning away. And in this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿of what is in﴾, may carry two meanings.

The first: the intended meaning is "what is in them" without regard to the attribute of being in them. It is as if He, Exalted, says: "Has he not been informed of the Tawhid (Oneness of God), the Resurrection, and other things that are mentioned in the scriptures of Moses?" An example: a person says to one who performed ablution with something other than water, "Perform ablution with what the Prophet ﷺ performed it with." According to this, the address is to everyone, because the polytheist and the People of the Book were informed by the Prophet ﷺ of what is in the scriptures of Moses.

The second: the intended meaning is what is in the scrolls together with its being in them, just as one who says in the example we mentioned, "Perform ablution with what is in the waterskin, not with what is in the jar," means that very thing and not its kind. According to this, the address is to the People of the Book, because they are the ones who were informed of it.

**The second issue:** Are the scriptures of Moses and Abraham collectively so called because they are many scrolls, or because they are attributed to two, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Your hearts have inclined﴾ (al-Tahrim 66:4)? The apparent meaning is that they are many, for God, Exalted is He, said, ﴿He took the tablets﴾ (al-A'raf 7:154), and He said, Exalted is He, ﴿and he threw down the tablets﴾ (al-A'raf 7:150), and every tablet is a scroll (sahifah).

**The third issue:** What is meant by "that which" (alladhi) in them? We say: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ and ﴿that man will have nothing but what he strives for﴾ (al-Najm 53:38–39), and what follows it of the matters mentioned, according to the reading of the one who reads anna (that) with a fatha, and according to the reading of the one who reads it with a kasra and says, ﴿and that to your Lord is the finality﴾ (al-Najm 53:42). In this there are several possibilities:

First: it is what is mentioned by His saying, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ (al-Najm 53:38), and this is the apparent meaning. Other things were only considered possible because the scriptures of Moses and Abraham do not contain this alone, and this is not the main purpose, unlike the reading with a fatha, for in it all the fundamentals are included, as has been explained.

Second: it is that the Hereafter is better than the first life, which is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ (al-A'la 87:18–19).

Third: all the fundamentals of the religion (usul al-din) are mentioned in all the books, and God did not leave any book devoid of them. For this reason He said to His Prophet ﷺ, ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ (al-An'am 6:90). The intended meaning is not the subsidiary rulings (furu'), because the subsidiary rulings of his religion differ from the subsidiary rulings of theirs, without doubt.

**The fourth issue:** Moses is mentioned first here, and He did not say it as He said in ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ (al-A'la 87:1). Is there a benefit in this? We say: Such a thing in the speech of the eloquent does not require a benefit to be sought for it. Rather, anteriority and posteriority are equal in their speech, so it is valid to limit oneself to this answer. It may also be said: the mention there was merely for the purpose of informing and warning, whereas here the purpose is to show the absence of excuses. Therefore, there He mentioned in the order of existence the scrolls of Abraham before the scrolls of Moses in the sending down. As for here, we have said that the address is to the People of the Book, who are the Jews, so He mentioned their scripture first. And if we say the address is general, the scrolls of Moses, peace be upon him, were abundant in existence. It is as if it was said to them: Look into them and you will know that the message is true, that messengers were sent before Moses, that monotheism is true, and that the Resurrection is certain. Since the scrolls of Moses were abundant among the Jews, He mentioned them first. As for the scrolls of Abraham, they were remote, and the admonitions in them were not well known among them, as were the scrolls of Moses, so He postponed their mention.

**The fifth issue:** God often mentioned Moses and postponed his mention, peace be upon him, because he was for the most part tested by those around him, and they were polytheists and Judaizers. The polytheists used to revere Abraham, peace be upon him, because he was their father. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿who fulfilled﴾, there are two interpretations.

The first: it is the fulfilling of the kind found in covenants. According to this, the doubling of the letter is for emphasis. It is said: waffa and waffa, like qata'a and qatta'a and qatala and qattala. This is clear, because he fulfilled the vow and laid his son down for slaughter. And it came concerning him: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ (al-Saffat 37:105), and God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, this is the manifest trial﴾ (al-Saffat 37:106).

The second: it is from tawfiyah, which is from wafa', meaning completeness, fulfilment, and completion. It is said: waffahu, that is, he gave it to him complete. According to this, it is from His saying, ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:124). It was also said: "waffa" means he gave the rights of God in his body. According to this, it is the opposite of the one about whom God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and gave a little and then ceased﴾ (al-Najm 53:34). He praised Abraham and did not describe Moses, peace be upon him.

We say: As for explaining his fulfilment, there is a subtle point in it: he never entered into a covenant without fulfilling it. He said to his father, ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ (Maryam 19:47), so he asked forgiveness and fulfilled the covenant, yet God did not forgive him. Thus he knew ﴿that man will have nothing but what he strives for﴾, and that his burden would not be borne by another soul. As for the praise of Abraham, peace be upon him, it is because it was agreed upon among the Jews, the polytheists, and the Muslims, and no one denied that he was faithful and one who fulfilled. Perhaps the polytheists hesitated in describing Moses, peace be upon him. Then God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and its interpretation has already been mentioned in Surah al-Mala'ikah (Fatir). What is appropriate to this place are the following issues:

The first: We have explained that the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿of what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾, is what He clarified by His saying, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear﴾. So this is a substitute (badal) for "ma" (what), and its estimation is: "Has he not been informed that no bearer of burdens shall bear?" And we mentioned two possibilities there:

The first: the intended meaning is that the Hereafter is better and more enduring.

The second: the fundamentals.

**Second issue:** *An-la* (أنْ) here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna* (إنَّ), as if he had said *annahu la tazru*. Lightening the heavy *inna* is sometimes obligatory and sometimes optional. It is obligatory when what follows it is a verb, or a particle that governs a verb. The reason is that this *inna* resembles the verb in both form and meaning, and a verb cannot be made to govern another verb. So it is removed from its resemblance to the verb and takes the form of a particle specific to verbs, which suits the verb and can therefore precede it.

**Third issue:** If someone says: the verse is revealed to show that the burden of the wrongdoer cannot be carried for him. This meaning is not achieved by this wording, because the bearer of a burden is already weighed down by her own load, so everyone knows she cannot carry anything. Had it said, "an empty-handed one does not carry the burden of another," it would have been more eloquent. We reply: it is not as you suppose. The intended meaning of "the bearer" (*al-wazirah*) is the one from whom a burden is expected, not the one who has already borne and carried it. This is like the saying, "the load has exhausted me," even when there is no load on him at that moment. Since that soul does not bear what is expected of it, how could it bear the burden of another? Thus the meaning is complete.

His exalted saying: ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strove for﴾ completes the explanation of the states of the accountable person (*mukallaf*). When He had shown that no one bears his evil deeds on his behalf, He showed that the good deeds of others are of no benefit to him. Whoever does not do righteousness does not attain good, so that he might complete himself by it. It also shows that the wrongdoer gains no reward because of the good deeds of others, and no one bears punishment for him. Regarding this verse there are also several issues:

**First:** ﴿For man﴾ (*lil-insan*) has two interpretations.

One: it is general, and this is the truth. It has been objected that reports state that what a living relative gives in charity or fasting reaches the dead, and supplication is also beneficial. Therefore man has something for which he did not strive. Also God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], and this is more than what he strove for. The answer is that if a person does not strive to have the charity of a relative through faith, that charity does not belong to him, so he has nothing except what he strove for. As for the increase, we say: when God promised the doer of good multiples, ten-fold, and multiplied increases, then if he does a good deed hoping that God will grant him what He bestows out of grace, he has striven for these multiples. If it is said: you have then taken striving (*sa'y*) to mean hastening toward a thing. One says, "he strove toward such-and-such" when he hastened to it. But the striving in His exalted saying ﴿except what he strove for﴾ means labour and work; one says "so-and-so strove," meaning he worked. Had it been as you mentioned, it would have said, "except what he strove *for* (*fihi*)." We say: on both interpretations an addition is necessary, for His exalted saying ﴿There is not for man except what he strove for﴾ does not mean that he has the very thing he strove for. Rather, the meaning, as you have stated, is that he has only the reward for what he strove for, or only the wage for what he strove for. Or it may be said that what he strove for is preserved for him, safeguarded from being nullified, so that on the Day of Resurrection he will have its result.

Two: the intended "man" is the disbeliever, not the believer. This is weak. It has also been said that His saying ﴿There is not for man except what he strove for﴾ belonged to the law of earlier communities, and then God abrogated it (*naskh*, the cancelling of a ruling by a later revelation) in the law of Muhammad (ﷺ) and made for man both what he strove for and what he did not strive for. This is false, since there is no need for such a legal obligation once the truth has become clear. According to what has been mentioned, His saying ﴿what he strove for﴾ is retained in its literal sense: he has the very thing he strove for, preserved with God, exalted is He, with no loss entering it, and then he is recompensed for it, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7].

**Second:** Is *ma* (ما) relative (*khabariyyah*, "that which") or verbal-infinitival (*masdariyyah*, "the act of striving")? We say that its being verbal-infinitival is more apparent, by the evidence of His exalted saying ﴿and that his striving will be seen﴾ [al-Najm: 40], meaning: "what is striven for will be seen." The verbal noun is often used in the sense of the object, as one says, "this is God's creation," meaning "His creature."

**Third:** Does the verse intend to explain the reward of righteous deeds, or to explain every deed? We say: the well-known view is that it applies to every deed, so good is rewarded and evil is punished. The apparent view is that it explains the good deeds. This is indicated by the *lam* (ل) in His exalted saying ﴿for man﴾, since *lam* denotes the return of benefits, while *ʿalā* (على) denotes the return of harms. One says, "this is for him" and "this is against him," and "it testifies for him" and "it testifies against him," in both benefits and harms.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 53, verses 40–41:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And that his striving will be seen﴾ ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾. That is, it will be presented to him and disclosed to him, from "araytuhu al-shay'" (I showed him the thing). In this there is good news for the believers, according to what we have mentioned. This is because Allah shows him his righteous deeds so that he may rejoice in them. Or it may be that He shows them to His angels and the rest of His creation, so that the doer may take pride in them, as is well known, and this is mentioned for the joy of the Muslim and the grief of the disbeliever. For his striving will be seen by creation and seen by himself. It is also possible to say that it is from "ra'a yara" (to see), so that it is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿And say: Work, for Allah will see your work, and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 105]. Concerning this and the verse after it, there are several issues:

The first: How is the deed seen after its existence and its passing? We say there are two aspects regarding it:

One of them: He sees it in a beautiful form if the deed was righteous.

The second: It is, according to our school, not far-fetched, for every existent is seen, and Allah is able to restore every non-existent, so after the act it is seen.

There is also a third aspect: that this is a metaphor for the reward, as one says: "You will see your kindness with the king," meaning his recompense for it. But this is far-fetched because of what He said after it: ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾.

The second issue: The pronoun "hu" refers to the striving, that is: then the person will be recompensed for his striving with the reward. "Al-jaza'" (recompense) is transitive to two objects, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He will reward them for what they endured with a garden and silk﴾ [al-Insan: 12], and one says: "May Allah reward you with good." It is transitive to three objects with a preposition, as one says: "Allah rewarded him for his deed with good, the Garden," and the preposition is omitted and the verb is connected, so one says: "Allah rewarded him his deed the good, the Garden." This is one aspect. There is another aspect, that the pronoun refers to the recompense, and its implied sense is: then he will be recompensed with a recompense, and His saying "al-jaza' al-awfa" (the fullest recompense) is an explanation or an apposition, like the Exalted's saying: ﴿And they conspired secretly, those who did wrong﴾ [al-Anbiya': 3], for the implied sense is: those who did wrong conspired secretly, those who did wrong. The fullest recompense, according to what we have mentioned, is befitting to the righteous believers, because it is the recompense of the righteous. And if the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Hell is your recompense, a full recompense﴾ [al-Isra': 63], it is answered that "awfa" is with regard to it: Hell's harm is far greater, together with the benefit of sins, so it is in itself the fuller.

The third issue: "Thumma" (then) indicates either the delay of the recompense or the delay of the speech, that is: then we say, he will be recompensed. If it indicates the delay of the recompense, how is the recompense delayed for the righteous, when it is established that the apparent meaning is that it is the righteous who are intended? We say: both aspects are possible, and the answer to the question is that the description "awfa" removes what you have mentioned, for Allah the Exalted, from the first moment the righteous person dies, recompenses him for his good, and delays for him the fullest recompense, which is the Garden. Or we say: "awfa" points to an increase, so it is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (husna)﴾ [Yunus: 26], which is the Garden, and ﴿and an increase (ziyadah)﴾, which is the vision. It is as if the Exalted said: ﴿And that his striving will be seen﴾, then he will be granted the vision. This aspect is befitting to the explanation of the wording, for "awfa" is unrestricted and unspecified, so He did not say "awfa than such-and-such," so it should be the fullest of every full thing, and nothing is described by it except the vision of Allah the Exalted.

The fourth issue: in explaining subtleties in the verses.

The first: Regarding the wrongdoer He said: ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and this indicates only the absence of carrying the burden from the bearer; it does not necessarily follow from the wording that the burden remains upon her, since it is possible that it falls from her and Allah erases that burden, so it does not remain upon her and no one else bears it on her behalf. But had He said: "No bearer bears except the burden of herself," it would necessarily follow from the exception that she bears. And regarding the doer of good He said: ﴿That man has nothing but what he strove for﴾, and He did not say: "He has nothing of what he did not strive for," because the second expression does not state that he has what he strove for, whereas in the first expression there is that he has what he strove for, in view of the exception. And He spoke regarding the wrongdoer with an expression that does not cut off his hope, and regarding the doer of good with an expression that cuts off his fear. All of this is an indication of the precedence of mercy over wrath.

And if the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Hell is your recompense, a full recompense﴾ [al-Isra': 63], it is answered that "awfa" is with regard to it: Hell's harm is far greater, together with the benefit of sins, so it is in itself the fuller.

The third issue: "Thumma" (then) indicates either the delay of the recompense or the delay of the speech, that is: then we say, he will be recompensed. If it indicates the delay of the recompense, how is the recompense delayed for the righteous, when it is established that the apparent meaning is that it is the righteous who are intended? We say: both aspects are possible, and the answer to the question is that the description "awfa" removes what you have mentioned, for Allah the Exalted, from the first moment the righteous person dies, recompenses him for his good, and delays for him the fullest recompense, which is the Garden. Or we say: "awfa" points to an increase, so it is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (husna)﴾ [Yunus: 26], which is the Garden, and ﴿and an increase (ziyadah)﴾, which is the vision. It is as if the Exalted said: ﴿And that his striving will be seen﴾, then he will be granted the vision. This aspect is befitting to the explanation of the wording, for "awfa" is unrestricted and unspecified, so He did not say "awfa than such-and-such," so it should be the fullest of every full thing, and nothing is described by it except the vision of Allah the Exalted.

The fourth issue: in explaining subtleties in the verses.

The first: Regarding the wrongdoer He said: ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, and this indicates only the absence of carrying the burden from the bearer; it does not necessarily follow from the wording that the burden remains upon her, since it is possible that it falls from her and Allah erases that burden, so it does not remain upon her and no one else bears it on her behalf. But had He said: "No bearer bears except the burden of herself," it would necessarily follow from the exception that she bears. And regarding the doer of good He said: ﴿That man has nothing but what he strove for﴾, and He did not say: "He has nothing of what he did not strive for," because the second expression does not state that he has what he strove for, whereas in the first expression there is that he has what he strove for, in view of the exception. And He spoke regarding the wrongdoer with an expression that does not cut off his hope, and regarding the doer of good with an expression that cuts off his fear. All of this is an indication of the precedence of mercy over wrath.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾. The well-known reading is with a fatha on the hamza, by coordination (ʿaṭf) upon "mā" (in "mā fī al-ṣuḥuf"), meaning that this too is in the scrolls, and it is the truth. It was also read with a kasra, as a new independent sentence (istiʾnaf). On this verse there are several issues.

The first: What is the intended meaning of the verse? We say: there are two views.

The first, which is the well-known one, is the explanation of the Return (al-maʿād): that for people there is standing before God. On this view, it connects with what preceded; for when God said "then he will be recompensed for it" (thumma yujzāhu), it was as if someone said: "You do not see the recompense; when will it be?" So He said: the return is to God, and at that point He rewards the grateful and requites the ungrateful.

The second: the intended meaning is Tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). The philosophers (ḥukamāʾ) have interpreted most of the verses in which there is "al-intihāʾ" (ending) and "al-rujūʿ" (return) with what we shall mention, though in some of them their interpretation is not evident, whereas in this place it is evident. We say: it is the demonstration of God's existence and His oneness. This is because when you consider contingent existents (al-mawjūdāt al-mumkina), you find no escape from an originator (mūjid). Then its originator may be supposed to be another contingent, such as the heat which is felt in a way that one supposes it comes from the rays of the sun or from fire; so it is said: "The sun and fire are contingent; from what do their existence come?" If they are dependent upon another contingent, the intellect finds no alternative but to terminate at a non-contingent, which is the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd). To Him the matter ends, so the Lord is the final end (al-muntahā). This, in this place, is evident, rational, and in agreement with what is transmitted. For it is related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "«And that to your Lord is the final end; there is no reflection upon the Lord»," meaning the matter terminates at the Necessary Existent, who does not have existence by another originator, and from Whom all existence comes. And Anas said, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "«When the Lord is mentioned, then stop»," and this admits of what we have mentioned. As for some people, they exaggerate and interpret every verse in which there is "al-rujʿā" (return) and "al-muntahā" and others with this interpretation, to the extent that it has been said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fāṭir: 10] is in this sense; and this is the proof of existence. As for the proof of oneness, it is that the intellect has terminated at the Necessary Existent insofar as He is Necessary Existent; for if He were not Necessary Existent, He would not be a terminus, but would have an originator. So the terminus is the Necessary insofar as He is necessary. This meaning is in reality one and the same in intellect, for there must be termination at this Necessary or at that Necessary, so no meaning is established for the Necessary other than that He is necessary; thus His necessity becomes remote. Therefore, if there were two necessary beings in existence, each would be before the terminus, since the totality before it would be the Necessary, and so it is the terminus. These are two proofs which I have mentioned in summary.

The second issue: God's saying ﴿to your Lord is the final end﴾. Regarding the addressee, there are two views.

The first: it is general, its implied meaning being "to your Lord, O hearer or intelligent one."

The second: the address is with the Prophet (ﷺ), and in it is a demonstration of the soundness of his religion, for every person was claiming a lord and a god, but when he (ﷺ) said: "«My Lord is He who is One and Eternal (al-Ṣamad)»," every contingent needs Him. So your Lord is the final end, and He is the Lord of lords and the Causer of causes. On this view, the kāf (your) is more fitting in its position. As for our view that the address is general, it is a forceful warning to the wrongdoer and a strong incitement to the good-doer; for His saying "O hearer, whoever you are, to your Lord is the final end" conveys both matters with complete thoroughness. As for our view that the address is with the Prophet (ﷺ), it is consolation for his heart, as if He says: "Do not grieve, for the final end is to God," which is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let not their saying grieve you; indeed We know what they conceal and what they reveal﴾, up to His saying at the end of the surah: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾; and similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an.

The third issue: the alif-lam (al-) on the first view is for specific reference (ʿahd), because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say that your return is certainly to God; so He said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾, the promised one mentioned in the Qur'an and the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ). On the second view it is for generality, i.e., to the Lord is every final end, and He is the origin. On this view we say: the final end of perceptions that perceive: a person first perceives apparent things, then he looks closely, and so terminates at God, and stops at Him.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

The first: According to our saying, "to your Lord is the final end" (al-muntaha), the purpose of these verses is to establish the Oneness (al-wahdaniyyah), and they establish matters on which Islam depends, among them the power of Allah the Exalted. Among the philosophers there are those who acknowledge that Allah is the final end and that He is One, but they say: "He is a necessitating cause (mujib), not a capable agent (qadir)." So Allah the Exalted said: He brought into existence two opposites, laughter and weeping, in one place, and death and life, and maleness and femaleness, in one substance. That can only come from a capable agent, and every intelligent person acknowledges it. And according to our saying, that His saying, ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾, is an explanation of the return (al-ma'ad), then it is an allusion to the explanation of His command. So just as He, in some of His servants, makes one laughing and joyful, and in some, weeping and sorrowful, so too is He dealing with them in the Hereafter.

The second issue: ﴿Causes laughter and causes weeping﴾ have no object (maf'ul) in this place, because they are brought in to express the power of Allah, not to specify the object of that power, so there is no need for an object. A speaker says: "So-and-so has in his hand the giving and the withholding; he gives and withholds," and he does not intend a thing withheld or a thing given.

The third issue: He chose these two attributes for the male and the female because they are matters that cannot be given a cause (la yu'allalan). No naturalist (tabi'i) can present a reason or cause for the specific attribute of laughing and weeping to humans. And if a thing has no cause, and it must have an originator, then it is Allah the Exalted. This is unlike health and sickness, for they say: their cause is the disturbance of temperament (mizaj) and its departure from balance (i'tidal). What indicates this is that when they mention for laughter a factor that causes laughter, they say: "the strength of wonder," and that is utterly false, because a person may be stunned at seeing astonishing things and not laugh. It was said: "the strength of joy," and that is not so either, because a person rejoices greatly and does not laugh, and the one who is in extreme grief may be made to laugh by a comedian. The same applies to weeping. And if it is said to the most knowledgeable of them about the matters that the naturalists claim, "Why does the tear come out of the eye at specific things?", he cannot give a sound explanation. And with the special properties, such as those found in the magnet and others, the naturalist comes to an end; just as at the configurations of the stars he comes to an end, as does the engineer who does not entrust his affair to the power and will of Allah the Exalted.

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾. The discussion of this is like that of laughing and weeping, except that in the first case God Almighty clarified the species-specific property (al-khassa), which is more specific than the genus, because it is more apparent and further from being explained by a cause. Then He joined to it what is more general than it and less remote from being explained by a cause, namely causing death and giving life. These are two opposite attributes, i.e., death and life, like laughing and weeping. On this view, death is not mere non-existence, for otherwise the non-existent would be dead. In any case, causing death and giving life are an existential matter, and they are among the properties of animal beings. The natural philosopher (al-tabi'i) says: life is the result of the balance of temperament (i'tidal al-mizaj). Temperament is composed of opposing elements (arkan): fire, air, water, and earth. These tend toward separation. Whatever has no composition of opposites has no death, because each of the opposites seeks to part from what is adjacent to it. God Almighty says: He who created and mixed the elements and preserved them for a period is able to preserve them for longer than that. So when a being dies, it is not out of necessity; it is by the act of a chooser, who is God Almighty: ﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾.

If it is said: When does He cause death and give life, so that one might know this? Rather, the observation of giving life and causing death is based on life and death. We say: there are several views on this:

First: it is by way of inversion, as if He had said: He gives life and causes death.

Second: it has the meaning of the future, since the matter is near. It is said: "So-and-so has arrived" and "the night has entered" when their place and time are near. Likewise, giving life and causing death.

Third: "He caused death" means He created death and stiffness in the elements and then composed them; and "He gave life" means He created sensation and motion in them.

* * *

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And that He created the pair, the male and the female﴾. This too is among the opposites that alternate upon the drop (nutfa) of semen: some of it is created male and some female. The understanding of the natural philosopher does not reach this, who says that it is due to coldness and moisture in the female. For many a woman has a drier temperament than a man. And how, when you look into the distinguishing features between the young and the old, you find them wondrous matters. Among them is the growth of the beard. The strongest thing they have said about the growth of the beard is that they said: hairs are formed from an oily vapour (bukhar dihani) that descends to the pores. When the pores are in an extreme state of moisture and dissolution, as in the temperament of the boy and the woman, hair does not grow, because those vapours exit easily through the moist pores before hair is formed. When they are in an extreme state of dryness and condensation, hair grows, because it has difficulty exiting through the narrow outlet. Then those substances are drawn to specific places and are propelled. Either they are propelled to the head, because it is created like a dome above the vapours and fumes, so these substances ascend to it; therefore the hair of the head is more abundant and longer. And in men there are places to which vapours and fumes are drawn: among them the chest, because of the heat of the heart, and heat draws moisture like a lamp draws oil; among them the area near the organ of reproduction, because the heat of desire also draws; and among them the cheeks (al-lihyan), for they move a great deal because of eating and speaking, and motion also draws. Then, if they are asked: What is the cause that necessitates the concomitance of the growth of beard hair and the organ of reproduction, for if the latter is cut off the beard does not grow? And what is the difference between the age of youth and the age of adulthood, and between woman and man? Some of these they are struck dumb about, and about others they speak with worthless claims. If they had referred these matters to divine wisdom, that would have been better.

There are two issues here:

The first: He said, ﴿And that He created﴾, and did not say, "And that it is He who created," as He said: ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and weep﴾. This is because laughing and weeping might be thought by someone to be by the act of a human being. As for causing death and giving life, although that supposition is remote, yet a fool might say it, as the one who argued with Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258]. So He emphasized that by mentioning the separating pronoun (al-fasl). As for the creation of the male and the female from the drop, no one could think that any human could do it. Therefore He did not emphasize it with the separating pronoun. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices﴾ [al-Najm: 48], where enriching was, in their belief, not attributed to God Almighty, and in their conviction that it was by their own act, as Qarun said: ﴿I was given it only on knowledge that is with me﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. Therefore He said: ﴿And that it is He who is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [al-Najm: 49], because they found it unlikely that the Lord of Muhammad was the Lord of Sirius. So He emphasized the attribution to God Almighty in the places where they found it unlikely, and did not emphasize it elsewhere.

The second issue: Are "al-dhakar" (male) and "al-untha" (female) names that are attributes, or names that are not attributes? The view well known among the lexicographers is the second. The apparent view is that they are among the names that are attributes. So "al-dhakar" is like "al-hasan" (the handsome), "al-'azab" (the unmarried), and "al-untha" is like "al-hubla" (the pregnant) and "al-kubra" (the great). We said that it is like "al-hubla" according to one opinion, because it is produced in its counterpart, not like "al-kubra." And if we say it is like "al-kubra" according to one opinion, that is also possible. We said that the apparent view is that they are attributes, because an attribute is what is applied to a thing to which something has become attached. For example, "the knower" (al-'alim) is applied to a thing that has knowledge, and "the moving" (al-mutaharrik) is said of a thing that has motion, unlike a tree or a stone. A tree is not said of a thing on condition that something becomes attached to it; rather, it is a name placed for a specific thing. "Male" is a name said of a thing to which something is attached, and for this reason it is used as a description, and "tree" is not used as a description. One says: "A male person came to me," or "a male human," but one does not say "a tree body." Those who went to the view that it is a name and not an attribute were led to it only because no verb has been formed from it. Attributes, in general, have verbs, like "knowing" and "ignorant," "unmarried," "great," and "pregnant." But this does not indicate what they claimed, because maleness and femaleness are among the attributes some of which do not change into others, so no verbs are derived for them, since the verb is for what is expected to renew itself in the usual case. For this reason no verbs were found for relational (idafi) terms such as fatherhood, sonship, and brotherhood, since they are not of the kind that changes. But verbs were found for changeable relational terms. One says: "He made him a brother" (wakhahu) and "he adopted him" (tabbanahu), since it was not established by nature, so with artifice it accepted change.

**Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 53, verses 46–47:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from a drop [nutfah]﴾, i.e., a piece of water.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when it is emitted﴾. It is from *amnā al-maniyy* (to emit the semen), when it is discharged, or from *mану yamnī* (to measure, to determine), when it is decreed. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿from a drop﴾, is a reminder of the perfection of power, because the drop (*nutfah*) is a body whose parts are proportionate. From it God the Exalted creates diverse organs and differing natures. The creation of the male and the female from it is the most wondrous of things, as we have explained. For this reason no one has been able to claim it, just as no one has been able to claim the creation of the heavens. Hence the Exalted said: ﴿And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say, "God"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 87], just as He said: ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, "God"﴾ [Luqman: 25].

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And that to Him is the other creation [al-nash'ah al-ukhrā]﴾. According to most of the exegetes, it refers to the Resurrection. What has become clear to me, after long reflection and inquiry, by the grace of God the Exalted, is the guidance toward the truth in this matter: it is possible that what is meant is the breathing of the human spirit into it. This is because the noble soul, not the commanding soul, mingles with dense, dark bodies, and by it God honoured the children of Adam. To this the Exalted refers in His saying: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced it as another creation﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 14]. This is other than the creation of the drop as a clot, the clot as a lump, and the lump as bones. By this other creation, man is distinguished from the kinds of animals and shares with the angel in perceptions. Thus, just as He said there, ﴿We produced it as another creation﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 14] after the creation of the drop, He says here, ﴿And that to Him is the other creation﴾. He makes the breathing of the spirit another creation, just as He made it another production there.

What necessitated saying this is that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [An-Najm: 42], according to most of them, is to explain the return (*al-i'adah*), and His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Then He will recompense him with the fullest recompense﴾ [An-Najm: 41] is likewise. So the mention of the other creation is a return. Also, because He said after this, ﴿And that He is the One who makes rich and gives contentment﴾ [An-Najm: 48], and this is among the affairs of this world. According to what we have mentioned, the sequence is of the utmost beauty: He, the Exalted, says, ﴿He created the male and the female﴾, and breathed into both the noble human spirit; then He enriched him with his mother's milk and his father's provision in his youth; then He gave him contentment through earning after his maturity.

If it is objected: the other creation for the Resurrection has been mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation; then God will produce the final creation"﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 20]. We say: *al-ākhirah* (the final) derives from *al-ākhir* (the last), not from *al-ākhar* (the other), because *al-ākhir* is an elative form. Moreover, it has already been stated that there, since the beginning (*al-bad'*) was mentioned, it was understood as the return. Here, however, the creation from a drop was mentioned, as in His saying: ﴿Then We made the drop a clot﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 14], and then He said: ﴿We produced it as another creation﴾.

In the verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** *'alā* (upon/for) indicates obligation, yet return is not obligatory upon God. What then is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And that to Him [*'alayhi*]﴾? Al-Zamakhshari said, in accordance with his own doctrine, that it is obligatory upon Him by reason, since wisdom requires recompense, and this is not complete except through the Resurrection; therefore return is obligatory upon Him by reason. We do not hold this view. We say that there are two aspects.

The first: it is incumbent upon Him by virtue of promise, for He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We are the One who gives life to the dead﴾. So it is incumbent upon Him by virtue of promise, neither by reason nor by revealed law.

The second: *'alā* here is for specification (*li-l-ta'yīn*). When a person is present among a group who have attempted a matter and failed at it, it is said: "It has become incumbent upon you, then, to do it," that is, it has become specifically assigned to him.

**Second issue:** It has been read as *al-nash'ah* as a verbal noun of the pattern *fa'lah*, like *al-darbah*, which denotes a single occurrence. One says: "I struck him two blows," meaning once after another. Here it means: a creation once more upon Him. It has also been read as *al-nashā'ah* with a long vowel, as a verbal noun of the pattern *fa'ālah*, like *al-kafālah*. Whichever reading is adopted, it is from *nasha'a*, which is intransitive. It would have been appropriate to say *'alayhi al-in<u>sh</u>ā'</u>* (upon Him is the producing), not *al-nash'ah*. We say: there is a benefit in it, namely that certainty is attained from this by the existence of creation once more. Had He said *'alayhi al-in<u>sh</u>ā'*, one might say: *in<u>sh</u>ā'* belongs to the pattern of causing to sit, as is said in ordinary usage: "I made him sit, but he did not sit," and "I made him stand, but he did not stand." Thus one would say: "He intended to produce him so that he would come into being, but it did not happen." But when He says *'alayhi al-nash'ah*, it means that He brings into being the bringing-into-being and makes it real, such that it certainly exists.

**Third issue:** Is there a difference between one who says *'alayhi al-nash'ah marratan ukhrā* ("upon Him is the creation once more") and His saying *'alayhi al-nash'ah al-ukhrā* ("upon Him is the other creation")? We say: yes. If one says *'alayhi al-nash'ah marratan ukhrā*, the creation has not been previously known. But when He says, ﴿upon Him the other creation﴾, the reality of the other creation has already been known, and so we say: that known thing is upon Him.

**Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 53, verses 46–47:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from a drop [nutfah]﴾, i.e., a piece of water.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when it is emitted﴾. It is from *amnā al-maniyy* (to emit the semen), when it is discharged, or from *mану yamnī* (to measure, to determine), when it is decreed. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿from a drop﴾, is a reminder of the perfection of power, because the drop (*nutfah*) is a body whose parts are proportionate. From it God the Exalted creates diverse organs and differing natures. The creation of the male and the female from it is the most wondrous of things, as we have explained. For this reason no one has been able to claim it, just as no one has been able to claim the creation of the heavens. Hence the Exalted said: ﴿And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say, "God"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 87], just as He said: ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, "God"﴾ [Luqman: 25].

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And that to Him is the other creation [al-nash'ah al-ukhrā]﴾. According to most of the exegetes, it refers to the Resurrection. What has become clear to me, after long reflection and inquiry, by the grace of God the Exalted, is the guidance toward the truth in this matter: it is possible that what is meant is the breathing of the human spirit into it. This is because the noble soul, not the commanding soul, mingles with dense, dark bodies, and by it God honoured the children of Adam. To this the Exalted refers in His saying: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced it as another creation﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 14]. This is other than the creation of the drop as a clot, the clot as a lump, and the lump as bones. By this other creation, man is distinguished from the kinds of animals and shares with the angel in perceptions. Thus, just as He said there, ﴿We produced it as another creation﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 14] after the creation of the drop, He says here, ﴿And that to Him is the other creation﴾. He makes the breathing of the spirit another creation, just as He made it another production there.

What necessitated saying this is that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [An-Najm: 42], according to most of them, is to explain the return (*al-i'adah*), and His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Then He will recompense him with the fullest recompense﴾ [An-Najm: 41] is likewise. So the mention of the other creation is a return. Also, because He said after this, ﴿And that He is the One who makes rich and gives contentment﴾ [An-Najm: 48], and this is among the affairs of this world. According to what we have mentioned, the sequence is of the utmost beauty: He, the Exalted, says, ﴿He created the male and the female﴾, and breathed into both the noble human spirit; then He enriched him with his mother's milk and his father's provision in his youth; then He gave him contentment through earning after his maturity.

If it is objected: the other creation for the Resurrection has been mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation; then God will produce the final creation"﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 20]. We say: *al-ākhirah* (the final) derives from *al-ākhir* (the last), not from *al-ākhar* (the other), because *al-ākhir* is an elative form. Moreover, it has already been stated that there, since the beginning (*al-bad'*) was mentioned, it was understood as the return. Here, however, the creation from a drop was mentioned, as in His saying: ﴿Then We made the drop a clot﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 14], and then He said: ﴿We produced it as another creation﴾.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said:

﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices (aghnā wa-aqnā).﴾ We have already mentioned its explanation, so we say: "Aghnā" means that He removed his need and did not leave him in need, because the poor (faqīr) stands in opposition to the rich (ghanī). So whoever is not left poor in any respect is rich absolutely, and whoever is not left poor in some respect is rich in that respect. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Enrich them from begging on this day," and this was interpreted as referring to zakat al-fitr (the charity of breaking the fast), and its meaning is: when there comes to him what he needs. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and suffices (aqnā)﴾, its meaning is that He added to it, and iqnā' (contentment/sufficiency beyond need) is above ighnā' (enrichment). What I think is that the letters are proportionate in meaning. So we say: since the place of articulation of the qāf is above the place of articulation of the ghayn, He made iqnā' a state above ighnā'. On this basis, ighnā' is what Allah gave him of sight and speech, and guided him to suckling in his infancy, or it is what Allah, exalted is He, gave him of food and clothing that he needs. In sum, everything with which Allah removes need is ighnā', and everything beyond that is iqnā'.
* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that it is He who is the Lord of Sirius (rabb al-Sh'ʿrā)﴾. This is an indication of the corruption of the saying of other people. For some people hold that poverty and wealth come from a person's own earning and effort: whoever earns becomes rich, and whoever is lazy becomes poor. Others hold that this is by fortune (bakht), and that this is by the stars. So He said: ﴿He is the one who enriches and suffices﴾. Whoever says that wealth comes from the stars is mistaken. We say: He is the Lord of the stars and the one who moves them, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He is the Lord of Sirius﴾. His saying ﴿He is the Lord of Sirius﴾, because of their denial of that, is emphasized with the pronoun of separation (al-fasl). Al-Sh'ʿrā is a bright star, and among the stars there are two Sh'ʿrās: one is Shamiyya and the other is Yamaniyya. The apparent meaning is that the Yamaniyya is intended, because they used to worship it.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 53, verse 52:

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿAd﴾. When He mentioned that He ﴿enriches and gives contentment﴾, and that this was by the grace of God and not by the gift of al-Shiʿra (Sirius), gratitude became obligatory toward the One who destroys. The condition of ʿAd, Thamud and others is a sufficient proof for them. As for ﴿ʿAdan al-ūlā﴾ (the first ʿAd), it was said: by the word "al-ūlā" it is distinguished from a people in Mecca who were the later ʿAd. It was also said: "al-ūlā" is to indicate their precedence, not to distinguish them. You say, "Zayd the scholar came to me," and you describe him, not to distinguish him, but to show his knowledge. There are readings of this: "ʿAdan al-ūlā" with the kasra on the nunation (tanwīn, the nasal "n" sound added to the end of indefinite nouns) because two consonants (sākinān) meet; and "ʿAda al-ūlā" with the nunation dropped, also because two consonants meet, like the reading "ʿUzayru ibnu Allāh" and ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ and ﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1, 2]. There is also "ʿAdan lūlā" with the nūn assimilated into the lām (idghām, assimilation of one letter into the next), and the damma of the hamza transferred to the lām; and "ʿAdan lʾūlā" with a hamza on the waw. This reader recited "ʿalā suʾqihi" (on its stalk), and its basis is weak. It could be argued in the place of "al-mu'qadah" and "al-mu'sadah", where the damma and the waw are present, so here it is substituted for the hamza; similarly in "suʾqihi", because the hamza exists in the original, and in "Mūsā". His statement is not good.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And Thamud, and He spared none﴾. He means: and He destroyed Thamud. His saying "fa-mā abqā" (and He spared none) refers back to ʿAd and Thamud, meaning: He did not spare them. Some of the exegetes said: "famā abqāhum," meaning He did not leave any of them alive. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 8]. Al-Hajjaj relied on His saying ﴿fa-mā abqā﴾ against those who claimed that the Thaqif are from Thamud.

﴿And the people of Nuh﴾, meaning He destroyed them ﴿before﴾. The issue of "qabl" (before) is well known. "Qabl" and "baʿd" (after) when cut off from the genitive construction become like a limit (ghāyah), and so they are built on the damma. As for their being built (mabnī, fixed in form), it is because they imply the genitive (iḍāfah). As for their being built on the damma, if they were built on the fatḥa, that would affirm what they would deserve by i'rāb (grammatical inflection), since they are time adverbs and so deserve the accusative and the fatḥa like it. If they were built on the kasra, the matter would be as i'rāb requires, which is the genitive after a preposition, so they were built on what differs from both their states of i'rāb.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed they were the most wrongdoing and the most transgressing﴾. As for injustice (ẓulm), it is because they were the first to begin it and the foremost in it. "Whoever establishes a bad practice will bear its burden, and the burden of whoever acts upon it" (“«ومَن سَنَّ سُنَّةً سَيِّئَةً فَعَلَيْهِ وِزْرُها ووِزْرُ مِن عَمِلَ بِها»”). The one who begins is more wrongdoing. As for "aṭghā" (more transgressing), it is because they heard the admonitions, the time stretched long upon them, and they did not desist, until their prophet prayed against them. A prophet does not pray against his people except after great persistence. The wrongdoer (ẓālim) is one who places a thing in other than its place. The transgressor (ṭāghī) is one who exceeds the limit. So the transgressor is more deeply within wrongdoing. It is like the "mughāyir" (different) and the "mukhālif" (opposed): the opposed is different with an additional attribute, and likewise the "mughāyir" and the "muḍādd" (contrary). Every opposite is different, but not every different is opposite. On this there is an objection: His saying ﴿and the people of Nuh﴾ intends to frighten the wrongdoer with destruction. If He says, "They were in the extreme of injustice and transgression, so they were destroyed," the wrongdoer would say, "They were more wrongdoing, so they were destroyed because of their exaggeration in injustice. We have not exaggerated, so we will not be destroyed." But if He said, "They were destroyed because they were wrongdoers," every wrongdoer would be frightened. So what is the benefit of His saying "aẓlam" (more wrongdoing)? We say: the purpose is to show their severity and the strength of their bodies. They did not proceed to severe injustice and transgression except through their persistence and the length of their lives. Despite that, none of them escaped. So what of those who are less than them in age and strength? It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Stronger than them in might﴾ [Qaf: 36].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 53, verse 53–54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down﴾. Al-Mu'tafikah is the overturned (al-munqalibah), and concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: it has been recited as "wal-mu'tafikat" (the plural). The well-known view is that these were the towns of the people of Lut, but they had places that were overturned, so they are called mu'tafikat. It is also possible to say that what is meant is everyone whose dwellings were overturned and whose places were effaced; this is why He concluded the destroyed ones with the mu'tafikat, like one who says: so-and-so died, and so-and-so, and everyone who was of their kind and likeness.

The second issue: ﴿Ahwa﴾ means He caused it to fall (asqatha), that is, He made it descend. It has been said: He made it descend to the earth from the point where Jibril, peace be upon him, carried it on his wing and then overturned it. It has also been said: their buildings were elevated, so He brought them down by the earthquake and made its highest part its lowest.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾, according to what I have said, is like the saying of one who says: "al-munqalibah qalabaha" (the overturned one overturned it). The overturning of the overturned is obtaining what is already obtained (tahsil al-hasil). We say: its meaning is not that the overturned cities overturned by themselves, but rather that Allah overturned them, so they were overturned.

The fourth issue: what is the wisdom in singling out al-Mu'tafikah with the name of a place in the mention, whereas for 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Nuh He said the name of a people? We say: the answer to this is from two aspects.

One of them: Thamud is the name of a place, so He mentioned 'Ad by the name of a people and Thamud by the name of a place, the people of Nuh by the name of a people and al-Mu'tafikah by the name of a place. This is to make known that a people cannot protect their places from the punishment of Allah, Exalted, nor can a place fortify a people against it. For in custom, at times the inhabitant is strong and defends his dwelling, and at other times the dwelling is strong and repels its inhabitant, but the punishment of Allah is not prevented by any preventer. This meaning was realized for the believers in two verses: one of them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He restrained the hands of people from you﴾ [al-Fath: 20], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. In the first, the inhabitant could not preserve his dwelling; in the second, the fortress could not preserve the inhabitant.

The second aspect: the matter of 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Nuh was already long past, and their dwellings had been effaced, but their affair was well known and widely transmitted. As for the people of Lut, their dwellings and the traces of the overturning were still apparent in them. So He mentioned, for each people, the more evident of the two matters.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So there covered them that which covered﴾. The word "ma" may be an object (maf'ul), which is the apparent reading, and it may be a subject (fa'il); one says: "darabahu man darabahu" (he was struck by whoever struck him). On this basis we say: the one who covered may be Allah, exalted is He, and it would be like His saying: ﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5]. And it may be that this is an indication of the cause of Allah's wrath upon them, that is, the cause covered them, in the sense that Allah became wrathful with them because of it. It is said of one who angered a king with words, and the king struck him: "Your words are what struck you."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down﴾. Al-Mu'tafikah is the overturned (al-munqalibah), and concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: it has been recited as "wal-mu'tafikat" (the plural). The well-known view is that these were the towns of the people of Lut, but they had places that were overturned, so they are called mu'tafikat. It is also possible to say that what is meant is everyone whose dwellings were overturned and whose places were effaced; this is why He concluded the destroyed ones with the mu'tafikat, like one who says: so-and-so died, and so-and-so, and everyone who was of their kind and likeness.

The second issue: ﴿Ahwa﴾ means He caused it to fall (asqatha), that is, He made it descend. It has been said: He made it descend to the earth from the point where Jibril, peace be upon him, carried it on his wing and then overturned it. It has also been said: their buildings were elevated, so He brought them down by the earthquake and made its highest part its lowest.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾, according to what I have said, is like the saying of one who says: "al-munqalibah qalabaha" (the overturned one overturned it). The overturning of the overturned is obtaining what is already obtained (tahsil al-hasil). We say: its meaning is not that the overturned cities overturned by themselves, but rather that Allah overturned them, so they were overturned.

The fourth issue: what is the wisdom in singling out al-Mu'tafikah with the name of a place in the mention, whereas for 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Nuh He said the name of a people? We say: the answer to this is from two aspects.

One of them: Thamud is the name of a place, so He mentioned 'Ad by the name of a people and Thamud by the name of a place, the people of Nuh by the name of a people and al-Mu'tafikah by the name of a place. This is to make known that a people cannot protect their places from the punishment of Allah, Exalted, nor can a place fortify a people against it. For in custom, at times the inhabitant is strong and defends his dwelling, and at other times the dwelling is strong and repels its inhabitant, but the punishment of Allah is not prevented by any preventer. This meaning was realized for the believers in two verses: one of them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He restrained the hands of people from you﴾ [al-Fath: 20], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 2]. In the first, the inhabitant could not preserve his dwelling; in the second, the fortress could not preserve the inhabitant.

The second aspect: the matter of 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Nuh was already long past, and their dwellings had been effaced, but their affair was well known and widely transmitted. As for the people of Lut, their dwellings and the traces of the overturning were still apparent in them. So He mentioned, for each people, the more evident of the two matters.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So there covered them that which covered﴾. The word "ma" may be an object (maf'ul), which is the apparent reading, and it may be a subject (fa'il); one says: "darabahu man darabahu" (he was struck by whoever struck him). On this basis we say: the one who covered may be Allah, exalted is He, and it would be like His saying: ﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾ [al-Shams: 5]. And it may be that this is an indication of the cause of Allah's wrath upon them, that is, the cause covered them, in the sense that Allah became wrathful with them because of it. It is said of one who angered a king with words, and the king struck him: "Your words are what struck you."

Then God Most High said: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ It has been said that this too is among what is in the scriptures. It has also been said that it is the beginning of a new statement, and the address is general, as if He were saying: "Which of the blessings, O listener, do you doubt or dispute?" It has also been said that it is an address to the disbeliever. It is possible that it is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ as well, and one should not object: "How is it permissible for Him to say to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿will you dispute﴾?" For we say that it belongs to the same category as: ﴿If you associate others with God, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. That is, there remains no possibility of doubt in him. Indeed, even if one were to suppose that the Prophet ﷺ were among those who doubt or dispute some hidden matters, it would not be possible for him to dispute the blessings of God. The general reading is the correct one, as if He were saying: "Which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute, O human being?" just as He said: ﴿O human being, what has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord?﴾ [al-Infitar: 6], and He said: ﴿And man is most of all things given to disputation﴾ [al-Kahf: 54]. If it is objected: "What was mentioned before were blessings, and the favours (ālāʾ) are blessings, so how can they be 'the favours of your Lord'?" We reply: when He had previously enumerated the blessings, namely the creation from a drop of semen, the breathing into it of the noble spirit, and the giving of sufficiency and contentment, and had mentioned that the disbeliever who was ungrateful for His blessings was destroyed, He said: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾, meaning: you will be struck by the like of what befell those who disputed before. Or you may say: when destruction was mentioned, He said to the doubter: "You have not been struck by what struck them, and that is by the protection of God over you." ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ We will elaborate on this in His saying: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ in several places.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾, and in it are several issues.

First issue: What is indicated by "this"? We say there are several views:

One: Muhammad ﷺ is of the same kind as the warners of old.

Two: The Qur'an.

Three: what He mentioned of the reports of those who were destroyed. Its meaning then is: "this is one of the matters that are warning." On our view that the intended referent is Muhammad ﷺ, then "warner" (nadhīr) means "one who warns," and the "min" (of) is to specify the kind. On our view that the intended referent is the Qur'an, "warner" may be a verbal noun (maṣdar) or may mean "one who warns" (fāʿil). That the reference is to the Qur'an is far-fetched, both verbally and in meaning. As for meaning: the Qur'an is not of the kind of the earlier scriptures, because it is a miracle, whereas those were not miracles. This is because, when He established the Oneness and said: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾, He said: ﴿This is a warner﴾, referring to Muhammad ﷺ and affirming the prophethood, and after that He said: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾, referring to the Resurrection; so that in these three verses there is the establishment of three principles in order: first God and His oneness, then the Messenger and his mission, then the gathering and the Resurrection. As for wording: if the warner is complete, then what He mentioned of the destruction of the perished is more fitting, since it is closer; and on this view "min" retains its true partitive meaning, i.e., "this which we have mentioned is part of what occurred and a fragment of what happened." Or it may be for the starting point of the end, meaning: "this is a warning from the earlier warners," as one says: "this is the book," and "this is the speech from so-and-so." On all these views, the mention of "of old" is not to specify the described thing and distinguish it from the later warners, as one says "the first group" to exclude the last group; rather, it is to describe the described thing, as one says: "Zayd the scholar came to me." So he mentions "the scholar" either to indicate that Zayd is learned, though you do not state it as a predicate and so bring it in the manner of description, or to praise Zayd by it, or for some other purpose. The more apt view, given the return to the plural form, namely "the warners" (al-nudhur), is that if it were meant in the singular sense he would have said "min al-nudhur al-awwalīn," as one says "min al-aqwām al-mutaqaddima" and "al-mutaqaddimīn," both in wording and in meaning.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near﴾ (azifat al-azifa). This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Inevitable Event has occurred﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 1].

It is also said: "kanat al-ka'ina" (the occurring event has come about). This usage occurs in several ways. Among them is when the doer has already become a doer of such an act before, and then the same act proceeds from him once more. So it is said: "fa'ala al-fa'il" (the doer did), meaning: the one who was already a doer has become a doer once again. It is said: "hakahu al-ha'ik" (the weaver wove it), meaning: the one who was previously occupied with that act has done it. Among them is when the doer becomes a doer by that act; from this comes the saying: "When the dead person dies, his deeds are cut off" (idha mata al-mayyit inqata'a 'amaluh), and when a usurper seizes property, he is liable for it. So His saying, "The Imminent Event has drawn near," may be of the first type, meaning: the Hour has drawn near, which every day grows nearer, so it is an imminent occurrence that is near and has increased in nearness. It may also be like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Inevitable Event has occurred﴾, meaning: its occurrence has drawn near, and "azifat" has as its real doer al-qiyama (the Resurrection) or al-sa'a (the Hour), as if He had said: "The Resurrection, the Imminent, has drawn near," or "the Hour," or "the like of it."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None besides God can avert it﴾ (laysa laha min duni Allahi kashifa), there are several aspects to it:

The first: there is no one who manifests it except God. Whoever knows it knows only through God's informing him of it and disclosing it to him. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, with God is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34], and His saying: ﴿None but He will reveal it at its time﴾ [al-A'raf: 187].

The second: none brings it about except God, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If God touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but Him﴾ [al-An'am: 17]. In this there are several issues:

The first: "min" (from) is extra (za'ida); its sense is "there is for it no revealer other than God." It enters upon negation and emphasizes its meaning, as you say: "ma ja'ani ahad" and "ma ja'ani min ahad" (no one came to me). According to this, it is possible that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its sense being: "there is for it no revealer apart from God," so it is a general negation with respect to revealers. It is also possible to say that it is not extra; rather the meaning of the statement is that there is no soul in existence that discloses it, i.e., informs about it as it truly is, and whenever its time is known by other than God, the one who discloses it discloses it from God, not from other than God. One says: "the disclosure of the matter from Zayd." "Dun" (apart from / besides) here carries the meaning of "ghayr" (other than), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?﴾ [al-Saffat: 86], i.e., other than God.

The second issue: "kashifa" is an attributive adjective for a feminine noun, i.e., "nafs kashifa" (a disclosing soul). It was also said that it is for emphasis (lil-mubalagha), as in "al-'allama" (the very knowing). According to this, it is not said that it is a negation that it has a revealer in the form of intensive emphasis, and it does not follow from "the superlative revealer" that the revealer itself is negated. For we say: if anyone were to reveal it, he would be a revealer in the complete sense; so there is no revealer of it, and no one discloses it. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants﴾ [Qaf: 29], in terms of negating that He is a wrongdoer in an intensive sense, and it does not follow from this that He is not a wrongdoer at all. We have stated there that if He were to wrong His weak servants without right, He would be in the utmost degree of wrongdoing, and He is not in the utmost degree of wrongdoing, so He does not wrong them at all.

The third issue: if you say that its meaning is "there is for it no disclosing soul," then "min duni Allah" is an exception according to the most well-known of the opinions. Then God would be a soul that is a disclosing one? We say: the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: there is no corruption in that. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I know not what is in Your soul﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116], relating from 'Isa, peace be upon him, and the meaning is the Essence (al-haqiqa).

The second: it is not the explicit exception, so it is permissible in it that it is not a soul.

The third: the exception is the disclosing, the intensive one.
